profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:38.037+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
Fèngchì Biānjí
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Zhōu considered himself a descendant of Guó Shū of the Zhōu dynasty.
During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods,
historical records state that among the descendants of Guó Shū, those who held states were called Guógōng,
later referred to as Guōgōng.
The pronunciations of Guó and Guō are similar.
Yú Grandee Gōng Zhīqí said: Guó Zhòng and Guó Shū,
were the descendants of Wáng Jì.
The surname Guō originated from the Zhōu,
so the state's name was established as Zhōu,
and the Comprehensive Mirror therefore refers to it as Later Zhōu.
First year of Guǎngshùn (Xīnhài, 951)
1 Spring,
first month,
Dīngmǎo,
the Hàn Empress Dowager issued a decree,
granting the Regent the imperial seals and symbols of authority,
and he ascended the throne.
The Regent entered the palace from Gāomén,
Gāomén,
was the name of a village outside the city of Dàliáng.
An edict stated:
"We are a descendant of the Zhōu house,
and of Guó Shū's line,
so the state's name should be Zhōu."
The era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, Wáng Zhāng, and others were all posthumously awarded official titles,
and the state arranged for their burial.
The deaths of Yáng Bīn and others are recorded in the previous year's section of the previous volume.
Wéi,
pronounced yú wèi fān.
Liǎn,
pronounced lì shàn fān.
All officials in charge of granaries, storehouses, and treasuries,
were prohibited from collecting extra measures (dǒu yú) or extra weight allowances (chēng hào);
dǒu yú,
refers to taking extra beyond the measured amount,
taking the remainder.
Chēng hào,
refers to taking extra beyond the weighed amount in catties, jun, or dan,
taking more to compensate for loss or wastage.
Now all these were abolished,
rectifying the harsh exactions of Wáng Zhāng.
Chēng,
pronounced chǐ zhèng fān.
All were abolished.
For those guilty of theft or adultery,
the punishments were to follow those in effect before the first year of Tiānfú of Jìn,
and unless the crime was rebellion or treason,
relatives were not to be executed,
nor family property confiscated.
This rectified the cruel punishments of Shǐ Hóngzhào.
The officials and palace women at the tomb of Hàn Gāozǔ,
the regular sacrifices, and the tomb-keeping households all remained as before.
Earlier,
with the decline of the Táng,
there was much banditry,
and the legal statutes were not used,
instead, harsher laws were enacted:
theft of goods worth three bolts of cloth was punishable by death;
during the Tiānfú period of Jìn,
this was increased to five bolts.
Adultery with a married woman,
regardless of whether it was forcible or consensual,
resulted in death for both man and woman.
Qiáng,
means the man used force against the woman,
and she had no choice but to commit adultery.
Hé,
means the man and woman were mutually attracted,
desire stirred and passion arose, leading to adultery.
Theft of even one coin or more was punishable by death;
also, for crimes other than rebellion or treason,
often entire clans were executed and property confiscated.
Therefore, when the Emperor ascended the throne,
he first reformed these abuses.
Earlier,
Yáng Bīn believed that many military governors who were meritorious officials or imperial relatives were not well-versed in administrative affairs,
xián,
means familiar or practiced.
These individuals, relying on their imperial appointments,
often acted arbitrarily and tyrannically,
and the military governors could not control them;
now they were all dismissed.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Chóngjǔ of Shàngdǎng, a close subordinate of Shǐ Hóngzhào, to seek out Hóngzhào's relatives.
Chóngjǔ reported:
"Hóngzhào's younger brother Hóngfú is still alive."
Earlier,
Hóngzhào had put Chóngjǔ in charge of the records of his family property,
so he knew all the assets,
and he handed them all over to Hóngfú.
The Emperor considered him worthy,
and assigned him to serve under the Emperor's son Róng.
2 Wùchén,
appointed the former Fùzhōu defense commissioner Wáng Yànchāo as acting Wǔníng military governor.
At that time, Liú Yūn's generals Gǒng Yánměi and others were defending Xúzhōu.
3 The Hàn Empress Dowager Li moved to the Western Palace.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
the Hàn Tàipíng Palace was probably the Western Palace.
Jǐsì,
she was honored with the title Zhāoshèng Empress Dowager.
4 The Kāifēng Prefect and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Liú Xūn died.
5 Guǐyǒu,
Wáng Jùn was appointed Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
6]Appointed the Minister of the Imperial Guard Liú Hào to oversee the funeral of the Hàn Yǐndì.
Since Liú Xūn had died,
there were no other close relatives.
7 Earlier,
when the Hé dōng military governor and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Liú Chóng heard of the Yǐndì's murder,
he intended to raise an army and march south.
Upon hearing that the Duke of Xiāngyīn was being welcomed to the throne,
he stopped,
saying:
"My son is becoming Emperor,
what more could I ask for!"
The Tàiyuán Deputy Prefect Lǐ Xiāng secretly advised Chóng:
"Observing Guō Gōng's intentions,
he ultimately wants to take the throne himself.
You should quickly lead troops across the Tàiháng Mountains,
occupy Mèngjīn,
and wait until the Lord of Xúzhōu ascends the throne.
The Duke of Xiāngyīn was originally the military governor of Xúzhōu,
hence this reference.
Then Guō Gōng would not dare to act;
otherwise,
you will be betrayed."
Chóng angrily said:
"Pedantic scholar,
trying to sow discord between me and my son!"
He ordered his attendants to drag him out and behead him.
Xiāng cried out:
"I, possessing talent for managing the world, have advised a fool,
and I accept death willingly!
I have an old wife at home,
I wish to die with her."
Chóng killed both him and his wife,
and reported it to the court,
to show he had no disloyal intentions.
When Yūn was deposed,
Chóng then sent an envoy requesting Yūn be returned to Jìnyáng.
An edict replied:
"The Duke of Xiāngyīn was recently in Sòngzhōu,
and is now being brought back to the capital.
We will certainly ensure he is properly settled,
do not worry about him.
If you can join forces and assist us,
you will be enfeoffed as a prince,
and permanently govern Hé dōng."
Gǒng Yánměi and Yáng Wēn heard that the Duke of Xiāngyīn had lost his position,
and they supported Yūn's wife, née Dǒng, in holding Xúzhōu and resisting,
awaiting reinforcements from Hé dōng.
Liú Yūn had ordered Gǒng Yánměi and others to defend Xúzhōu,
as recorded in the previous year's section of the previous volume.
Yánměi and Wēn wanted to surrender but feared death.
The Emperor again sent a letter to Yūn:
"Considering these men served their lord with all their heart,
their loyalty and righteousness deserve reward.
How can we blame them for regrets or faults?
When the new military governor enters the city,
the new military governor,
refers to Wáng Yànchāo.
you can further instruct them with detailed orders."
In the late Táng, when a commander-in-chief gave written instructions to his officers,
it was generally called wěiqū.
8 When the Khitan attacked Nèiqiū,
as recorded in the previous year's section of the previous volume,
there was also a lunar eclipse,
and many strange omens occurred in the army.
The Khitan ruler became fearful,
and did not dare to advance deeply,
leading his troops back.
The northern tribes in warfare,
use the moon as an indicator.
A lunar eclipse,
and many strange omens,
so they feared and did not dare advance.
Yāo,
pronounced yī yáo fān.
Huán,
pronounced cóng xuān fān,
also as the usual pronunciation.
Coinciding with the fall of Hàn,
the Ānguó military governor Liú Cí sent their envoy to Dàliáng.
The Emperor sent the Left Thousand Ox Guard General Zhū Xiàn on a return embassy,
explaining the reason for the dynastic change,
and presented him with gold vessels and a jade belt.
9 The Emperor considered Yèdū crucial for pacifying Héběi,
and controlling the Khitan,
and wanted a trusted confidant stationed there.
Yǐhài,
appointed the Níngjiāng military governor and Commander of the Imperial Guard Wáng Yīn as the Yèdū Military Commissioner, Tiānxióng military governor, and Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
retaining his military command as before,
still leading the Imperial Guard.
On the 10th day, Bingzǐ,
the Emperor led the officials to the Western Palace,
where they performed mourning rites and donned mourning garments for the Later Han's Hidden Emperor,
all according to the rites for a Son of Heaven.
Last year,
the Hidden Emperor's coffin had been moved to the Western Palace,
as recorded in the previous scroll.
The character "帥"
is read as "率".
The character "為"
is pronounced with the tone "yú wèi fān".
11. Mùróng Yànchāo sent an envoy to present tribute.
The Emperor, concerned that he might be suspicious and fearful,
issued an edict to comfort and reassure him,
saying:
"Now, your elder brother's affairs have come to this point,
I do not wish to speak at length,
but hope that you, my younger brother, will support [me],
so that we may together bring peace to the millions."
Hàn Gāozǔ was the elder brother of Mùróng Yànchāo.
The phrase "今兄"
appears in the *Old History of the Five Dynasties* as
"令兄",
which should be followed.
12. On the Wùyín day,
the Duke of Xiāngyīn was killed in Sòngzhōu.
13. On this day,
Liú Chóng ascended the throne as emperor in Jìnyáng.
Liú Chóng
was the younger brother of the same mother as Hàn Gāozǔ.
The territory he held consisted of twelve prefectures: Bìng, Fén, Xīn, Dài, Lán, Xiàn, Lóng, Wèi, Qìn, Liáo, Lín, and Shí.
Sòng Bái said: Xiànzhōu
was originally the Lóufán Pasturage.
In the first year of the Lóngjì era of Táng Zhāozōng,
Lǐ Kèyòng petitioned to establish Xiànzhōu.
When Sòng Tàizōng pacified Tàiyuán,
Zhé Yùqīng joined forces from Fǔzhōu to attack Liú Jìyuán,
first capturing Kělán Army,
then capturing Lóngzhōu,
and then capturing Lánzhōu.
Thus, Lóngzhōu was likely established during the Jìn and Hàn periods,
its location being between Kělán and Lángǔ.
The character "沁"
is pronounced "qiān zhèn fān".
The observation judge, Zhào Huá of Xíngyáng, was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue,
and concurrently Tongpingzhangshi.
He appointed his second son, Chéngjūn, as Commander of the Imperial Guard and Chief of Tàiyuán,
and the deputy military commissioner, Lǐ Cúnhuái, as Defense Commissioner of Dàizhōu.
The subordinate general, Zhāng Yuánhuī of Wǔ'ān, was appointed as Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Wǔ'ān County belongs to Míngzhōu,
located 95 *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
The Northern Hàn ruler said to Lǐ Cúnhuái and Zhāng Yuánhuī:
The *Zizhi Tongjian* refers to the Hàn in Lingnan as Southern Hàn,
and the Hàn in Hédōng as Northern Hàn.
"I see the enterprise of Gāozǔ fallen in a single day;
today, my title and position
are assumed out of necessity.
But consider, what kind of Son of Heaven am I,
and what kind of military commissioners are you!"
For this reason, he did not establish ancestral temples,
and sacrifices were conducted as in a common family.
The monthly salary for the chancellor was only one hundred strings of cash,
and for military commissioners, only thirty strings.
According to the salaries of officials during the Táng dynasty,
after the Huìcháng era,
they were not increased or decreased.
The Three Preceptors received two million,
the Three Dukes 1.6 million,
the Zhongshu Ling 1.5 million,
the Zhongshu Ling, Vice Directors of the Two Departments, the Two Chiefs of Staff, and the Three Preceptors of the Eastern Palace 1.4 million,
the Ministers, the Censor-in-Chief, and the Three Junior Preceptors of the Eastern Palace one million,
and military commissioners 300,000.
By the fifth year of the Kāipíng era of Liáng,
the salary for a chancellor was 200,000 cash.
In the fourth year of the Tóngguāng era of Later Táng,
it was determined that deputy military commissioners would receive a monthly stipend of 40,000 cash,
so military commissioners likely received even more.
Now, the Northern Hàn ruler reduced all these amounts.
The character "俸"
is pronounced "fú yòng fān".
Therefore, there were few honest officials in his state.
The Guest Reception Commissioner, Lǐ Guāngměi of Hénán, had once served as a Direct Service Official.
The Three Departments had Direct Service Officials;
whenever officials visited the chancellor,
they were assigned a Direct Service Official to guide them.
Their duties were similar to those of receptionists in external military towns.
The institutions and regulations of the Northern Hàn court
all originated from Guāngměi.
When the Northern Hàn ruler heard of the death of the Duke of Xiāngyīn,
he wept and said:
"I did not heed the words of loyal ministers,
and thus have come to this!"
He established a shrine for Lǐ Xiāng,
offering sacrifices seasonally.
14. On the Jǐmǎo day,
Féng Dào was appointed as Zhongshu Ling,
Dòu Zhèngù was additionally appointed as Shìzhōng,
and Sū Yǔguī as Minister of Works.
15. Wáng Yànchāo reported sending an envoy with an imperial decree to Xúzhōu,
but Gǒng Tíngměi and others hesitated and refused to open the gates.
An edict was issued to advance troops and attack them.
16. The Emperor said to Wáng Jùn:
"I rose from humble origins,
having endured all manner of hardships.
Encountering an era of chaos and destruction,
I suddenly became emperor.
How dare I indulge in lavish living to the detriment of the common people!"
He ordered Jùn to list all the rare and exquisite foods presented as tribute from various regions.
On the Gēngchén day,
he issued an edict abolishing them all.
According to the *Old History of the Five Dynasties*, the edict stated:
"All the delicious foods and delicacies formerly presented as tribute by the prefectures of the realm
should be reduced or eliminated.
These include fine wines, seafood, ginger, and melons from Liǎngzhè;
mùyóuzi tea, milk sugar, white sugar, and olives from Húnán;
high-quality rice and water pears from Zhènzhōu;
chestnuts from Yìdìng;
white pear, rice flour, mung bean flour, and jade-like wheat bran from Hédōng;
red glutinous rice from the imperial fields and new barley bran from Yǒngxīng;
suzi chestnuts from Xīngpíng;
musk, antelope horn, bear bile, otter liver, red persimmons, and bear fat from Huàzhōu;
red dates, schisandra berries, and light maltose from Hézhōng;
stone-hard cakes from Tóngzhōu;
grapes and yellow snow pears from Jìn and Jiàng;
phoenix-roost pears from Shǎnfǔ;
purple ginger, new bamboo shoots, and oranges from Xiāngzhōu;
polished glutinous rice and fermented flavors from Ānzhōu;
water pears from Qīngzhōu;
various fruits from Héyáng;
imperial plums from Xǔzhōu;
new bamboo shoots and goose pears from Zhèngzhōu;
cold-food apricot kernels from Huáizhōu;
ránghé from Shēnzhōu;
bìxiè from Bózhōu;
and Huái white fish from prefectures along the Huái River.
From now on, these need not be presented."
"What is presented is only for my person,
but the harm extends to the common people."
He also said:
"Accumulating these in government offices
results in useless items."
Another edict stated:
"I grew up in the military,
not having studied closely,
and am unaware of the way to govern the realm.
Civil and military officials who have strategies beneficial to the state and the people
should each submit sealed memorials to inform me.
All should write directly about the matters,
without embellishing with rhetoric."
The Emperor bestowed Sū Féngjí's residence upon Wáng Jùn.
Jùn said:
"This is how Féngjí caused the extermination of Lǐ Sōng's clan!"
This matter is recorded in the first year of the Qiányòu era of the Hàn dynasty, scroll 288.
If Wáng Jùn, while in a position of power,
always maintained such a mindset,
he would certainly not have met with the disaster in Shāngzhōu.
The character "處"
is pronounced "chāng lǚ fān".
17. Earlier,
when the Khitan ruler returned north,
as seen in the twelfth year of the Tiānfú era of Hàn Gāozǔ, scroll 287,
the Khitan ruler appointed Yùniǎn as the Southwest Route Pacification Commissioner.
When the Northern Hàn ruler ascended the throne,
the Khitan ruler sent Yùniǎn to deliver a letter to Liú Chéngjūn.
The Northern Hàn ruler had Chéngjūn reply,
stating:
"Our dynasty has fallen,
and I have succeeded to the imperial throne.
Wishing to follow the precedent of the Jìn dynasty,
I seek assistance from the Northern Court."
The Khitan ruler was greatly pleased.
The Northern Hàn ruler dispatched troops to station at Yīndì, Huángzé, and Tuánbǎi.
Those stationed at Yīndì intended to spy on Jìn and Xí;
those at Huángzé aimed to observe Xíng and Zhào;
and those at Tuánbǎi watched Zhèn and Dìng.
On the Dīnghài day,
Chéngjūn was appointed as Pacification Commissioner,
and together with Deputy Pacification Commissioner Bái Cónghuī and Supervisor Lǐ Cúnhuái, led ten thousand infantry and cavalry to invade Jìnzhōu.
Cónghuī
was a Tǔyùhún.
18. Guō Chóngwēi changed his name to Chóng,
and Cáo Wēi changed his name to Yīng.
Both avoided the Emperor's personal name.
The character "更"
is pronounced "gōng héng fān".
On the 19th day of the second month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
the emperor appointed his son, the Yá Nèi Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ of Tiānxióng, Róng, as the Jiédù Shǐ of Zhènníng.
He selected court officials to serve as his subordinates,
appointing Shì Yùshǐ Wáng Mǐn as the Jiédù Pànguān,
Yòu Bǔquē Cuī Sòng as the Guānchá Pànguān,
and Jiàoshū Láng Wáng Pǔ as the Zhǎng Shūjì.
This lays the groundwork for Wáng Pǔ's future service under Shìzōng.
(Wáng Pǔ was the son of Wáng Xíe;
Cuī Xíe served as chancellor under Hòutáng Míngzōng.
He was from Dōngpíng.)
On the 20th day, Wùxū,
the Northern Hàn army attacked Jìnzhōu in five columns.
The Jiédù Shǐ, Wáng Yàn, closed the city gates and did not venture out.
Liú Chéngjūn thought he was cowardly,
and his troops swarmed up the walls like ants.
Wáng Yàn then unleashed his ambushing troops who fought fiercely,
and the Northern Hàn army suffered over a thousand casualties.
Chéngjūn sent his Deputy Bīngmǎ Shǐ, Ān Yuánbǎo, to set fire to the western city of Jìnzhōu,
but Yuánbǎo came and surrendered.
Chéngjūn then shifted his army to attack Xízhōu.
(The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Jìnzhōu northwest to Xízhōu is 250 lǐ.)
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Xízhōu Cìshǐ Xǔ Qiān sent his Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ, Sūn Jìyè, to intercept the Northern Hàn army at Chángshòu Village.
(In the second year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Chángshòu County was established from part of Shílóu in Xízhōu.
It was abolished and merged back into Shílóu in the first year of the Zhēnguān era.)
He killed them.
Not long after,
the Northern Hàn army attacked the prefectural city.
After several days of failing to capture it,
and suffering heavy casualties,
they withdrew.
(Xǔ Qiān
was from Yùnzhōu.)
On the 21st day, Jiǎchén,
the King of Chǔ, Xī'è, sent his Zhǎng Shūjì, Liú Guāngfǔ, to present tribute to the Táng court.
(The Kǎoyì states: According to the Húxiāng Gùshì,
"Guāngfǔ"
is written
as "Guānghàn."
We now follow the Shíguó Jìnián.)
On the 22nd day, the emperor took out several dozen precious jade vessels from the Hàn palace
and smashed them in the courtyard,
saying:
"What use does an emperor have for such things!
I have heard that the Hàn Yǐndì spent his days amusing himself with his favorites inside the palace,
with rare treasures never leaving his side.
This event is not far in the past,
and it should serve as a warning."
He then admonished his attendants,
"From now on, objects that are merely dazzling and pleasing to the eye
are not to be brought into the palace."
On the 23rd day, Dīngwèi,
the Khitan ruler sent his official, Wūyī Gǔzhī, to come together with Zhǔ Xiàn,
to congratulate him on his accession.
On the 24th day, Wùshēn,
an edict was issued allowing former officials to reside as they pleased in outer prefectures.
(In the winter of the second year of the Qiányòu era of Hàn Yǐndì,
Yáng Bīn memorialized that former officials should reside separately in the two capitals.
This matter is recorded in scroll 288.)
Chén Sīràng had not yet reached Húnán
when Mǎ Xī'è had already captured Chángshā.
Sīràng remained stationed at Yǐngzhōu,
and an imperial order summoned him to return.
(Last November,
the Hàn court discussed sending troops to rescue Tánzhōu,
but internal troubles arose and it was not carried out.
During the change of surname between the Liú and Guō clans,
they certainly had no leisure to send generals southward.
It is unknown under which court Chén Sīràng was dispatched;
this should be examined.
According to the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ,
when Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he sent Chén Sīràng to lead a detachment to Ān and Yǐng
to plan an advance.
After Chángshā fell,
he then withdrew his troops.
Thus, he was dispatched by the emperor.)
On the 26th day, Dīngsì,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng Tián Mǐn was sent as an envoy to the Khitans.
The ruler of Northern Hàn sent his Tōngshì Shèrén Lǐ Biànyán as an envoy to the Khitans.
("Biànyán"
is a vulgar form
of the character "biàn"
, composed
of "biàn"
and "yán".
Sòng Jǐngwén's Shǒujì states: During the Northern Qí period,
it was common among the populace to create false characters,
beginning with using
"qiǎo yán"
to represent
"biàn".
By the Suí dynasty, there was Liǔ Biànyán,
whose name used the character
"biàn"
in place of
"qiǎo".)
An edict was issued adding the title Zhōngshū Lìng to Tàiníng Jiédù Shǐ Mùróng Yànchāo,
and Hànlín Xuéshì Yú Chóngliàng was sent to Yǎnzhōu to convey the imperial intent.
(Chóngliàng
was originally Chóngyuǎn.
Yú Chóngliàng had previously changed his name to avoid the taboo of the Hàn ancestor's name.)
In the third month, on the first day, Rénxū,
an edict was issued in reply, stating:
"Previously, due to the former dynasty's lack of virtue,
and the young ruler's use of slander,
in a moment of urgency,
you were summoned to the court.
You immediately rushed to respond to the command,
reaching the capital within two nights,
rescuing the nation's crisis without regard for yourself,
hearing your lord's summons without waiting for your carriage;
until Heaven ended the Hàn mandate,
and the army scattered outside Liáng,
with surrendering generals and defeated troops
arriving one after another,
you then turned your horse's head
and directly returned to Guīyīn.
(Yǎnzhōu lies north of Guī Mountain.
Mùróng Yànchāo's journey to Dàliáng
and return to Yǎnzhōu are both recorded in the previous scroll of last year.)
You had a beginning and an end.
This is what is called 'in danger and chaos, one sees the integrity of a loyal minister; in strong winds, one knows the heart of sturdy grass.'
If all subjects could be like this,
then what ruler would not wish to employ them!
Regarding what you said about when I was the hidden dragon in Héshuò,
and during the pacification of troubles at Jùnjiāo,
because I did not receive your informing words,
I also could not send anyone to the traveling court.
Moreover, in the way of serving one's lord,
why must it be like this!
If one were to be disloyal to the Hàn court,
how could one then be loyal and trustworthy to the Zhōu house!
To be fearful on this account,
is that not excessive!
You need only exert your strength and devote your heart,
pacifying the people and embodying the state.
Your service to me,
as you served your former lord,
will not only bring peace to the common people,
but also be a reliance for the altars of grain and soil.
Just firmly set an example;
there is no discussion of replacing you.
The sincere words from my heart
are all spoken here."
(Because Mùróng Yànchāo was uneasy,
this edict was issued to pacify and instruct him.)
On the 28th day, the Táng court appointed the King of Chǔ, Xī'è, as Tiāncè Shàng Jiāngjūn, Jiédù Shǐ of Wǔ'ān, Wǔpíng, Jìngjiāng, and Níngyuǎn, concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng and King of Chǔ.
They appointed Yòu Púyè Sūn Jì
(Sūn Jì was Sūn Shèng.
The Ōu Shǐ states: Shèng had another name, Jì,
and also another name, Fèng.)
On the 29th day, Bǐngyín,
the former Cízhōu Cìshǐ Chén Sīràng was sent to lead troops to garrison Cízhōu,
to hold the Huángzé road.
(Cízhōu lies northwest at the pass of Huángzé Guān.
Cí is pronounced like qiáng.)
After the King of Chǔ, Xī'è, achieved his ambition,
he dwelled much on old grudges,
killing without restraint.
Day and night, he indulged in wine and debauchery,
entrusting all military and governmental affairs to Mǎ Xīchóng.
Xīchóng, in turn, was often selfish and unfair,
and administration and punishments fell into disorder.
The government storehouses had already been exhausted by the disorderly troops,
so they requisitioned the people's wealth to reward the soldiers.
Sometimes they would seal people's doors and take their possessions,
yet the soldiers still complained of unfairness and harbored resentment.
Even the old generals and aides from Lǎngzhōu who had come with Xī'è
were all displeased,
and their hearts were turning away.
When Liú Guāngfǔ went to present tribute to the Táng court
(presenting tribute, see last month),
Guāngfǔ secretly said:
"In Húnán, the people are exhausted and the ruler is arrogant;
it can be taken."
The Táng ruler then appointed the Yíngtún Dū Yúhòu Biān Hào as the Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ,
leading troops to garrison Yuánzhōu,
secretly planning an advance to seize it.
The minor gate officer Xiè Yǎnyóng,
originally a household slave of Xī'è,
was favored by Xī'è due to his handsome appearance,
handsome appearance,
meaning the allure of a catamite.
He relied on this favor to act arrogantly and tyrannically.
He often walked shoulder-to-shoulder with Xīchóng,
or even patted him on the back;
according to the Book of Rites: if someone is twice one's age,
one should serve them as a father;
if ten years older,
one should serve them as an elder brother;
if five years older,
one should walk shoulder-to-shoulder with them.
The commentary states: walking shoulder-to-shoulder means
walking alongside them but slightly behind.
As for patting the back,
it indicates excessive familiarity.
According to precedent,
during official banquets,
minor gate officers would stand guard with weapons outside the door;
Xī'è allowed Yǎnyóng to sit at the banquet,
sometimes even placing him above the generals,
which shamed all the generals.
Xī'è, because the official residence had been burned down,
ordered the Lǎngzhōu Jìngjiāng commanders Wáng Kuí and deputy Zhōu Xíngféng to lead over a thousand of their troops to repair it,
the labor was extremely arduous,
and there were no rewards or gifts,
so the soldiers all resented it,
whispering among themselves:
"Prisoners spared from death are forced into labor.
We followed the Great King through countless dangers to seize Húnán,
what crime have we committed to be treated like prisoners and forced into labor!
Moreover, the Great King indulges in drinking and singing all day long,
how could he know of our toils and hardships!"
Kuí and Xíngféng heard this,
and said to each other:
"The resentment among the troops runs deep,
if we do not plan early,
disaster will befall us."
On the morning of Rénshēn,
they led their troops, each armed with long-handled axes and white clubs,
and fled back to Lǎngzhōu.
Kē,
means the handle of an axe.
Tǐng,
pronounced as tǐng.
The attendants did not dare to report it;
on Guǐyǒu,
they finally reported it.
Xī'è sent the Húnán commander Táng Shīzhù to lead over a thousand men in pursuit,
but they failed to catch up,
and went straight to Lǎngzhōu;
Kuí and others, taking advantage of their exhaustion,
set an ambush and launched a fierce attack,
the soldiers were almost entirely killed or wounded,
and Shīzhù escaped back alone.
Kuí and others deposed the acting governor Mǎ Guāngzàn,
last year,
Mǎ Xī'è had his son Guāngzàn garrison Lǎngzhōu.
Guānghuì,
was the son of Xīzhèn.
Xīzhèn,
was the legitimate eldest son of Mǎ Yīn.
Kuí and others, along with Hé Jìngzhēn and the various army commanders Zhāng Fǎng, jointly decided military and governmental affairs.
Xī'è reported the situation in detail to the Táng,
the Táng ruler sent an envoy with generous rewards to summon and instruct them;
Kuí and others accepted the rewards,
released the envoy,
but did not reply to the edict,
and the Táng also did not dare to question them.
31 Wáng Yànchāo reported the capture of Xúzhōu,
killing Gǒng Tíngměi and others.
Gǒng Tíngměi and others were defeated and died due to lack of reinforcements.
32 The Northern Hàn's Lǐ [AS-FDB3] [AS-FBEC]yán arrived in Qìdān,
the Qìdān ruler sent Yèlà Méilǐ to respond to him.
33 On Bǐngzǐ,
an imperial decree:
"The court and the Táng originally have no enmity,
the armies and towns along the Huái River,
each should guard their own territories,
and must not allow soldiers or civilians to trespass into Táng territory;
merchants and travelers coming and going,
must not be prohibited."
34 On Jǐmǎo,
Lùzhōu sent over two hundred and sixty captured Northern Hàn generals and soldiers from Shè County,
each was bestowed with shirts, trousers, towels, and shoes before being sent back.
Shè,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to Lùzhōu in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: located 198 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
35 Added to Wúyuè King Qián Hóngchù the title of Commander-in-Chief of the Armies of All Circuits.
36 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Rénchén, the first day,
the prefectures and towns along the Huái River reported:
"Famine-stricken people from Huáinán are crossing the Huái to buy grain,
we dare not prohibit them."
An edict stated:
"Their people,
how are they different from ours?
It is appropriate to order the prefectures, counties, ferries, and posts not to prohibit them."
37 The Shǔ's General Memorials Officer Gāo Yánzhāo firmly declined the position of Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
on Dīngwèi,
the former Yún'ān Salt Monopoly Officer of Tàiyuán, Yī Shěnzhēng, was appointed as General Memorials Officer,
and Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Yún'ān,
was the territory of the Qúrǔ County of Bā Commandery in the Hàn,
Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu established Yún'ān County,
it belonged to Kuízhōu in the Táng,
because it produced salt,
the Yún'ān Salt Monopoly was established.
He was the son of the Shǔ高祖's younger sister, Princess Bāoguó,
from a young age he was intimate and familiar with the Shǔ ruler,
and upon becoming Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
all matters of governance, big and small, were consulted with him.
Shěnzhēng also took managing state affairs as his own responsibility,
but he was greedy, extravagant, and deceitful,
colluding with Wáng Zhāoyuǎn,
and the Shǔ's governance thus gradually declined.
38 The Wúyuè King Qián Hóngchù moved the deposed king Qián Hóngzōng to reside in the Eastern Capital,
moving from the Yìjǐn Army to reside in the Eastern Capital.
Wúyuè used Yuèzhōu as the Eastern Capital.
He built gardens and parks,
to amuse and please him,
and the annual provisions and gifts were very generous.
39 The Qìdān ruler sent an envoy to the Northern Hàn,
informing them that the Zhōu envoy Tián Mǐn had come,
agreeing to pay an annual tribute of one hundred thousand strings of cash.
The Northern Hàn ruler sent Zhèng Gǒng with generous bribes to thank the Qìdān,
calling himself
"Nephew Emperor sends a letter to Uncle Heaven-bestowed Emperor,"
requesting the performance of the investiture ceremony.
40 In the fifth month,
on Jǐsì,
sent the Left Imperial Guard General Yáo Hànyīng and others as envoys to the Qìdān,
the Qìdān detained them.
Because the Northern Hàn's dealings with them were generous,
the Qìdān thus detained the Zhōu envoys.
41 On Xīnwèi,
the Northern Hàn's Minister of Rites and Vice Director of the Secretariat, Zhèng Gǒng, died in Qìdān.
Examination of discrepancies: Jìnyáng Jiànwén Lù states:
"After Zhèng Gǒng reached the barbarian court,
the barbarian ruler treated him with generous courtesy.
The barbarian custom is to boast of pools of wine and forests of meat,
even those who do not drink, like Wéi Yào and his ilk,
are also forced to drink,
even if they become ill,
they are not believed.
Gǒng was tall and strong, good at drinking,
subjected to limitless coercion,
after the banquet,
he was carried back,
and one night his ribs rotted away in the felt tent of the yurt,
and his body was carried back to report the mission."
Jiǔguó Zhì states:
"The Qìdān feasted and rewarded Hàn envoys,
always providing ample wine and meat,
to show off their extravagance.
When Gāozǔ garrisoned Hédōng,
he once sent Wéi Yào as an envoy north,
Yào was frail and thin and could not drink,
the barbarians forced him,
and he died."
Note: Wéi Yào,
was Wéi Zhāo from the time of Sūn Hào,
who could not drink.
Wáng Bǎohéng cited this as literary embellishment,
but Lù Zhèn said he was a person from Gāozǔ's time,
which is an error.
42 On Jiǎxū,
the Yìwǔ military governor Sūn Fāngjiǎn avoided the taboo of the imperial father's name,
and changed his name to Fāngjiàn.
43 The Dìngnán military governor Lǐ Yíyīn sent an envoy to present a memorial to the Northern Hàn.
"Military governor"
below,
should have
character.
Nán,
pronounced nán.
44 In the sixth month,
on Xīnhài,
appointed the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner and Vice Director of the Secretariat Wáng Jùn as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Vice Director of the Chancellery,
Deputy Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner and Vice Minister of War Fàn Zhì, and Administrator of
the Three Departments Lǐ Gǔ as Vice Directors of the Secretariat,
all concurrently Vice Directors of the Secretariat,
Gǔ still administered the Three Departments.

Minister of Education and Palace Attendant Dòu Zhēngù, Minister of Works and Vice Director of the Secretariat and Vice Director of the Secretariat Sū Yǔguī were both dismissed to their original offices.
On Guǐchǒu,
Fàn Zhì participated in the administration of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
On Dīngsì,
appointed the North Court of the Palace Reception Commissioner Zhái Guāngyè concurrently as Deputy Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner.
Initially,
when the Emperor campaigned against Hézhōng,
he was already the one whom popular sentiment favored;
(The Emperor's campaign against Hézhōng is recorded in volume 288, the first year of the Hàn dynasty's Qiányòu era.)
Favor,
read as *zhǔ*.
The Emperor repeatedly hinted at him with subtle words,
but Lǐ Gǔ only responded with the duty of a subject to fulfill his loyalty,
and for this, the Emperor esteemed him.
Upon ascending the throne,
he first appointed him as chancellor.
At that time, the state was newly established,
and there were many troubles from all directions.
Wáng Jùn devoted himself day and night,
doing everything he knew to do,
and his military strategies
were of great benefit.
Fàn Zhì was intelligent, quick-witted, and had a strong memory,
strictly adhering to laws and regulations.
Lǐ Gǔ was resolute, composed, and had strategic insight;
when discussing matters before the Emperor,
his words were impassioned and fervent,
adept at using analogies to enlighten the Emperor's mind.
45. The military commissioner of Wǔpíng, Mǎ Guānghuì,
was foolish, cowardly, and fond of drinking,
unable to command the respect of the generals.
Wáng Kuí, Zhōu Xíngféng, and Hé Jìngzhēn conspired to support Liú Yán, the prefect of Chénzhōu from Lúlíng, who was brave and had won the hearts of the barbarian tribes.
(Liú Yán followed Péng Gān to flee to Chǔ,
and thus became a general of Chǔ.)
Liú Yán knew that Kuí and the others would be difficult to control,
and said:
"If I do not go,
they will attack me."
So he went alone on horseback to meet them.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chénzhōu is 566 *lǐ* east of Lǎngzhōu.)
The masses deposed Guānghuì,
sent him to Táng,
and elected Yán as acting military commissioner of Wǔpíng,
setting the stage for Wáng Kuí and others to later kill Liú Yán.
The people of Táng did not approve;
they also pledged allegiance to Zhōu.
46. The King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngchù, believing that the former commander of the inner and outer cavalry and infantry, Qián Rénjùn, was innocent,
restored his official position and title.
(Qián Rénjùn's imprisonment is recorded in volume 285, the second year of the Jìn dynasty's Qíwáng Kāiyùn era.)
47. The Khitan sent the Prince of Yān, Shùzhá, and others to confer upon the ruler of Běi Hàn the title of Great Hàn Divine and Martial Emperor,
and to establish an empress.
The ruler of Běi Hàn changed his name to Mín.
48. In autumn,
the seventh month,
according to the *Wǔdài Huìyào*,
in this month,
Zhōu posthumously honored four ancestral temples.
Bóxīng
was originally Bóchāng County of Qīngzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
During the Later Táng, to avoid the taboo of the name of the honored ancestor,
it was changed to Bóxīng.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: The county is 120 *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.)
He requested troops to attack Zhōu.
49. In the eighth month,
on the *rénxū* day,
the Hàn Emperor Yǐndì was buried at Yǐnglíng.
(Yǐnglíng is located in Yángzhái County, Xǔzhōu.)
50. The military commissioner of Yìwǔ, Sūn Fāngjiàn, came to the court.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
he was transferred to be the military commissioner of Zhènguó,
and his younger brother, the prefect of Yìzhōu, Sūn Xíngyǒu, was appointed acting military commissioner of Yìwǔ.
Also, the military commissioner of Jiànxióng, Wáng Yàn, was transferred to Xúzhōu,
and the military commissioner of Wǔníng, Wáng Yànchāo, replaced him.
(Wáng Yàn and Wáng Yànchāo exchanged their respective commands.)
51. On the *wùwǔ* day,
the late Lady Chái was posthumously established as empress.
(Lady Chái had died earlier;
last year, she did not die at the hands of Liú Shū.)
52. In the ninth month,
the ruler of Běi Hàn sent the commander Lǐ Cúnhuái to lead troops from Tuánbǎi to invade.
The Khitan intended to lead troops to join him,
(The word "ruler" should follow "Khitan.")
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* states: Eighty *lǐ* east of Jǔyáng City is Mùniú Mountain,
at the foot of which are the Ninety-Nine Springs,
which are the source of the Cāng River.
According to Wèi Shōu's *Wèi Shū*: In the third year of Tiāncì,
in the eighth month,
the ruler of Wèi ascended the northern plain of Wǔyào,
to view the Ninety-Nine Springs.
(Wǔyào County was the seat of the Eastern Commandant of Dìngxiāng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.)
Sòng Bái said: The Ninety-Nine Springs
are over a thousand *lǐ* northwest of Yōuzhōu.
The Khitan ruler forced him,
and on the *guǐhài* day,
they reached Huǒshéndiàn in Xīnzhōu.
Although the Khitan had defeated Jìn,
their strength was also exhausted.
The various tribes had not yet recovered from their wounds,
and were weakened and depleted,
so they did not wish to invade the south.
(Sòng Bái said: Huǒshéndiàn is west of Xīnzhōu.
Forced, read as *qiǎng*.
Diàn, read as *diàn*.
Shallow water is called *diàn*.)
They assassinated the Khitan ruler and established Shùzhá.
The son of the Khitan ruler Déguāng,
Shùlǜ, fled into the southern mountains.
The various tribes supported Shùlǜ to attack Shùzhá and Ōusēng,
killed them,
and exterminated their clans and factions.
They established Shùlǜ as emperor,
and changed the era name to Yìnglì.
From Huǒshéndiàn, he entered Yōuzhōu,
and sent an envoy to inform Běi Hàn.
The ruler of Běi Hàn sent the Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Wáng Dézhōng from Shàngdǎng, to the Khitan,
to congratulate him on his accession,
and again treated him as an uncle,
requesting troops to attack Jìnzhōu.
The Khitan ruler was young,
fond of amusement and games,
and did not attend to state affairs.
Every night he drank heavily,
staying up until dawn before sleeping,
and rising only around noon.
His people called him the Sleeping King.
He later changed his name to Míng.
53. On the *rénshēn* day,
Shǔ appointed the Minister of Personnel and Censor-in-Chief, Fàn Rénshù, as Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Minister of Personnel, participating in determining governmental matters.
54. The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Xī'è, after capturing Chángshā,
did not reward Xǔ Kěqióng.
(Xǔ Kěqióng's surrender to Xī'è is recorded in the previous volume, the third year of the Hàn Emperor Yǐndì's Qiányòu era.)
He sent him out to be the prefect of Méngzhōu.

(In the fifth year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty, Suíhuà County of Lìzhōu was separated to establish Nángōngzhōu. In the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era, it was renamed Méngzhōu. In the fifth year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng dynasty, Méngzhōu was abolished, and Lìshān County was placed under Zhāozhōu. Sòng Bái said: Méngzhōu is the territory of Lìpǔ County of the Hàn dynasty. The Táng established Méngzhōu because east of the prefecture is Méng Mountain, at the foot of which is a spring that flows into the Méng River. The people at the foot of the mountain all have the surname Méng, hence the name.)
To defend against the troops of Lǎng,
he did not comfort the laborers,
so the officers and soldiers were all resentful and angry,
and plotted to rebel.
Xīchóng knew of their plot.
On the *wùyín* day,
Xī'è held a banquet for his officers,
but Xú Wēi and others were not invited,
and Xīchóng also excused himself due to illness and did not attend.
Wēi and others first sent over a dozen horses that kicked and bit into the mansion,
and then led their followers armed with axes and clubs,
claiming to tie up the horses,
and suddenly rushed to the seats,
striking people left and right,
knocking them to the ground.
Xī'è climbed over the wall and fled,
but Wēi and others captured and imprisoned him.
(The *Shíguó Jìnián* records this as the *dīngchǒu* day. According to the *Húxiāng Gùshì*, it was on the nineteenth day; now we follow that.)
They hacked him from head to toe.
They established Xīchóng as acting military commissioner of Wǔ'ān,
and allowed the soldiers to plunder freely.
They imprisoned Xī'è in Héngshān County.

(During the Three Kingdoms period, Wú separated Héngshān County from Xiāngnán County. In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Héngzhōu. In the fourth year of the Chúnhuà era of the Sòng dynasty, it was placed under Tánzhōu. The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Héngshān County is 320 *lǐ* southwest of Tánzhōu.)
When Liú Yán heard that Xī Chóng had taken the throne,
he dispatched troops toward Tánzhōu,
proclaiming he was marching to punish Xī Chóng for the crime of usurpation.
On the rénwǔ day,
his army camped west of Yìyáng.
Xī Chóng grew fearful.
On the guǐwèi day,
he sent out two thousand soldiers to resist them,
and also dispatched an envoy to Lǎngzhōu to sue for peace,
requesting to become a neighboring vassal.
The administrative secretary, Lǐ Guānxiàng of Guìlín, advised Yán, saying:
(People of that time called Guìzhōu "Guìlín".)
(Shuì means to persuade.)
(Shì, ruì fān.)
"Xī È's old generals and aides are still in Chángshā.
They certainly do not wish to be neighbors with you.
It would be better to first send a dispatch to Xī Chóng demanding their heads.
After that, we can plan for Húnán,
and we may be able to annex it."
Yán followed this advice.
Xī Chóng, fearing Yán,
immediately beheaded more than ten people, including the military judge Yáng Zhòngmǐn, administrative secretary Liú Guāngfǔ, palace guard commander Wèi Shījìn, and chief officer Huáng Qíng,
and sent the former magistrate of Chényáng County, Lǐ Yì, to deliver the heads to Lǎngzhōu.
(Chényáng is a place name.
The Mǎ family established it as a county,
belonging to Chénzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Chénxī County
was originally the Hàn dynasty's Chénlíng County.
In the Later Hàn it was called Chényáng,
because the county was on the north bank of the Chén River.
The Sui dynasty changed it to Chénxī.
Thus, the Mǎ family used the Later Hàn county name.)
Yán, along with Wáng Kuí and others, all believed these were not the heads of Zhòngmǐn and the rest.
They angrily reprimanded Yì,
and Yì, terrified, committed suicide.
After Xī Chóng usurped the throne,
he also indulged in wine and debauchery,
governed unjustly,
and his words were often deceitful and false,
so the people of the state did not support him.
Initially, when Mǎ Xī È entered Chángshā,
(events seen in the twelfth month of the previous year in the previous scroll)
he still had Shī Gǎo beaten on the back and dismissed to commoner status.
Xī Chóng thought Shī Gǎo must harbor resentment against Xī È,
so he sent Xī È to Héngshān under Shī Gǎo's escort,
actually hoping Shī Gǎo would kill him.
Shī Gǎo said:
"Do you want to make me a regicide?"
He served Xī È with even greater respect.
On the bǐngxū day,
they reached Héngshān.
The Héngshān commander, Liào Yǎn,
was the son of Liào Kuāngtú.
(In the fourth year of the Later Jìn Tiānfú reign, Liào Kuāngtú died fighting the barbarians.)
"My family has received the Mǎ family's favor for generations.
Now Xī È is the eldest but has been deposed.
He will certainly not escape disaster.
Why don't we join together to assist him?"
Thereupon, he led the estate tenants and local villagers, all forming troops.
(Tenants who farmed the lands of powerful families and paid them rent were called estate tenants.)
(Shuài is read as lǜ.)
They used the county as a provisional headquarters,
blocked the river to build a stockade,
and wove bamboo into warships.
They appointed Shī Gǎo as the military governor of Wǔqīng.
(The military governor of Wǔqīng was a title Liào Yǎn and the others bestowed upon themselves.)
Within a few days,
their numbers reached over ten thousand,
and many prefectures and counties responded to them.
They sent administrative officer Liú Xūjǐ to seek aid from the Táng.
Xú Wēi and others, observing Xī Chóng's actions,
knew he would certainly not succeed.
They also feared the pressure from Lǎngzhōu and Héngshān,
worried that one day they would be defeated,
and all would be implicated in disaster.
They wanted to kill Xī Chóng to extricate themselves.
Xī Chóng vaguely sensed this,
grew greatly afraid,
and secretly dispatched the guest general Fàn Shǒumù to submit a memorial requesting troops from the Táng.
The Táng sovereign ordered Biān Hào to lead ten thousand troops from Yuánzhōu westward toward Chángshā.
55 In winter,
tenth month,
on the xīnmǎo day,
the Lùzhōu patrol commander Chén Sīràng defeated the Northern Hàn army at Sītíng.
56 The Táng's Biān Hào led troops into Lǐlíng.
(The Old Tángshū Geography Treatise states: Within the boundaries of the Hàn dynasty's Línxiāng County was Lǐlíng.
The Later Hàn established it as a county.
The Sui abolished it.
In the fourth year of the Táng Wǔdé reign, Lǐlíng County was created from part of Chángshā County,
and both belonged to Tánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: Lǐlíng County is 160 lǐ east of Tánzhōu.
Fàn Chéngdà's Travel Record: From Píngxiāng County in Yuánzhōu to Lǐlíng County in Tánzhōu is a journey of two days.)
On the guǐsì day,
the King of Chǔ, Xī Chóng, sent an envoy to reward the army.
On the rényín day,
he sent the Tiāncè Mansion academician Tuòbá Héng to deliver a letter to Hào requesting surrender.
Héng sighed, saying:
"I have lived so long without dying, only to deliver a surrender document for a child!"
On the guǐmǎo day,
Xī Chóng led his younger brothers and nephews to welcome Hào,
bowing upon seeing the dust of his approach.
Hào dismounted and proclaimed an imperial edict to comfort them.
On the jiǎchén day,
Xī Chóng and others followed Hào into the city.
Hào took up residence in the Liúyáng Gate tower.
All the generals and officials of Húnán came to offer congratulations,
and Hào richly rewarded them all.
At that time, Húnán was suffering famine.
Hào extensively distributed grain from the Mǎ family's granaries for relief,
greatly pleasing the people of Chǔ.
Mǎ Yīn occupied Tán and Lǎng,
passing them to his sons Xī Shēng, Xī Fàn, Xī Guǎng, Xī È, and Xī Chóng.
By now, they were destroyed.

(When Chǔ returned the defeated Wú general Miáo Lín, Xǔ Déxūn said to him: "Wait until the colts fight over the manger and stable, and then Hú and Xiāng can be taken." Now it indeed happened as he said.)
57 The Qìdān sent the Zhāngguó military governor Xiāo Yǔjué to lead fifty thousand Xī and Qìdān troops to join the Northern Hàn army in an invasion.
The Northern Hàn sovereign personally led twenty thousand troops from Yīndì Pass to invade Jìnzhōu.
On the dīngwèi day,
they camped north of the city,
setting up encampments on three sides,
attacking day and night.
Their roaming troops reached Jiàngzhōu.
At that time, Wáng Yàn had already left his post,
and Wáng Yànchāo had not yet arrived.
The patrol commander Wáng Wǎngǎn temporarily took charge of Jìnzhōu,
joining with the Lóngjié capital commander Shǐ Yànchāo and the Hǔjié commander Hé Huī to resist them together.
(The Basic Annals of the Old History of the Five Dynasties: In the first year of the Guǎngshùn reign,
the names of the Imperial Guard cavalry and infantry armies were changed.
The cavalry army, formerly called Hùshèng, was changed to Lóngjié;
the infantry army, formerly called Fèngguó, was changed to Hǔjié.
[Shǐ Yànchāo] was from Yúnzhōu.)
58 On the guǐchǒu day,
the Táng's Wǔchāng military governor Liú Rénshàn led two hundred warships to capture Yuèzhōu,
pacifying and accepting surrenders and submissions,
so that people forgot about their state's destruction.
(Liú Rénshàn was skilled at command, hence he was later able to steadfastly defend Shòuzhōu for the Táng.
He was the son of Liú Jīn.
Liú Jīn was a general under the Yáng family.)
The Táng officials all congratulated each other on the pacification of Húnán.
The diarist Gāo Yuǎn said:
"We took advantage of Chǔ's chaos to seize it, which was very easy.
But judging by the talents of our generals, I fear holding it will be difficult!"
(Yuǎn was from Yōuzhōu.)
The retired minister of education, Lǐ Jiànxūn, said:
"Disaster will likely begin from this!"
(The Táng's disaster and defeat later indeed happened as these two ministers predicted.)
Since ascending the throne,
the Táng sovereign had never personally performed the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices.
The ritual officials requested it,
and the Táng sovereign said:
"Wait until the world is united as one family, then I will report and give thanks."
After capturing Chǔ in one move,
he believed the various states could be settled with a wave of his hand.
Wèi Cén, while attending a banquet, said:
"When I was young, I traveled to Yuánchéng [in Wèibó] and enjoyed its customs and land.
I beg that after Your Majesty pacifies the Central Plains,
you grant me the military governorship of Wèibó."
The Táng sovereign agreed,
and Cén hurried down to bow and give thanks.
Their sovereign was so arrogant and their ministers so fawning.
Mǎ Xī È hoped the Táng would establish him as the military governor of Tán,
but the people of Tán despised Xī È
and jointly requested Biān Hào be made military governor.
The Táng sovereign then appointed Hào as the military governor of Wǔ'ān.
(This sets the stage for Biān Hào later being driven out by the Lǎng troops.)
59 Wáng Jùn had an old acquaintance named Shēn Shīhòu,
who had once served as a deputy commander in Yǎnzhōu,
but lost his position and suffered hunger and cold.
Seeing Wáng Jùn's horse, he bowed and paid his respects on the road.
At that time, the acting military governor of Liángzhōu, Zhébū Jiāshī, submitted a memorial to the court requesting a military governor.
Zhébū
was a Qiāng tribal name,
which he thus adopted as his surname.
The court sought to recruit an official from the Crown Prince's Guard who was willing to go.
The Crown Prince's Guard
refers to the ten guard offices of the Eastern Palace.
No one responded to the recruitment.
Wáng Jùn recommended Shīhòu to the Emperor.
On Dīngsì day,
Shīhòu was appointed as the Military Governor of Héxī.
60 The Táng general Biān Hào urged Mǎ Xīchóng to lead his clan to the court.
The Mǎ clan gathered and wept together.
They wanted to heavily bribe Biān Hào,
requesting permission to remain in Chángshā.
Biān Hào smiled faintly and said:
"Our state and your family have been enemies for generations,
nearly sixty years,
yet we have never dared to harbor any intention of coveting your state.
Now, you brothers are fighting among yourselves,
and in your dire straits, you have come to us of your own accord.
If you waver again,
I fear there will be unforeseen calamities."
Xīchóng had no reply.
In the eleventh month,
on Xīnyǒu day,
he and his clan members, along with over a thousand officers and soldiers, boarded boats wailing and lamenting.
Those seeing them off all wept,
the sound shaking the valleys.
61 The Emperor, concerned that the forces of the Northern Hàn and the Qìdān were still at Jìnzhōu,
on Jiǎzǐ day,
appointed Wáng Jùn as Field Commander of the Campaign Army,
ordering him to lead troops to relieve it.
An edict commanded all armies to accept Wáng Jùn's command,
allowing him to act according to circumstances,
and to select his own officers and officials.
On Yǐchǒu day,
Jùn set out,
and the Emperor personally went to the west of the city to bid him farewell.
This refers to the west of Dàliáng city.
62 The Deputy Military Governor of Chǔ's Jìngjiāng Army and Administrator of Guìzhōu, Mǎ Xīyǐn,
was the youngest son of King Wǔmù, Mǎ Yīn.
The Chǔ kings Mǎ Xīguǎng and Mǎ Xī'è were contending for the state.
The Southern Hàn ruler appointed the palace attendant Wú Huái'ēn as the Northwestern Pacification Commissioner,
leading troops to station at the border,
waiting for an opportunity to secretly plan an advance.
Xīguǎng dispatched Commander Péng Yànhuī to lead troops and station at Lóngdòng to guard against him.
South of the stream in Guìzhōu was Báilóng Cave,
located halfway up a mountain on flat ground.
Xīyǐn disliked this,
and secretly sent someone to inform the Prefect of Méngzhōu, Xǔ Kěqióng.
Kěqióng, fearing the pressure from Southern Hàn,
immediately abandoned Méngzhōu
and led his troops towards Guìzhōu.
Méngzhōu and Guìzhōu were over four hundred lǐ apart.
Qù
is pronounced qūyù.
Yànhuī was defeated
and fled to Héngshān.
Kěqióng remained stationed at Guìzhōu.
Wú Huái'ēn occupied Méngzhōu,
advanced his troops to raid and plunder,
causing great disturbance in the Guì region.
Xīyǐn and Kěqióng did not know what to do,
and could only drink together and weep facing each other.
The Southern Hàn ruler sent a letter to Xīyǐn,
stating:
"King Wǔmù possessed the entire Chǔ,
which was wealthy, strong, peaceful, and stable for over fifty years.
It is precisely because the thirty-fifth uncle and the thirtieth uncle brothers took up arms,
and began preying on each other,
— the thirty-fifth uncle
refers to Xīguǎng;
the thirtieth uncle,
refers to Xī'è.
The Hàn ruler Liú Yǎn married a daughter of King Mǎ Yīn of Chǔ,
hence he addresses Xīguǎng and others as uncles.
You faced a northern enemy.
This refers to the entire state submitting to Táng.
I privately reckon that Guìlín will subsequently be taken by them.
Our court has long been your allied state,
further bound by marriage ties.
Seeing this perilous situation,
how can we bear not to come to your rescue!
We have already dispatched a large army advancing by both land and water.
We shall ensure that you, sir and uncle, forever hold the commander's tally,
and permanently govern a region."
Xīyǐn received the letter,
and discussed surrendering with his subordinates.
Administrative Assistant Pān Xuánguī considered it unacceptable.
On Bǐngyín day,
Wú Huái'ēn led troops and suddenly arrived at the city walls.
Xīyǐn and Kěqióng led their followers,
broke through the gates at night and fled to Quánzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Guìzhōu north to Quánzhōu is one hundred and sixty-three lǐ.
During the reign of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn,
the Mǎ family changed the name of Xiāngyuán County in Yǒngzhōu to Qīngxiāng County,
and established Quánzhōu.
Originally the territory of Táoyáng County of the Hàn,
the Táo River is north of Qīngxiāng County.
Shuài
is pronounced shuài.
Huái'ēn subsequently used his troops to conquer and pacify Yí, Lián, Wú, Yán, Fù, Zhāo, Liǔ, Gōng, Xiàng, and other prefectures.
In the second year of the Qiánfēng era of Táng,
they recruited and settled the raw Lǎo tribes,
and established Yánzhōu in the former territory of the Guìlín Commandery of Qín.
Fùzhōu was likely established in Fùchuān County of Hèzhōu.
63 On Xīnwèi day,
the Táng general Biān Hào sent Vanguard Commander Lǐ Chéngjiǎn to lead troops to Héngshān,
to urge Mǎ Xī'è to come to court.
On Gēngchén day,
Xī'è, along with over ten thousand officers and soldiers, went east downriver from Tánzhōu.
64 Wáng Jùn remained at Shǎnzhōu for ten days.
The Emperor, concerned that the Northern Hàn's attack on Jìnzhōu was urgent,
feared it could not be held,
and considered personally leading troops via the Zézhōu route to join forces with Jùn and relieve it.
The Emperor intended to go west from Zézhōu,
while Wáng Jùn would cross the river north from Shǎn,
take Jiàngzhōu, and rendezvous at Jìnzhōu.
Shǎn
is pronounced shǐrǎn.
Jiàng
is pronounced jíliàng.
In the twelfth month,
on Wùzǐ, the first day,
an edict was issued to march west on the third day.
When the messenger reached Shǎn,
Jùn used the messenger to relay a message to the Emperor:
"The walls of Jìnzhōu are strong,
and it will not be easily captured.
Liú Chóng's military momentum is currently sharp,
and we cannot contend with him by force.
The reason for stationing troops here
is to wait for his vigor to decline,
it is not that I am timid.
Your Majesty has newly ascended the throne,
and should not move lightly.
If the imperial carriage departs from Sìshuǐ,
then Mùróng Yànchāo will lead troops into Biàn,
and the great enterprise will be lost!"
The Emperor heard this,
and with his own hand pulled his ear, saying:
"That nearly ruined our affairs!"
Wáng Jùn's words
addressed a precaution the Emperor had not considered,
and struck him as profoundly correct,
hence he unconsciously pulled his own ear.
Jī
is pronounced jīyī.
Bài
is pronounced bǔmài.
On Gēngyín day,
an order was issued to cancel the personal campaign.
Earlier,
the Military Governor of Tàiníng and concurrently Grand Councillor Mùróng Yànchāo, upon hearing that Xúzhōu had been pacified,
believed Gǒng Tíngměi and others were dead.
He then recruited fugitives,
stockpiled firewood and grain,
and secretly sent letters to ally with the Northern Hàn.
An official intercepted his letter and reported it.
He also sent people disguised as merchants to seek aid from Táng.
The Emperor sent the Interpreter-Aide Zhèng Hǎoqiān to convey reassurance and instructions,
and made an oath with him.
Yànchāo grew increasingly uneasy.
He repeatedly sent his Chief Ya Officer Zhèng Lín to the court,
pretending to express sincere allegiance,
but actually to spy on opportunities.
He also presented a letter from the Military Governor of Tiānpíng, Gāo Xíngzhōu,
whose contents all slandered the court and expressed intentions to ally with Yànchāo.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"This is Yànchāo's trickery!"
He showed the letter to Xíngzhōu.
Xíngzhōu submitted a memorial thanking the Emperor for his grace.
Early in the Hàn dynasty,
Yànchāo and Xíngzhōu jointly attacked Wèi,
and thus developed a rift.
Moreover, Yǎnzhōu and Yùnzhōu were neighboring provinces.
If Yànchāo raised troops,
he feared Xíngzhōu would threaten his rear,
so he forged this letter
intending to sow discord;
the Emperor instead showed the letter to Xíngzhōu to secure his loyalty.
On Bǐngshēn day,
the Emperor dispatched the Gate Commissioner Zhāng Níng to lead troops to Yùnzhōu for inspection and patrol to guard against him.
Zhíguān Fēn Jì: The Gate Commissioner and Deputy
are in charge of serving the imperial carriage,
court assemblies, imperial tours, grand banquets, and ushering in imperial princes, chief ministers, all officials, and foreign guests for audiences and farewells,
and correcting breaches of etiquette.
Since the Five Dynasties period,
these posts have often been held by military officers,
sent on diplomatic missions and commanding armies.
On the Gēngzǐ day (65th),
Wáng Jùn arrived at Jiàngzhōu.
On the Yǐsì day,
he led his troops towards Jìnzhōu.
South of Jìnzhōu was Méngkēng,
an extremely strategic and crucial location.
Jùn feared the Northern Hàn troops would occupy it.
That day,
hearing that his vanguard had already crossed Méngkēng,
he joyfully said:
"My task is accomplished!"
(66) Mùróng Yànchāo submitted a memorial requesting to enter the court.
The Emperor knew it was deceitful,
and immediately granted it;
but soon after, Yànchāo again claimed there were many bandits within his territory,
and he dared not leave his post.
(67) The ruler of Northern Hàn attacked Jìnzhōu,
but could not capture it for a long time.
He had attacked Jìnzhōu on the Gēngzǐ day of the tenth month this year,
and by now over fifty days had passed.
The people gathered together to defend the mountain strongholds,
leaving the countryside with nothing to plunder,
and the army lacked food.
The Khitan troops longed to return home.
Hearing that Wáng Jùn had reached Méngkēng,
they burned their camp and fled at night.
Jùn entered Jìnzhōu.
His generals urged him to pursue immediately,
but Jùn hesitated and did not decide;
the next day,

he then dispatched the Field Army Cavalry Commander-in-Chief Qiú Hóngchāo, the Formation Marshal Yào Yuánfú, the Left Wing Formation Marshal Chén Sīràng, and Kāng Yánzhǎo to lead the cavalry in pursuit.
They caught up at Huòyì.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Huòyì
is located 135 lǐ north of Jìnzhōu.
Many Northern Hàn soldiers fell to their deaths in the cliffs and valleys.
The road at Huòyì was narrow.
Yánzhǎo, being timid and cowardly, did not press the pursuit urgently,
thus allowing the Northern Hàn troops to cross.
Yào Yuánfú said:
"Liú Chóng mobilized all his forces,
relying on the Hu cavalry to come,
with the ambition to swallow Jìn and Jiàng.
Now their morale is low and strength exhausted,
fleeing in disarray.
If we do not take this opportunity to crush them,
they will surely become a future trouble."
The other generals did not wish to advance.
Wáng Jùn again sent a messenger to stop them,
and they thus returned.
By the time the Khitan reached Jìnyáng,
they had lost thirty to forty percent of their men and horses;
Xiāo Yǔjué, ashamed of having achieved nothing,
nailed a great chieftain to the market,
and over ten days later, executed him.
The ruler of Northern Hàn then ceased his intentions for further advances.
Northern Hàn's land was barren and its people poor.
Internally, it supplied the army and state,
externally, it served the Khitan.
Taxes were numerous and corvée labor heavy,
making life unbearable for the people.
Many fled into Zhōu territory.
(68) The ruler of Táng appointed Sòng Qíqiū, the Military Commissioner of Zhènnán and concurrently Secretariat Director, as Grand Tutor.
He appointed Mǎ Xī'è as Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngnán Xīdào,
to govern
Hóngzhōu,
and additionally bestowed upon him the title of Prince of Chǔ.
He appointed Mǎ Xīchóng as Military Commissioner of Yǒngtài,
to govern
Shūzhōu.
Táng had established the Yǒngtài Army in Shūzhōu.
Those of high rank were appointed as Prefects, Generals, or Ministers and Supervisors;
those of lower rank received official posts in order.
The ruler of Táng praised the loyalty of Liào Yǎn and Péng Shīgǎo,
appointing Yǎn as Left Palace Duty Army Commissioner and Prefect of Láizhōu.
Láizhōu belonged to Zhōu territory,
so Liào Yǎn held the title in name only.
He bestowed generous gifts upon them.
The prefects of Húnán all went to the Táng court to pay homage.
Only Wáng Yūn, the Prefect of Yǒngzhōu, arrived late,
and the ruler of Táng had him poisoned to death.
(69) The ruler of Southern Hán dispatched the Palace Attendants Bureau Assistant Pān Chóngchè
(Táng's Palace Attendants Bureau had a Director and
a Vice Director,
but never had an Assistant;
this was a position created by Southern Hán)
and Táng's Biān Hào to send troops to rescue them.
Chóngchè defeated the Táng troops at Yìzhāng,
and then captured Chēnzhōu.
Biān Hào requested to appoint prefects for Quán and Dào prefectures to prepare against Southern Hán.
On the Bǐngchén day,
the ruler of Táng appointed Liào Yǎn as Prefect of Dàozhōu,
and appointed the Black Cloud Commanding Officer Zhāng Luán to administer Quánzhōu.
Quán and Dào prefectures bordered the three prefectures of Hè, Zhāo, and Guì of Southern Hán.
(70) That year,
the ruler of Táng appointed Wáng Yánzhèng, the Military Commissioner of Ānhuà and Prince of Póyáng, as Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào.
Xīngyuán,
Shānnán Xīdào,
belonged to Shǔ.
Táng had Wáng Yánzhèng hold the title in name only.
Previously,
the garrison commander of Méngchéng, Xián Shīlǎng, led his troops to surrender to Táng.
(See the second year of the Qiányòu era of Hàn, scroll 288.)
Jiàng,
pronounced as liàng.
He followed Biān Hào in pacifying Húnán.
Táng confiscated all the gold, silk, treasures, playthings, granary stores, and even the beautiful boats, pavilions, and flowers and fruits of Húnán,
and moved them to Jīnlíng.
They dispatched the Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors Yáng Jìxūn and others to collect the taxes and levies of Húnán to support the garrison troops.
Jìxūn and others were extremely harsh and exacting,
causing the people of Húnán to lose hope.
The Field Army Provisions Commissioner Wáng Shàoyán reduced the soldiers' grain rations and allowances.
The Fèngjié Commanding Officers Sūn Lǎng and Cáo Jìn angrily said:
"In the past, we followed Lord Xián in surrendering to Táng.
Did Táng treat us as well as they treat the Húnán generals and soldiers today?
Now, having achieved merit, our salaries and allowances are not increased,
but are instead reduced.
It would be better to kill Shàoyán and Hào,
seize Húnán,
return to the Central Plains,
and seek wealth and honor!"
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
at night,
Sūn Lǎng and Cáo Jìn led their followers in rebellion.
They bundled straw and secretly set fire to the government gate,
but the fire did not catch.
Biān Hào detected them,
sent out troops to fight,
and ordered drums and horns to be sounded.
Lǎng, Jìn, and others thought dawn was approaching,
broke through the gate, and fled to Lǎngzhōu.
Wáng Kuí asked Lǎng:
"In the past, I followed the Martial and Solemn King,
and repeatedly achieved victory in battles against Huáinán.
(Mǎ Yīn was posthumously titled the Martial and Solemn King.)
Now I wish to use the forces of Lǎngzhōu to retake Húnán.
Is it possible?"
Lǎng said:
"I was in Jīnlíng for several years,
and saw all aspects of their governance.
The court has no worthy ministers,
the army has no good generals.
Loyalty and flattery are not distinguished,
rewards and punishments are inappropriate.
Under such circumstances,
it is fortunate the state still exists;
how could they have the leisure to annex others?
I request to serve as your vanguard.
Taking Húnán will be as easy as picking up a mustard seed!"
Kuí was pleased,
and treated him generously.
2. On the Rénxū day,
50,000 laborers from the Kāifēng Prefecture were conscripted to repair the walls of Dàliáng,
and the work was completed in ten days.
3. Mùróng Yànchāo mobilized local militia to enter the city,
diverted the Sì River water to fill the moat,
as preparation for offense and defense;
he also gave many banners and flags to the various garrison commanders,
ordering them to recruit bandits,
plunder neighboring territories,
and everywhere reported his rebellious actions.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
an edict was issued that Yí and Mì prefectures would no longer be subordinate to the Tàiníng Army.
This was to first take control of his patrol jurisdictions to weaken Mùróng Yànchāo.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
To campaign against Yànchāo,
the Zhāowǔ Army,
Lìzhōu,
belonged to Shǔ,
so Cáo Yīng held the title in name only.
The Imperial City Commissioner Xiàng Xùn of Hénèi was appointed as the Army Supervisor.
Xiàng
is a surname.
Originally, from the branch of Duke Wén of Sòng of the Yīn-Shāng, Xiàng Wéngàn,
his grandson Shù took his grandfather's courtesy name as his surname.
According to my examination of the "Zuǒzhuàn" from the Spring and Autumn period,
Xiàng Shù
was a descendant of Duke Huán of Sòng.
Xiàng,
pronounced shì liàng fān.
Jiān,
pronounced gǔ xián fān.
The Emperor, considering Yuánfú a veteran general,
(Yào Yuánfú had served Táng, Hàn, and Jìn,
and had achievements as a general.)
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Both men treated him as a father.
The ruler of Táng dispatched five thousand troops,
stationing them at Xiàpī,
to support Yǎn Chāo;
upon hearing that Zhōu troops were about to arrive,
they retreated and encamped at Shùyáng.
Xiàpī County,
belonged to Xúzhōu,
located a hundred lǐ southeast to Shùyáng County.
Liú Xù said: Shùyáng,
was the Hàn dynasty's Lǐnqiū County,
renamed Shùyáng in the Later Wèi,
and belonged to Hǎizhōu in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is one hundred and eighty lǐ southwest of Hǎizhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Shùyáng County of Hǎizhōu,
was the territory of Hàn's Yuánqiū County,
with Tóngyáng Commandery established there by the Liáng.
Shù,
is pronounced shí yù fān.
They heavily defeated the Táng troops,
killing and drowning over a thousand men,
and captured their general Yān Jìngquán.
Initially,
Yǎn Chāo, believing the Zhōu house was newly established,
thought it easily shaken,
so he summoned Běi Hàn and the Qìdān from the north,
and enticed the Táng people from the south,
to invade the border regions,
hoping the court would be too busy responding to emergencies,
and then he would act taking advantage of the situation.
After Běi Hàn and the Qìdān retreated north from Jìnzhōu,
and Táng troops were defeated at Shùyáng,
Yǎn Chāo's momentum was thus thwarted.
Yǒngxīng military governor Lǐ Hóngxìn,
considering himself a close relative of the Hàn house,
felt uneasy in his heart,
Lǐ Hóngxìn,
was a distant cousin of the Hàn Empress Dowager Lǐ.
While Wáng Jùn was in Shǎn,
under the pretext of rescuing Jìnzhōu,
he mobilized several hundred of his troops.
After the Běi Hàn troops fled,
he sent over a thousand imperial guards to garrison Cháng'ān;
Hóngxìn became fearful,
and thus entered the court.
4 On Rénshēn,
Wáng Jùn returned from Jìnzhōu,
and had an audience.
5 Cáo Yīng and others arrived at Yǎnzhōu,
setting up a long siege.
Mùróng Yǎn Chāo repeatedly came out to fight,
but Yào Yuánfú defeated him each time,
so Yǎn Chāo dared not venture out again.
After more than ten days,
the long siege was completed,
and they then launched an assault.
Initially,
when Yǎn Chāo was about to rebel,
his administrative assistant Cuī Zhōudù admonished him, saying:
"Lǔ,
is a state of poetry and books,
since Bóqín, it has never been able to dominate the feudal lords,
yet by upholding ritual and righteousness,
it can endure for generations.
Your Lordship holds no personal grievance against the state,
why harbor suspicions yourself!
Moreover, the sovereign has earnestly and thoroughly instructed and enlightened,
if you dismantle your defenses and submit sincerely,
then you can sit and enjoy the security of Mount Tài.
Have you not seen what ultimately became of Dù Zhōnglìng, Ān Xiāngyáng, and Lǐ Hézhōng!"
Dù Zhōnglìng,
refers to Dù Chóngwēi,
Ān Xiāngyáng,
refers to Ān Cóngjìn,
Lǐ Hézhōng,
refers to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn,
all of whom rebelled and were defeated and died,
events all recorded in previous annals.
When the government troops besieged the city,
Yǎn Chāo requisitioned the wealth of the soldiers and civilians to supply the army,
and many were executed for sitting on hidden wealth.
Former Shǎnzhōu military administrator Yán Hónglǔ,
was the son of Yán Bǎo,
Yán Bǎo betrayed Liáng and submitted to Táng,
and served as a military governor.
He offered all his family wealth,
but Yǎn Chāo still suspected he had hidden more,
and ordered Zhōudù to search his house.
Zhōudù said to Hónglǔ:
"Your life or death,
depends on the abundance or scarcity of your wealth,
you should hold nothing back."
Hónglǔ tearfully bowed to his wives and concubines, saying:
"Bring out everything to save my life."
They all said:
"It is all exhausted!"
Zhōudù reported this to Yǎn Chāo,
but Yǎn Chāo did not believe it,
and arrested Hónglǔ and his wife, imprisoning them.
A wet nurse found a gold bracelet in the mud,
and presented it,
hoping to ransom her master.
Yǎn Chāo said:
"What he has
hidden must still be plentiful."
He had Hónglǔ and his wife flogged,
until their flesh rotted and they died.
Accusing Zhōudù of shielding them,
he had him beheaded in the marketplace.
6 Běi Hàn sent troops to raid Fǔzhōu,
but defense commissioner Shé Déyǐ defeated them,
killing over two thousand men.
In the second month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Déyǐ reported capturing Běi Hàn's Kělán Army,
and garrisoned troops there.
Old Tángshū Geography Treatise says: Lángǔ County of Lánzhōu,
was the old Kělán Army,
located in the northern boundary of Yífāng County, Lánzhōu;
in the second year of Cháng'ān,
it was separated from Yífāng,
and Lángǔ County was established at the old Kělán Army site;
in the second year of Shénlóng,
the county was abolished,
and the army was established;
in the twelfth year of Kāiyuán, the county was re-established.
This was probably the army re-established by Later Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Kělán Army administered Lángǔ County,
located ninety lǐ south of Lánzhōu.
Kě,
is pronounced kū wǒ fān.
7 On Jiǎchén,
the Emperor released Yān Jìngquán and others, sending them back to Táng,
and said to the ruler of Táng:
"A treacherous minister,
is hated by all under heaven,
I did not expect the ruler of Táng to assist him,
could this be an unwise plan!"
The ruler of Táng was greatly ashamed,
and all the Central Plains people he had previously captured,
he treated with courtesy and returned them.
Táng officials who discussed affairs still proposed strategies for seizing the Central Plains,
but Secretariat Drafter Hán Xīzǎi said:
"Though the Guō house has ruled for a short time,
its governance is already solid,
if we rashly mobilize troops,
it will surely bring harm without benefit."
Since the time of Lièzǔ of Táng,
the Táng ruler Lǐ Shēng,
temple name Lièzǔ.
they wished to join with them to control the Central Plains,
exchanging gifts,
and swearing brotherhood.
However, the Qìdān coveted their goods,
and merely engaged in empty exchanges of words,
never truly aiding Táng.
The ruler of Táng was fond of literature,
so Xīzǎi and Féng Yánjǐ, Yánlǔ, Jiāng Wénwèi, Pān Yòu, Xú Xuàn, and their like all attained high office.
Yòu,
was from Yōuzhōu.
At that time, Táng's literary elegance surpassed that of other states,
yet it had never established imperial examinations,
often appointing officials based on memorials submitted discussing affairs.
At this time,
he first ordered Hanlin Academician Jiāng Wénwèi to oversee the examinations,
and Jìnshì Lúlíng's Wáng Kèzhēn and two others passed.
Lúlíng,
a Hàn dynasty county,
in Táng times was attached to Jízhōu.
Wèi,
is pronounced yū wù fān.
"How does your selection of scholars compare with the previous dynasty?"
He replied:
"The previous dynasty mixed public recommendation and private solicitation,
I solely rely on utmost impartiality!"
The ruler of Táng was pleased.
Secretariat Drafter Zhāng Wěi,
who had passed the examinations under the previous dynasty,
heard this and bore a grudge.
At the time, those in power had not come through the examinations,
and together they obstructed and slandered,
ultimately abolishing the examinations.
When Nán Táng abolished the examinations,
the Central States had not yet abolished them.
8 In the third month,
on Wùchén,
he appointed the Palace Reception Commissioner and Ēnzhōu militia commissioner, Jìnyáng's Zhèng Rénhuì, as Deputy Military Commissioner.
According to this, at that time the Central States had no Ēnzhōu,
this refers to Nán Hàn's Ēnzhōu,
Zhèng Rénhuì merely held the militia commissioner title remotely.
In the eighth year of Sòng Qìnglì,
after suppressing Wáng Zé,
Bèizhōu was renamed Ēnzhōu,
and to distinguish it, the Ēnzhōu in Lǐngnán was renamed Nán'ēnzhōu.
9 On Jiǎxū,
the Wēishèng Army was renamed the Wǔshèng Army.
Previously, Dèngzhōu was the Wēishèng Army,
now it was renamed to avoid the Emperor's personal name.
10 The Tang ruler appointed the Grand Protector of the Grand Younger Brother and Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, Féng Yánjǐ, as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
the former Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi, Xú Jǐngyùn, as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat,
and together with Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Sūn Shèng, all were made Participating Managers of Affairs with Equaling Authority.
After the edict was proclaimed,
the Minister of Revenue Cháng Mèngxī loudly declared in the midst of the crowd:
"The white hemp paper edict is excellent,
but it is not as good as Jiāng Wénwèi's memorial!"
(Jiāng Wénwèi's memorial is seen in the 287th scroll, in the twelfth year of the Hàn Tiānfú era.)
He said to others:
"Golden cups and jade bowls,
are they used to store dog excrement!"
Féng Yánjǐ said to the Tang ruler:
"Your Majesty personally attends to all affairs,
therefore the chief ministers cannot fully utilize their talents,
this is why the way of governance has not been achieved!"
The Tang ruler then entrusted all governmental affairs to him,
merely approving memorials.
Soon, Yánjǐ was unable to diligently handle affairs,
documents were all left to be completed by petty clerks,
military matters were entrusted to border generals,
and before long,
governance became even more ineffective,
so the Tang ruler resumed personally reviewing them.
The Minister of Justice Xiāo Yǎn despised Yánjǐ's character,
and repeatedly submitted memorials attacking him.
It happened that Yán Yǎn was implicated for wrongly sentencing someone to death,
and Zhōng Mó, Lǐ Démíng and others insisted on having him executed.
Yánjǐ said:
"Yǎn mistakenly killed one woman,
you gentlemen believe he deserves death.
Yǎn is one of the Nine Ministers,
can he be mistakenly killed?"
He alone submitted a memorial stating:
"Yǎn has always had a reputation for integrity,
and the crime he is implicated in has already been covered by an amnesty,
he should be treated with leniency."
Yǎn was thus spared;
people also praised Yánjǐ for this.
Jǐngyùn was soon dismissed and made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
(Note: Since the Tang court had already established officials for the Grand Younger Brother,
there should not also be a Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent;
this should be examined.)
11 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day of the month, Bǐngxū,
there was a solar eclipse.
12 The Emperor, because Cáo Yīng and others had attacked Yǎnzhōu for a long time without success,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
issued an edict to personally campaign,
appointing Lǐ Gǔ as acting Capital Guardian of Dōngjīng and concurrently Administrator of Kāifēng Prefecture,
Zhèng Rénhuái as acting Grand Palace Metropolitan Patrol
and Inspector,
and also appointing the Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry Army Guō Chóng as acting Capital Metropolitan Patrol Inspector.
13 After the Tang ruler had conquered Húnán,
he dispatched his general Lǐ Jiànqī to garrison Yìyáng to plan against Lǎngzhōu,
and appointed the Administrator of Quánzhōu Zhāng Luán concurrently as Guìzhōu Pacification Commissioner to plan against Guìzhōu.
After a long time,
there was no success.
The Tang ruler said to Féng Yánjǐ and Sūn Shèng:
"The people of Chǔ sought respite with us,
(meaning the people of Húnán,
suffering under their ruler's tyrannical governance and harsh exactions, sought respite from the Táng.)
