This is not the way to meet their hopes for deliverance;
(The Book of Documents says: 'The later one brings deliverance.'
This means the people of Chǔ hoped the Táng would bring them rest, but the Táng instead raised military campaigns to weary them,
not meeting their hopes.
If the Tang ruler's words could be matched by actions,
not swayed by public opinion,
how could there be defeat later on!)
Should we withdraw the garrison from Yìyáng,
and bestow the command tally and ceremonial staff upon Liú Yán,
what do you think?"
Shèng believed it should be so.
(Should be so,
meaning it should be like this.)
Yánjǐ said: "We dispatched a deputy general and took Húnán,
startling all near and far;
now suddenly we have lost two-thirds,
gaining Tán but losing Lǎng and Guì,
(hence saying lost two-thirds.
Lost,
read as 'sàng'.)
I request to entrust border generals to observe the situation."
The Tang ruler then dispatched the Commander-in-Chief Hóu Xùn to lead five thousand troops from the Jízhōu route towards Quánzhōu,
to join forces with Zhāng Luán and attack Guìzhōu.
The Southern Hàn set ambushes in the mountain valleys;
when Luán and others first arrived at the city walls,
exhausted and weary,
ambushing troops rose from all sides,
troops from within the city came out and attacked them from both sides,
the Tang troops were greatly defeated,
Xùn died,
and Luán gathered several hundred scattered soldiers and fled back to Quánzhōu.
14 In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng;
on the day Wùchén,
he arrived at Yǎnzhōu.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Emperor sent someone to summon and instruct Mùróng Yànchāo,
but the people on the city walls spoke insolently;
on the day Gēngwǔ,
he ordered the various armies to attack.
Previously,
a diviner had deceived Yànchāo, saying:
"The star Zhènxíng has moved to Jiǎo and Kàng,
(Jiǎo and Kàng correspond to Yǎnzhōu's division,)
there is fortune below it."
Yànchāo then erected a shrine and prayed to it,
ordering all among the people to erect yellow streamers.
(The color of earth is yellow;
Yànchāo ordered streamers erected to match its color.
If the people's hearts are pleased, then Heaven's will is obtained;
if people are disloyal,
what use are apotropaic rituals!)
The government troops attacked the city urgently,
yet he still buried and hid treasures,
thus the people had no will to fight,
and generals and soldiers successively came out to surrender.
On the day Yǐhài,
the government troops captured the city.
Yànchāo was just then praying at the Zhènxíng shrine,
he led his troops in fierce battle,
but was not victorious,
then burned the Zhènxíng shrine,
and with his wife threw himself into a well and died;
his son Jìxūn fled,
was pursued and captured,
and killed.
The government troops plundered extensively,
nearly ten thousand people died in the city.
Initially,
when Yànchāo was about to rebel,
he recruited bandits and placed them under his command,
over two thousand came,
all were fierce and unruly from the mountains and forests,
but in the end they were of no use.
The Emperor wanted to execute all of Yǎnzhōu's generals and officials,
the Hanlin Academician Dòu Yí met with Féng Dào and Fàn Zhì,
and together with them reported to the Emperor, saying:
"They were all coerced into following."
He then pardoned them.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
he appointed the Academician of the Duānmíng Hall Yán Kàn as acting Administrator of Yǎnzhōu Affairs.
He pardoned
Yànchāo's partisans within the jurisdiction of Yǎnzhōu,
those in hiding were given a period of one month to voluntarily surrender,
and the relatives of those already executed were pardoned.
On the day Guǐwèi,
he demoted the Tàiníng Army to a Defense Prefecture.
(Because Mùróng Yànchāo occupied Yǎnzhōu and defied orders,
the military command was demoted to a Defense Prefecture.)
15 The retired Táng Minister of Works Lǐ Jiànxūn died.
As he was dying,
he admonished his family, saying:
"The affairs of the times are like this,
it is fortunate that I can die a natural death!
Do not mound earth or erect a stele,
let people cultivate the land above it,
to avoid it becoming a marker for excavation in the future."
When Jiāngnán fell,
(meaning when the Sòng pacified Jīnlíng.)
only Jiànxūn's grave site was unknown.
(Lǐ Jiànxūn knew the state's affairs were not right and his bones were able to be preserved in their burial place;
can this not be called wise!)
On the 16th day of the sixth month,
the first day of the month (yǐyǒu),
the Emperor went to Qūfù,
to pay homage at the temple of Confucius.
In ancient times, Shǎohào shì moved from Qióngsāng to Qūfù;
it was the residence of Bóqín, the Marquis of Lǔ,
the ruins of Shǎohào shì.
Yìng Shào said: Qūfù is within the city of Lǔ,
winding and extending seven or eight lǐ.
Liú Zhāo said: In Qūfù there is Quèlǐ,
where Confucius lived,
and later generations built a temple to Confucius.
Since the Táng dynasty,
Yǎnzhōu was governed from Xiáqiū,
and Qūfù became a subordinate county.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is forty lǐ east of the prefecture.
In the fifth year of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era of the Sòng dynasty,
Qūfù was renamed Xiānyuán County.
As he was about to bow,
his attendants said:
"Confucius,
was a minister's minister,
it is not appropriate for the Son of Heaven to bow to him."
The Emperor said:
"Confucius is the teacher of emperors and kings for a hundred generations,
how dare I not show respect!"
He then bowed.
He also bowed at the tomb of Confucius,
ordered the repair of the temple of Confucius,
and prohibited woodcutting in the forest of Confucius.
The temple of Confucius is located in the southwest corner of Qūfù city, at Quèlǐ.
The tomb of Confucius is north of Qūfù city on the Sì River,
one lǐ from the city,
the burial ground covers about one qǐng,
the mound is ten paces from north to south,
thirteen paces from east to west,
and twelve chǐ high.
In front there are tiles,
forming an altar for sacrifices,
six chǐ square,
level with the ground.
Within the cemetery there are over a hundred unusual trees,
all brought by his disciples from various regions,
planted in the cemetery,
which the people of Lǔ could not identify.
He appointed them as Magistrate of Qūfù and Registrar.
On bǐngxū,
the Emperor departed from Yǎnzhōu.
On the 17th, yǐwèi,
the Shùndé Grand Lady Wú of Wúyuè passed away.
On the 18th, dīngyǒu,
a great flood entered Chéngdū in Shǔ.
During the Qín period,
the governor of Shǔ, Lǐ Bīng, channeled two rivers through Chéngdū,
both navigable by boat.
The Jùnxiàn Zhì states: Lǐ Bīng excavated Líduī,
and opened two canals,
one passing from Yǒngkāng through Xīnfán into Chéngdū,
called the Outer River;
the other canal,
passing from Yǒngkāng through Pí into Chéngdū,
called the Inner River.
Before Gāo Pián built the Luó city wall,
both the Inner and Outer Rivers entered from the west of the city.
After Pián built the city wall,
he constructed the Mízǎo Weir to the northwest,
causing the Outer River to circle north of the city and flow east to Héjiāng,
while the Inner River followed south of the city and joined the Outer River to flow into the river.
The river comes from the west,
the terrain is high,
hence the flood disaster.
Over five thousand people drowned,
and four chambers of the Grand Temple were destroyed.
On wùxū,
Shǔ issued a great amnesty,
and provided relief to families affected by the flood.
On the 19th, jǐhài,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
He returned from Yǎnzhōu to Dàliáng.
The Shòufāng military commissioner and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, the Prince of Chénliú, Féng Huī, passed away.
His son, the Yánèi Dū Yúhòu Jìyè, killed his elder brother Jìxūn,
and took charge of the military government affairs himself.
Lǐ Tāo, the Crown Prince's Guest, had a younger brother, Huàn,
who served as a Qínzhèngdiàn Academician among the Qìdān,
and was on good terms with the Yōuzhōu military commissioner, Xiāo Hǎizhēn.
Hǎizhēn
was the brother-in-law of the Qìdān ruler, Wùyù.
Huàn persuaded Hǎizhēn to submit to the central dynasty,
and Hǎizhēn gladly agreed.
Huàn then had the spy from Dìngzhōu, Tián Zhòngbà, deliver a silk memorial to inform the court,
and also sent a letter to Tāo,
saying:
"The Qìdān ruler is childish and foolish,
devoted solely to feasting and pleasure,
with no long-term ambitions,
unlike his predecessors,
(predecessors,
referring to Ābǎojī, Déguāng, etc.)
we will surely overcome;
if not,
making peace,
we will surely succeed.
Both options benefit from speed,
considering the situation,
in the future they will ultimately be unable to effectively support Hédōng."
On rényín,
Zhòngbà arrived at Dàliáng,
but as the central dynasty was preoccupied with many matters,
they did not proceed with the plan.
The north did not obtain Yān and Yún,
the west did not obtain Hé, Shàn, Líng, and Xià,
which the Sòng people considered a regret for the ages.
Observing Wēn Gōng's account of this matter,
then at the beginning of the Yuányòu era, abandoning Mǐzhī and the other four strongholds,
they knew the strength of the central dynasty was insufficient.
On xīnhài,
Féng Jìyè was appointed as Shòufāng Liúhòu.
The Privy Councilor Wáng Jùn,
was by nature frivolous and impulsive,
full of schemes,
fond of power and profit,
and liked people to attach themselves to him.
He considered the empire his own responsibility.
Whenever he spoke on matters,
if the Emperor agreed he was pleased,
but if at times he did not consent,
Jùn would become angry and resentful,
often uttering disrespectful words;
the Emperor, because of their old friendship,
and because he had contributed to the founding of the dynasty,
(from the Emperor's entry from Yèdū into Biàn until his accession,
Wáng Jùn's contributions were many.)
often tolerated him.
Jùn was older than the Emperor,
and after the Emperor ascended the throne,
he still addressed him as elder brother,
or by his courtesy name,
and Jùn became increasingly arrogant because of this.
The Deputy Commissioner Zhèng Rénhuì, the Imperial City Commissioner Xiàng Xùn, and the Ēnzhōu Tuánliànshǐ Lǐ Chóngjìn,
were all trusted generals and aides of the Emperor when he was a military governor,
and after the Emperor ascended the throne,
they were gradually promoted and employed.
Jùn was jealous of them in his heart,
repeatedly submitting memorials claiming illness,
requesting to be relieved of his duties,
to test the Emperor's intentions.
The Emperor repeatedly sent attendants to urge and instruct him,
but Jùn's tone towards the envoys was haughty and severe.
He also sent letters to the military commissioners of various circuits seeking guarantees;
the various circuits each presented his letters,
and the Emperor was shocked and alarmed for a long time.
He again sent attendants to console and encourage him,
ordering him to attend to his duties,
and said:
"If you do not come,
I will personally go to you."
Still he did not come.
The Emperor knew that the Zhīshūmì Zhí Xuéshì Chén Guān was on good terms with Jùn,
and ordered him to convey his intentions.
Guān said:
"Your Majesty need only announce that you will visit his residence,
and Jùn will surely not dare not to come."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on wùzǐ,
Jùn came to court,
and the Emperor consoled and encouraged him, ordering him to attend to his duties.
Chóngjìn
was from Cāngzhōu,
his mother was the Emperor's sister, the Grand Princess Fúqìng.
Lǐ Gǔ slipped,
injuring his right arm,
and was on leave for over a month;
the Emperor, because Gǔ's duties were numerous and pressing,
urged him to come to court.
(On leave,
means on vacation.
Urge,
is read as cù.
Court,
is read as zhí yáo fān;
the same below.)
On guǐsì,
an edict exempted him from court attendance,
but ordered him to attend to his duties.
25. The Minister of Works of Shǔ, Guō Yánjūn, who was also the Military Commissioner of Wǔdé, treated the Military Supervisor Wáng Chéngpī disrespectfully.
Chéngpī plotted to start a rebellion.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
the Left Fèngshèng Capital Commandant Āncì Sūn Qīn
(Āncì County
belonged to Yōuzhōu.
Sūn Qīn was originally a man of Yān but served in Shǔ.)
went to bid farewell to Chéngpī.
Chéngpī invited him to go together to see the Prefectural Lord;
the Prefectural Lord
refers to Guō Yánjūn.
"Lord"
is an honorific title for a person;
the one respected in a prefecture,
thus called the Prefectural Lord.
He followed him.
When Chéngpī arrived,
he ordered his attendants to strike and kill Yánjūn,
slaughtering his family.
He claimed to be acting on an imperial edict to handle the military prefecture,
then opened the government storehouses to reward the soldiers,
released the prisoners,
and mobilized the garrison troops.
When all the officers had gathered,
Qīn said to Chéngpī:
"Now that Yánjūn has already been punished for his crimes,
you should produce the imperial edict to show the crowd."
Chéngpī said:
"I can bring you wealth and honor;
do not ask about the edict."
Qīn then realized that Chéngpī was rebelling.
He thus deceived him, saying:
"Now that internal and external affairs are not yet settled,
I request to lead my troops to patrol for you."
He then leaped onto his horse and rode out.
Chéngpī repeatedly called after him,
but he did not stop.
Qīn returned to camp,
enlightened his troops,
led them into the prefectural headquarters,
and attacked Chéngpī.
Chéngpī's attendants wanted to resist,
but Qīn shouted at them,
and they all abandoned their weapons and fled.
He then captured Chéngpī,
beheaded him,
along with his close associates,
and sent their heads to Chéngdū.
26. The Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng and concurrently Secretariat Director Gāo Xíngzhōu died.
Xíngzhōu was brave and understood righteousness,
had high achievements but was not arrogant.
When he rode his horse to face the enemy,
his shouts stirred the wind.
In daily life, when feasting with guests and subordinates,
he was dignified yet amiable,
and people respected him for this.
27. On the Guǐmǎo day,
the ruler of Shǔ sent the Commissioner of Diplomatic Reception Zhào Jìzhá to Zǐzhōu
to console and pacify the officials and people,
because they had just experienced the rebellion of Wáng Chéngpī.
28. Under the Hàn law,
those who violated the salt and yeast monopolies,
regardless of the amount, were sentenced to death.
A commoner from Zhèngzhōu had received salt from the government as payment for house tax.
When passing through the prefectural city,
the officials considered it private salt,
seized and killed him;
his wife appealed the injustice.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
an edict was first issued stipulating that punishments for salt and yeast violations would vary according to the weight.
At that time, an imperial order specified punishments for various salt and yeast violations:
for violations involving one jin or less down to one liǎng,
eighty strokes with the cane,
and penal servitude;
for more than one jin but less than five jin,
three years of imprisonment;
for five jin or more,
a severe beating,
and execution.
Punctuated by Róng Zàozǔ, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial order
Later
In the second year of Guǎngshùn (Rénzǐ, 952)
1. In the ninth month,
on the first day, Jiǎyín,
the Chancellor of Wúyuè, Péi Jiān, died.
The Prefect of Táizhōu, Wú Yánfú, was appointed to jointly participate in the affairs of the Chancellor's Office.
2. On the Gēngwǔ day,
an imperial order was issued forbidding officials and people in the northern border regions from entering the territory of the Qìdān to capture and plunder.
3. The Qìdān general Gāo Móhàn crossed the Húlú River using reed rafts to invade.
The Húlú River
lies between Shēnzhōu and Jìzhōu,
stretching for several hundred li.
Dīng Dù said: The Húlú River
is another name for Héngzhāng.
The Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, Hé Fújìn, sent the Longjié Capital Commandant Liú Chénghuì and others to station at Bèizhōu to resist them.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Bèizhōu
is 120 li north to Jìzhōu.
They hastily led their troops north across the river;
the several hundred strong men from Jìzhōu who had been captured by the Qìdān,
upon seeing the government troops,
clamored in unison,
wanting to attack the Qìdān.
The government troops did not dare to respond,
and the Qìdān killed them all.
4. The Military Commissioner of Shǔ's Shānnán Xīdào, Lǐ Tíngguī, reported that the Zhōu were gathering troops in Guānzhōng,
and requested additional troops for defense.
The ruler of Shǔ sent the Capital Inspector of the Imperial Guard, Zhào Jìn, to lead troops toward Lìzhōu.
Later, upon hearing that the Zhōu were gathering troops to prepare against the Northern Hàn,
he withdrew his troops.
5. The Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān of the Táng, Biān Hào,
was dim-witted, cowardly, and indecisive.
In Húnán,
governance came from multiple authorities,
and he did not win the hearts of the people.
Ōuyáng Guǎng from Jíshuǐ submitted a memorial,
(Jíshuǐ
was the ancient territory of Jíyáng County,
long abandoned.
The Táng established Jíshuǐ County,
belonging to Jízhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 40 li northeast of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: In the tenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Jíyáng County was abolished and merged into Lúlíng County.
In the Dàyè era, eleven villages east of the water in Lúlíng County were separated to form Jíshuǐ County.)
stating: "Hào is not a talent for generalship;
he will surely lose Húnán.
We should select another capable commander
and increase troops to rescue from defeat."
There was no response.
The ruler of Táng ordered Hào to manage Lǎngzhōu.
Those who came from Lǎngzhōu
mostly said that Liú Yán was loyal and obedient,
so Hào did not make preparations.
The ruler of Táng summoned Liú Yán to court,
but Yán did not go.
He said to Wáng Kuí:
"The Táng will surely attack us;
what should we do?"
Kuí said:
"Wǔlíng relies on the natural barriers of rivers and lakes.
(Lǎngzhōu
is Wǔlíng Commandery.)
How can we fold our hands and submit to others!
Biān Hào governs without proper methods,
and the officials and people do not support him.
He can be captured in one battle."
Yán hesitated and could not decide.
Zhōu Xíngféng said:
"Military affairs value speed;
if we delay, they will make preparations,
and we cannot succeed."
Yán then appointed Kuí, Xíngféng, and the subordinate generals Hé Jìngzhēn, Zhāng Fǎng, Pú Gōngyì, Zhū Quánxiù,
Yǔwén Qióng, Péng Wànhé, Pān Shūsì, and Zhāng Wénbiǎo—ten men in total—as commandants,
and assigned them to mobilize troops.
Shūsì and Wénbiǎo
were both from Lǎngzhōu.
Xíngféng was skilled in strategy,
Wénbiǎo excelled in battle,
and Shūsì was decisive and brave.
The three often relied on each other for success,
and their relationship was very close.
The generals wanted to summon the tribal chieftain of Xùzhōu, Fú Yàntōng, for support.
Xíngféng said:
"The barbarians are greedy and without righteousness.
The year before last, they followed Mǎ Xī'è into Tánzhōu
and burned and looted everything.
(This event is recorded in the 289th volume, in the third year of Qiányòu of the Hàn Emperor Yǐndì.)
They go wherever they cannot be defeated.
Why use such people,
allowing them to brutally harm the common people!"
They then stopped.
However, they also feared that Yàntōng would become a future threat.
Since the tribal chieftain and local militia commandant Liú Táo was feared by the Yáo barbarians,
he was appointed as the Western Border Defense Commander to guard against them.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wáng Kuí and others led troops in separate routes towards Chángshā.
They appointed Sūn Lǎng and Cáo Jìn as vanguard commanders.
Sūn Lǎng and Cáo Jìn fled to Lǎngzhōu.
See the first month of this year in the previous scroll.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Wáng Kuí and others captured Yuánjiāng,
capturing the regional inspector Liú Chéngyù.
The deputy general Lǐ Shīdé led five hundred of his troops and surrendered to them.
On the Rénchén day,
Wáng Kuí and others ordered their soldiers to hold up small boats to shield themselves,
heading directly to Yìyáng,
and entered the camp from all sides by chopping through the stockade,
thus capturing it,
killing two thousand garrison soldiers.
Biān Hào urgently reported to the Táng.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Wáng Kuí and others captured Qiáokǒu and Xiāngyīn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: There is a Qiáokǒu town in Chángshā County, Tánzhōu.
On the Yǐwèi day,
they reached Tánzhōu.
Biān Hào defended the city walls and held out;
reinforcements had not arrived,
and the troops in the city were few.
On the Bǐngshēn night,
Biān Hào abandoned the city and fled,
and both officials and civilians scattered in disarray.
The bridge at the Lǐlíng Gate collapsed.
The Lǐlíng Gate
is the east gate of Tánzhōu city.
Collapsed,
meaning it broke and overturned.
The prefect of Dàozhōu, Liào Yǎn, was killed by the disorderly troops.
At dawn on the Dīngyǒu day,
Wáng Kuí entered the city,
proclaiming himself Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng and acting administrator of the military prefecture.
"Wǔpíng"
should be
"Wǔ'ān".
The military prefecture
refers to the military prefecture of Tánzhōu.
He sent Jìng Zhēn and others to pursue Biān Hào,
but they did not catch up,
and beheaded five hundred men.
Pú Gōngyì attacked Yuèzhōu.
The Fēngsú Tōng states: In the Hàn dynasty, there was a Chamberlain Pú Chāng.
Also, the Jìnshū Zǎijì records: The ancestor of the Dí chieftain Pú Hóng
had rushes growing in his family pond,
which grew to fifty feet long,
shaped like bamboo.
At that time, people all called them
"the Pú family",
and thus they took it as their surname.
Later, they changed their surname to Fú.
Thus, the origin of the surname Pú has two sources.
Liú Yán appointed Pú Gōngyì as acting prefect of Yuèzhōu.
The Táng generals guarding the various prefectures in Húnán,
upon hearing that Chángshā had fallen,
fled one after another.
Liú Yán completely recovered the former territory of the Mǎ family north of the mountains,
except for Chēn and Lián, which were taken by the Southern Hàn.
6. In the Qìdān territories of Yíng, Mò, and Yōuzhōu, there was a great flood.
Refugees entering the passes and scattered throughout Héběi numbered several hundred thousand people.
The Qìdān prefectures and counties did not prohibit them.
An edict was issued ordering the local authorities to provide relief and settle them.
Among the Central Plains people who had previously been captured,
five or six out of ten were able to return.
7. On the Dīngwèi day,
Gǔ, due to a long-unhealed arm illness—
Lǐ Gǔ's arm illness began in the sixth month of this year in the previous scroll—
"Gǔ"
must have
"Lǐ"
above it
for the text to be clear.
[Chapter note: The twelve-line edition correctly has
"Lǐ"
character;
the Kǒng edition is the same;
the Xióng collation states that the Sòng edition does not have
"Lǐ"
character,
but it is unknown which Sòng edition this is based on.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to convey his intention, saying:
"Your responsibilities are extremely important—
referring to Lǐ Gǔ's management of the Three Departments' finances and grain—
if your duties can be accomplished,
why must you attend court rituals!
I will now await you in the informal hall,
you may come in briefly for an audience."
Gǔ entered and had an audience at the Jīnxiáng Hall,
personally expressing his sincerity;
the Emperor did not permit it.
Gǔ had no choice but to resume his duties.
Gǔ was unable to hold a brush,
so an edict was issued stating that due to the heavy workload of the Three Departments,
he was ordered to have a name seal carved and use it.
8. On the Xīnhài day,
an imperial decree stated:
"If the people have lawsuits,
they must first go through the county, prefecture, and observation commissioner for judgment.
If they are not satisfied,
then they may bring their case to
the central departments.
If they are unable to write the petition themselves,
and ask someone else to write it for them,
they must write the name and residence of the person asked.
If there is no one to ask,
they are allowed to submit plain paper.
The lawsuit must concern their own affairs;
they are not allowed to lodge lawsuits on behalf of others out of personal motives."
9. The prefect of Qìngzhōu, Guō Yànqīn, was greedy by nature.
The Yějī tribe had many sheep and horses.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The Dǎngxiàng Yějī tribe
lived north of Qìngzhōu.
The Yějī tribe then rebelled,
plundering merchant convoys.
The Emperor ordered Níngzhōu and Huánzhōu to combine their forces to suppress them.
The Táng established Wēizhōu at the ancient Míngshā location,
and the Zhōu changed it to Huánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Níngzhōu is 120 lǐ north to Qìngzhōu;
Huánzhōu is 180 lǐ south to Qìngzhōu.
10. Liú Yán sent an envoy to report,
stating:
"Húnán has served the court for generations,
but unfortunately was invaded by a neighboring enemy—
neighboring enemy,
referring to the Táng—
so we gathered righteous troops,
and pacified the old territory."
Meaning they pacified the old territory of the Chǔ in Húnán.
The Táng sovereign stripped Biān Hào of his official titles and ranks,
and exiled him to Ráozhōu.
Initially,
Biān Hào, as the capital patrol commissioner, followed Chá Wénhuī in capturing Jiànzhōu.
This event is recorded in the 285th scroll, in the second year of the Kāiyùn era of the Jìn Prince of Qí,
which was the third year of the Bǎodà era of the Táng sovereign.
The people of Jiàn called him
"Biān the Buddha-child".
When he captured Tánzhōu,
the markets did not change their shops,
as recorded in the first scroll of the previous year,
which was the ninth year of the Bǎodà era of the Táng.
"Biān the Bodhisattva".
Later, when he became military commissioner,
his administration lacked discipline,
and he only held daily vegetarian feasts,
extensively conducting Buddhist ceremonies.
The people of Tán were disappointed,
and called him
"Biān the Monk"
instead.

The Left Vice Director of the Chancellery with the title of Tongpingzhangshi Féng Yánjǐ and the Right Vice Director of the Chancellery with the title of Tongpingzhangshi Sūn Chéng submitted memorials requesting punishment;
both were pardoned.
Sūn Chéng repeatedly pleaded for punishment,
so he and Féng Yánjǐ were both dismissed from their additional posts and retained only their original official titles.
The Táng sovereign, because military campaigns in recent years had been unsuccessful,
then discussed resting the troops and giving the people respite.
Someone said:
"If Your Majesty refrains from using troops for several decades,
we can achieve modest prosperity!"
The Táng sovereign said:
"I intend to refrain from using troops for my entire lifetime,
why only several decades!"
People are not made of metal or stone;
did the Táng sovereign truly believe he could enjoy boundless longevity!
However, just as he wished to refrain from using troops for his entire lifetime,
the Zhōu troops had already reached the Huái River.
He was appointed magistrate of his home county.
Because Ōuyáng Guǎng had said that Biān Hào would certainly be defeated,
his words proved true.
11. In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
the Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì, Shé Cóngruǎn, was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Jìngnán.
Shé Cóngruǎn moved from Shǎnzhōu to Bīnzhōu.
Nán,
is pronounced nǎi dàn fān;
the same below.
On the Guǐyǒu day (the 12th),
an imperial edict was issued:
"Regarding the cowhides submitted annually by the common people,
reduce the quota by two-thirds;
for every ten qǐng of farmland,
tax one hide.
The remainder may be used or traded by the people themselves,
but selling them to enemy states is strictly prohibited."
Previously,
since the outbreak of military conflicts,
private trading of cowhides had been banned,
with all hides required to be submitted to the government for compensation.
During the reign of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng,
officials only compensated with salt;
in the Tiānfú era of the Later Jìn,
even salt was no longer provided.
Under the laws of the Later Hàn,
anyone found trading even an inch of cowhide privately would face the death penalty.
However, cowhides were indispensable for daily use among the people.
The Emperor had long been aware of these abuses,
and at this time,
Lǐ Gǔ proposed
distributing the burden equally based on farmland,
which benefited both the state and the people.
On the 13th day of the twelfth month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
the Yellow River breached at Zhèngzhōu and Huázhōu,
and envoys were dispatched to inspect and oversee repairs.
On the Jiǎwǔ day (the 14th),
the former Jìngnán military governor Hóu Zhāng offered a thousand bolts of silk and five hundred taels of silver for a banquet.
The Emperor refused to accept them,
saying:
"When feudal lords come to pay homage to the Son of Heaven,
they should be feasted and rewarded—
how can this depend on purchasing it?
During the Five Dynasties period,
not only did regional governors purchase banquets upon entering the court,
but in the second year of the Tiānchéng era of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng, in the third month,
when the emperor visited the Huìjié Garden,
his ministers also purchased a banquet.
Thus, even court officials purchased banquets.
The term 'reward' (kào)
is pronounced kǔ dào fān.
All such offerings were refused."
Wáng Kuí led troops and fifty thousand cave barbarians to attack Chēnzhōu.
The Southern Hàn general Pān Chóngchè came to its aid
and encountered them at Háo Shí.
Háo Shí
is located in Yìzhāng County, Chēnzhōu.
The character '蠔' (háo)
is pronounced háo.
He said:
"They are weary and disorganized—
they can be defeated."
He launched an attack
and routed them decisively,
leaving corpses strewn across eighty lǐ.
The Hanlin academician Xú Táifú requested the execution of Gé Yányù and Lǐ Chéng, who had falsely accused Lǐ Sōng.
The false accusation against Lǐ Sōng is recorded in the 288th volume, in the first year of the Qiányòu era of the Later Hàn.
Xú Táifú had long been on good terms with Lǐ Sōng,
hence he pleaded for the execution of the false accusers.
The request was not granted.
Wáng Jùn admired Xú Táifú's sense of justice,
and reported it to the Emperor.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Yányù and Chéng were arrested
and executed.
Liú Yán submitted a memorial stating that Tánzhōu was devastated,
requesting to move the administrative seat to Lǎngzhōu,
and asking to present tribute and sell tea
according to the precedents set by the Mǎ family.
This was approved.
The Chǔ king Mǎ Xī'è, the Jiāngxī observation commissioner of the Southern Táng, came to court.
The Southern Táng ruler detained him,
and several years later,
he died in Jīnlíng,
posthumously honored as Gōngxiào.
Earlier,
the local magnate Yáng Xìn of Línzhōu had appointed himself prefect,
receiving recognition from the Later Zhōu.
After Xìn's death,
his son Chóngxùn succeeded him.
A textual note states:
"Chóngxùn"
is sometimes written as
"Chóngxūn."
The Shízōng Shílù records it as
"Chóngxùn,"
likely because he later changed his name to avoid the taboo of Prince Liáng Zōngxùn.
According to the textual note,
"Chóngxùn"
should be written as
"Chóngxùn."
At this time,
he was besieged by the Qiāng tribes,
and once again pledged allegiance,
seeking aid from Xiàzhōu and Fǔzhōu.
Xiàzhōu was under Lǐ Yíyīn;
Fǔzhōu was under Shé Déyǐ.
The Jiǔyù Zhì records: Línzhōu
is 120 lǐ northwest to Xiàzhōu,
and 120 lǐ northeast to Fǔzhōu.
In spring,
the first month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
Liú Yán, the acting military commissioner of Wǔpíng, was appointed as the military commissioner of Wǔpíng,
with authority over military affairs in Wǔ'ān, Jìngjiāng, and other regions, and granted the title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Wáng Kuí was appointed as the military commissioner of Wǔ'ān,
Hé Jìngzhēn as the military commissioner of Jìngjiāng,
and Zhōu Xíngféng as the行军司马 of Wǔ'ān.
After Wáng Kuí gained control of Tánzhōu,
he killed Hé Jìngzhēn;
after killing Hé Jìngzhēn,
he attacked Liú Yán and annexed Lǎngzhōu.
An edict was issued to Shé Cóngruǎn:
"If the Yějī tribe can reform,
grant them official positions and bestow gold and silk.
Otherwise, advance troops to subdue them."
On the Rénxū day,
Cóngruǎn reported:
"Apart from the chieftain Lǐ Wànquán and others who received the edict and swore allegiance,
the remainder still refuse to submit,
and we are preparing to attack them."
In earlier times, military agricultural colonies were all established in border regions,
with garrison soldiers farming them.
By the end of the Táng dynasty,
with troops stationed in the Central Plains,
agricultural colonies were set up everywhere to cultivate wasteland;
later, wealthy households were recruited to pay taxes and farm the land.
The Ministry of Revenue established a separate office to oversee this,
not subordinate to prefectures or counties.
Some households had many laborers but no corvée duties,
while others harbored criminals,
and local authorities could not investigate them.
When Liáng Tàizǔ attacked Huáinán,
he seized thousands upon thousands of oxen,
as recorded in the 265th volume, in the first year of the Tiānyòu era of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng.
These oxen were made to pay annual rent.
For decades thereafter,
even after the oxen died, the rent was not abolished,
causing great hardship for the people.
The Emperor had long been aware of these abuses.
When the Gé mén shǐ and acting prefect of Qīngzhōu, Zhāng Níng, submitted a proposal,
requesting the abolition of the agricultural colonies,
and Lǐ Gǔ also spoke in favor,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
an edict was issued:
"Abolish all agricultural colonies under the Ministry of Revenue,
and place the people under the jurisdiction of prefectures and counties.
The farmland, houses, oxen, and farming tools
shall all be granted to the current tenants as permanent property,
and all ox-rent taxes are abolished."
That year,
the Ministry of Revenue registered over thirty thousand additional households.
Once the people obtained permanent property,
they dared to repair houses and plant trees,
reaping several times the previous benefits from the land.
Some suggested:
"Some of the agricultural colony lands are fertile—
why not sell them
to raise hundreds of thousands of strings of cash for the state?"
The Emperor replied:
"If the people benefit,
it is as if the state benefits.
What would I do with such money?"
The prefect of Láizhōu, Yè Rénlǔ,
was an old subordinate of the Emperor.
Regarding Yè Rénlǔ,
he was a trusted general of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Later Hàn.
In the twelfth year of the Tiānfú era,
he once defeated the Khitans at Chéngtiān Army.
Now, as an old subordinate of the Emperor,
he must have served under him in the Bureau of Military Affairs,
or during the campaigns against Hézhōng or while garrisoning Yèdū.
He accepted a bribe of a thousand strings of cash.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
he was ordered to commit suicide.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to bestow wine and food upon him, saying:
"You have brought this upon yourself by violating the law of the state.
There is nothing I can do!
I will care for your mother."
Rénlǔ wept in gratitude.
The Emperor was troubled by the Yellow River breach,
and Wáng Jùn volunteered to inspect it in person.
This was approved.
The Zhènníng military commissioner, Guō Róng, repeatedly requested to come to court.
Jùn, wary of his talent and integrity,
often obstructed him.
In the intercalary month,
Róng again requested to come to court.
As Jùn was away at the river,
the Emperor granted permission.
6 The Khitan invaded Dìngzhōu,
besieging the Yìfēng Army,
at that time the Yìfēng Army was stationed in Yìfēng County of Dìngzhōu.
They suffered heavy losses,
and the Khitan fled.
They also invaded Zhènzhōu,
but were driven off by the local troops.
7 On Bǐngshēn,
Zhènníng Military Commissioner Guō Róng came to court.
Mǎ Quányì, a former cavalryman under Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, accompanied Guō Róng to court.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience,
appointed him as a Palace Front Commandant,
and said to his attendants:
"Quányì was loyal to his master;
in the past at Hézhōng,
he repeatedly thwarted our armies,"
referring to the period of Hàn Qiányòu,
when the Emperor was campaigning against Lǐ Màozhēn.
Wáng Jùn, hearing that Guō Róng had come to court,
hurried back from the river,
and on Wùxū,
arrived at Dàliáng.
8 Zhāngwǔ Military Commissioner Gāo Yǔnquán died.
His son, Yá'nèi Commandant Gāo Shàojī, plotted to inherit his father's position.
He falsely claimed that Yǔnquán was ill,
and submitted a memorial stating that he himself was managing the military prefecture's affairs.
Observation Judge Lǐ Bīn earnestly remonstrated,
Shàojī became angry,
and executed him.
On Xīnwèi,
he reported that Bīn had plotted rebellion.
9 Wáng Jùn persistently requested to be granted a military governorship.
The Emperor had no choice,
and
appointed Jùn to concurrently serve as Pínglú Military Commissioner.
10 Gāo Shàojī repeatedly memorialized about various barbarians invading the border,
hoping to secure the inheritance.
The Emperor sent the Six Residences Commissioner Zhāng Rénqiān to Yánzhōu for an inspection tour.
The *Zhíguān Fēnjì* states: The Táng established the Ten Residences and Six Residences Commissioners,
named after the residences of the various princes,
sometimes collectively called the Sixteen Residences,
later simply called the Six Residences.
Only then did he begin the mourning period for his father.
11 On Wùshēn,
Shé Cóngruǎn reported the surrender of twenty-one tribes of Yějī.
12 A commoner of the Táng, Shào Táng, submitted a statement:
Commoners without court appointments
are called "cǎozé" (grass and marshes).
"Shàng"
is pronounced "shí zhǎng fān."
"Recently traveling in Huáishàng,
I heard that the Zhōu ruler is respectful and frugal,
and is enhancing virtuous governance.
Our troops were recently defeated at Tán and Lǎng,"
referring to Biān Hào's defeat at Tánzhōu.
"We should make preparations."
Men of wisdom and knowledge—
what state lacks them!
It only depends on whether they are employed or not.
13 Earlier,
after Wáng Kuí gained control of Tánzhōu,
as seen in the tenth month of the previous scroll.
Zhū Quánxiù served as Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān,
Zhāng Wénbiǎo as Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng,
and Zhōu Xíngféng as Military Commander of Wǔ'ān.
Hé Jìngzhēn and Zhū Quánxiù each maintained their own personal troops,
and shared the hall with Kuí to conduct affairs,
so officials and people did not know whom to follow.
At banquets and gatherings,
the various generals indulged in drinking,
brawling like a marketplace,
with no distinction between superior and subordinate.
Only Xíngféng and Wénbiǎo served Kuí with full propriety,
and Kuí was fond of them.
Jìngzhēn was at odds with Kuí,
resigned, and returned to Lǎngzhōu.
Yet he also could not serve Liú Yán,
and plotted rebellion with Quánxiù.
Yán had always been wary of Kuí's strength,
suspected that Kuí had sent Jìngzhēn to spy on him,
and was about to attack him.
Kuí heard of this,
and was greatly alarmed.
Xíngféng said:
"Liú Yán has never been of one mind with us.
Hé Jìngzhēn and Zhū Quánxiù are ashamed to be beneath you.
You should deal with them early."
Kuí was pleased and said:
"Together we will eliminate the villainous faction,
and jointly govern Tán and Lǎng."
Zhōu Xíngféng's seizure of Tán and Lǎng
began from this point.
"Zhì"
is pronounced "zhí zhī fān."
Just then, the Southern Hàn invaded Quán, Dào, and Yǒngzhōu.
Xíngféng requested:
"I will go personally to Lǎngzhōu to persuade Yán,
to send Jìngzhēn and Quánxiù south to campaign,
the southern campaign being
to resist the Southern Hàn troops.
Then we can capture them by stratagem,
as easily as something in the palm of the hand."
Kuí agreed.
Xíngféng went to Lǎngzhōu.
Yán appointed Jìngzhēn as Southern Front Field Commandant,
and Quánxiù as Vanguard Commander,
leading over a hundred personal troops to join the Tánzhōu forces in defending against the Southern Hàn.
The two men arrived at Chángshā.
Kuí went out to the suburbs to welcome them,
they met with great cordiality,
feasting and drinking for several days,
often using beautiful singing girls to entice them,
so Jìngzhēn lingered and did not advance.
Lǎngzhōu Commandant Lǐ Zhòngqiān had long been garrisoned at Tánzhōu with three thousand troops.
Jìngzhēn ordered him to set out first,
heading toward Lǐngběi.
Quán, Dào, and Yǒngzhōu are all north of the Dàyǔ Ridge.
"Qù"
is pronounced "qī yù fān."
He forced Zhòngqiān to return to Lǎngzhōu.
Kuí took advantage of Jìngzhēn's drunkenness,
had someone pretend to be a messenger from Yán,
and rebuked Jìngzhēn, saying:
"The southern invaders have penetrated deeply,
yet you do not urgently defend against them but instead devote yourself to wild feasting.
The Grand Tutor orders you to be shackled and returned to the Western Prefecture."
The Grand Tutor
refers to Liú Yán.
The Lǎng prefecture is west of Tánzhōu,
hence called the Western Prefecture.
Quánxiù fled,
and troops were sent to pursue and capture him.
In the second month,
on the first day Xīnhài,
Jìngzhēn was executed and his head displayed.
Not long after,
Quánxiù and more than ten of his accomplices were captured,
and all were executed.
14 On Guǐchǒu,
Zhènníng Military Commissioner Guō Róng returned to Chánzhōu.
The Privy Councilor, Military Commissioner of Pínglú, and Tongpingzhangshi Wáng Jùn,
in his later years became increasingly arrogant and impetuous.
He petitioned to have the Duanmingdian Academician Yǎn Kàn
and the Privy Council Academician Chén Guān replace Fàn Zhì and Lǐ Gǔ as chancellors.
The Emperor said:
"The appointment and dismissal of chief ministers
cannot be done hastily;
wait for me to consider it further."
Jùn forcefully argued his case,
and his language gradually became disrespectful.
As the day approached noon,
the Emperor had not yet eaten.
Jùn continued to argue relentlessly.
The Emperor said:
"It is currently the Cold Food Festival;
wait until the holiday is over,
and I will act according to your petition."
Jùn then withdrew.
According to the old system,
the Cold Food Festival holiday lasted a total of five days before and after.
The character for 'holiday'
is pronounced 'jū' with a surprised tone.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Emperor urgently summoned the chancellors and privy councilors to enter,
and confined Jùn in a separate place.
The Emperor saw Féng Dào and others,
and wept, saying:
"Wáng Jùn has bullied me excessively.

The Jìn dynasty had eight Chief Clerks in the Department of State Affairs,
with a rank of 200 shi,
who together with the Left and Right Vice Directors oversaw the affairs of the Department.
The Liáng dynasty had five,
called the Five Chief Clerks.
In the Suí dynasty, during the Kāihuáng reign period,
the title Chief Clerk was changed to Chief Administrator,
with eight appointed.
The Later Wèi established Chief Clerks in the various bureaus of the Department of State Affairs.
The Suí dynasty also established Chief Clerks in the various ministries;
Emperor Yáng removed the 'Clerk' from the title,
changing it to simply Chief.
Initially, scholars were mixed in these posts,
but by the Táng dynasty, only those outside the regular official stream were used.
By the Five Dynasties period, the Privy Council also established Chiefs.
When Lǐ Shǒuzhēn rebelled,

Zhōu Xíngféng disliked the Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng, Zhāng Fǎng,

Since the end of the Táng dynasty,

In Shǔ, Wú Zhāoyì used his private wealth of a million to establish schools,

From then on, literary culture flourished again in Shǔ.
Since Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and Yáng Xióng of the Hàn dynasty,

the blocks were completed,

The carving and printing of the Nine Classics began with 277 volumes in the third year of the Chángxīng era of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng,

Even in a time of disorder,

The history records that the reason the Way of the Sages did not perish

"Their people and ours are the same,

First year of Xiǎndé (Jiǎyín, 954)
1. In spring,
the first month,

3. On the day Gēngchén,
Prince of Jìn, Chái Róng, was additionally appointed as Shìzhōng,

4. Among the soldiers, there were rumors that the rewards for the suburban sacrifice were less than in the time of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng.
Emperor Míngzōng of Táng, due to soldiers' rumors, granted excessive rewards,

and they were unwilling to exert themselves in service.
How is that worthy of emulation!

"Since I ascended the throne,

and the enthronement took place on the Bǐngshēn day.
11 Earlier,
the Military Commissioner of Jìnghǎi, Wú Quán, had died.
(Wú Quán occupied Jiāozhōu; see volume 281, the third year of the Tiānfú era of Jìn Gāozǔ,
which corresponds to the eleventh year of the Dàyǒu era of Southern Hàn Gāozǔ.)
Chāngjí died,
and his younger brother Chāngwén succeeded him.
This month,
he began requesting recognition from the Southern Hàn,
and the Southern Hàn appointed Chāngwén as Military Commissioner of Jìnghǎi and concurrently Protector-General of Ānnán.
12 The ruler of Northern Hàn, upon hearing of Tàizǔ's passing,
was greatly pleased
and planned a major invasion,
sending an envoy to request troops from the Qìdān.
In the second month,
the Qìdān sent their Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng and Chief Administrator of Government Affairs Yáng Gǔn to lead over ten thousand cavalry to Jìnyáng.
Textual analysis note: The Jìnyáng Eyewitness Account states:
"Gǔn led fifty to seventy thousand cavalry,
claiming to be one hundred thousand, to join forces."
Here, we follow the Shìzōng Veritable Records.
He appointed the Military Commissioner of Yìchéng, Bái Cónghuī, as Field Commander,
and the Military Commissioner of Wǔníng, Zhāng Yuánhuī, as Vanguard Commanding Officer.
(The Yìchéng Army
was based in Huázhōu;
the Wǔníng Army,
in Xúzhōu;
both belonged to Zhōu.
Bái Cónghuī and the others also held these titles in absentia.)
Textual analysis note: The Shìzōng Veritable Records states:
"The enemy general Zhāng Huī led three thousand cavalry as the vanguard."
Here, we follow the Jìnyáng Eyewitness Account.
13 The Left Kuāngshèng Infantry and Cavalry Commanding Officer and Military Commissioner of Bǎoníng of Shǔ, Ān Sīqiān, had slandered and killed Zhāng Yè
and deposed Zhào Tíngyǐn.
(Both events are recorded in volume 288, the first year of the Qiányòu era of Hàn.)
The ruler of Shǔ sent him to lead troops to rescue Wáng Jǐngchóng,
but Sīqiān delayed and achieved nothing.
(See volume 288, the second year of the Qiányòu era of Hàn,
which corresponds to the twelfth year of the Míngdé era of Shǔ.)
(Note: The character "橈"
is pronounced as "nú jiào fān.")
He felt uneasy.
Since Zhāng Yè's execution,
the palace gate guards had been strengthened,
and Sīqiān suspected this was directed at him,
often speaking disrespectfully.
Sīqiān, in charge of the palace guards,
frequently killed soldiers to establish his authority.
When the ruler of Shǔ inspected the guards,
there were some still in their prime whom Sīqiān had dismissed;
the ruler reinstated them to the guard roster,
but Sīqiān killed them,
which deeply displeased the ruler of Shǔ.
Sīqiān had three sons:
Yǐ, Sì, and Yì.
Relying on their father's power, they were violent and tyrannical,
becoming a scourge to the people.
The Hanlin Commissioner Wáng Zǎo
(according to the Zhíguān Fēnjì: The Táng dynasty had Hanlin Commissioners
who managed artisans and those awaiting appointments.
The Five Dynasties had Hanlin Tea and Wine Commissioners;
Shǔ likely followed the old Táng system)
was about to rebel.
On the Dīngsì day,
when Sīqiān entered the court,
the ruler of Shǔ ordered strong men to strike and kill him
along with his three sons.
Zǎo was also implicated for submitting a memorial that stirred up border troubles,
and was executed as well.
14 The Northern Hàn troops encamped at Liánghóu Station.
The Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, Lǐ Yún, sent his general Mù Lìngjūn to lead two thousand infantry and cavalry to engage them,
while Yún personally led the main army to camp at Tàipíng Station.
(Sòng Bái said: Liánghóu Station
is south of Tuánbǎi Valley,
northwest of Tàipíng Station.
Tàipíng Station
is eighty lǐ southeast of Lùzhōu.)
Feigning defeat and retreating,
Lìngjūn pursued them,
where an ambush was sprung,
killing Lìngjūn
and capturing or killing over a thousand soldiers.
Yún fled back to Shàngdǎng.
(Lùzhōu was administered from Shàngdǎng.)
(Yún
is the same as Lǐ Róng.
In the twelfth year of the Tiānfú era,
Lǐ Róng had the merit of expelling Má Dá;
see volume 287.)
When Shìzōng heard that the ruler of Northern Hàn had invaded,
he wished to personally lead troops to resist him.
The ministers all said:
"Since Liú Chóng fled from Píngyáng,
(referring to the first year of the Guǎngshùn era when Liú Chóng besieged Jìnzhōu
but failed to capture it and withdrew;
see the previous volume for details)
he certainly would not dare to come personally.
Your Majesty has newly ascended the throne,
the imperial tomb construction is scheduled,
people's hearts are easily shaken,
it is not appropriate to act lightly;
you should order a general to resist him."
The emperor said:
"Chóng takes advantage of our great mourning,
looking down on me for being young and newly enthroned,
with the ambition to swallow the world.
He will certainly come personally,
and I cannot but go."
Féng Dào firmly opposed this,
but the emperor said:
"In the past, when Táng Tàizōng pacified the world,
he never failed to lead personally.
How dare I seek ease and comfort!"
Dào said:
"I wonder if Your Majesty can be like Táng Tàizōng?"
The emperor said:
"With the strength of my troops,
crushing Liú Chóng will be like a mountain crushing an egg!"
Dào said:
"I wonder if Your Majesty can be the mountain?"
(Féng Dào served eight different regimes,
holding the position of chief minister,
yet was not known for offering good advice,
except for opposing Shìzōng's personal campaign.
Only Wáng Pǔ encouraged the expedition,
and the emperor followed his advice.)
15 In the third month,
on the first day, Yǐhài,
the ruler of Shǔ promoted the Pěngshèng Kòngquè Commanding Officer and concurrently Director of the Secretariat Sūn Hànsáo to Military Commissioner of the Wǔxìn Army,
bestowed upon him the title of Prince of Lè'ān,
and relieved him of his military duties.
(This means he was relieved of his command over the imperial guards.)
He ordered the Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào Lǐ Tíngguī and nine others to separately command the imperial guards.
16. The Northern Hàn took advantage of their victory to advance and press upon Lùzhōu.
This was following their victory at Liánghóu Station.
On Dīngchǒu,
an edict was issued ordering Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng Fú Yànqīng to lead troops from Cízhōu’s Gùzhèn to emerge behind the Northern Hàn army.
Cízhōu’s Wǔ'ān County had a Gùzhèn.
From there, heading northwest,
one reached the north of Liáozhōu.
The Hàn army at that time had already attacked Lùzhōu.
If Fú Yànqīng reached the border of Liáozhōu,
he would then emerge behind them.
Cí
is pronounced like qiáng.
Another edict ordered Military Commissioner of Hézhōng Wáng Yànchāo to lead troops east from Jìnzhōu to intercept the Northern Hàn,
with Deputy Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì Hán Tòng as his deputy;
also ordered Commander of the Cavalry Fán Àinéng, Military Commissioner of Níngjiāng, and Commander of the Infantry Hé Huī, Military Commissioner of Qīnghuái,
(The Níngjiāng Army
was in Kuízhōu,
belonging to Shǔ.)
(The Qīnghuái Army
was in Shòuzhōu,
belonging to Táng.)
Fán and Hé also held these titles remotely.
Defensive Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu Shǐ Yànchāo and former Tuanlian Commissioner of Yàozhōu Fú Yànnéng led troops first toward Zézhōu,
with Xuānhuī Commissioner Xiàng Xùn overseeing them.
(Chóngzàn
was from Xiànzhōu.)
17. On Xīnsì,
a general amnesty was declared.
18. On Guǐwèi,
the Emperor ordered Féng Dào to escort the imperial coffin to the mountain tomb.
(The mountain tomb
was in Xīnzhèng County, Zhèngzhōu.)
On Yǐyǒu,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng;
on Gēngyín,
he reached Huáizhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: From Dàliáng to Huáizhōu is 325 lǐ.)
Commander of the Kònghè Army Zhào Cháo from Zhēndìng privately said to Interpreter Attendant Zhèng Hǎoqiān:
"The enemy's momentum is currently strong;
we should be cautious to wear them down."
Hǎoqiān reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor angrily said:
"How dare you say such things!
You must have been instigated by someone.
Name the person and you will live;
otherwise, you will surely die."
Hǎoqiān replied truthfully,
and the Emperor ordered both Cháo to be shackled and imprisoned in the prefectural jail.
(The jail of Huáizhōu.)
On Rénchén,
the Emperor passed through Zézhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: From Huáizhōu north to Zézhōu is 120 lǐ.)
The Northern Hàn ruler did not know the Emperor had arrived.
Passing Lùzhōu without attacking it,
he led his troops south.
That evening,
they encamped south of Gāopíng.
(Liú Xù said: Gāopíng
was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Xuànshì County.
Sòng Bái said: The Hàn dynasty's Xuànshì County
was changed to Xuánshì by the Later Wèi,
and changed to Gāopíng by the Northern Qí.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Gāopíng County is 65 lǐ northeast of Zézhōu.)
On Guǐsì,
the vanguard encountered the Northern Hàn army
and attacked them.
(Examination of discrepancies: The Shízōng Shílù states:
"On Jiǎwǔ,
the enemy arrayed themselves on the high plain south of Gāopíng."
Considering that below there is also a Jiǎwǔ,
this must be an error for Guǐsì.
Now follow the Shíguó Jìnián.)
The Emperor, concerned they might flee,
urged all armies to advance quickly.
The Northern Hàn ruler arrayed his central army at Bāgōng Plain,
with Zhāng Yuánhuī's army to the east,
and Yáng Gǔn's army to the west.
Their ranks were quite orderly and strict.
At that time, Military Commissioner of Héyáng Liú Cí, leading the rear army, had not yet arrived.
The troops were anxious and fearful,
but the Emperor's morale grew even sharper.
He ordered Bái Chóngjìn and Deputy Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry Lǐ Chóngjìn to lead the left army positioned on the west.
("Bái Chóngjìn"
should be
"Bái Chóngzàn."
[Chapter note: The twelve-line edition correctly has
"zàn";
the eleven-line edition B is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same;
the Zhāng collation is the same;
the Tuìzhāi collation is the same.
) Xiàng Xùn and Shǐ Yànchāo led elite cavalry positioned in the center,
while Commander of the Palace Front Zhāng Yǒngdé led the imperial guards to protect the Emperor.
The Emperor, armored and mounted, personally went to the front lines to oversee the battle.
The Northern Hàn ruler, seeing the Zhōu army was few,
regretted summoning the Khitan.
He said to his generals:
"Using only our Hàn army, we can defeat them.
(The Northern Hàn ruler, before the battle, already had a contemptuous attitude toward the enemy;
it was fitting he was defeated.)
Today, not only will we conquer Zhōu,
we will also make the Khitan submit in their hearts."
All the generals agreed.
Yáng Gǔn rode forward to observe the Zhōu army,
then retreated and said to the Northern Hàn ruler:
"They are a formidable enemy;
do not advance lightly!"
The Northern Hàn ruler, stroking his beard, said:
"The opportunity must not be lost.
Please, sir, say no more.
Just watch me fight."
Gǔn fell silent, displeased.
At that time, the northeast wind was strong,
but suddenly it shifted to a south wind.
The Northern Hàn Deputy Privy Councilor Wáng Yánsì had the Director of the Astrological Bureau Lǐ Yì report to the Northern Hàn ruler:
"Now is the time to fight."
The Northern Hàn ruler agreed.
Academician of the Privy Council Wáng Dézhōng grabbed his horse's bridle and admonished:
"Yì should be beheaded!
With the wind like this,
how can it be aiding us?"
The Northern Hàn ruler said:
"My plan is already decided.
Old scholar, do not speak recklessly,
or I will behead you!"
He waved for the eastern army to advance first.
Zhāng Yuánhuī led a thousand cavalry to attack the Zhōu right army.
Not long after the battle joined,
Fán Àinéng and Hé Huī led their cavalry in flight first,
and the right army collapsed.
Over a thousand infantrymen removed their armor and shouted "Long live,"
surrendering to the Northern Hàn.
The Emperor, seeing the army's situation was critical,
personally led his personal guards through arrows and stones to oversee the battle.
The future Emperor Tàizǔ was then a guard general.
He said to his comrades:
"Our lord is in such peril;
how can we not fight to the death!"
He also said to Zhāng Yǒngdé:
"The enemy's morale is arrogant;
fighting fiercely can defeat them!
Among your troops are many capable of left-handed archery.
I ask you to lead troops to take the high ground and form the left wing,
while I lead troops as the right wing to attack them.
The safety of the state
rests on this one action!"
Yǒngdé agreed,
and each led two thousand men forward into battle.
The future Emperor Tàizǔ personally led the charge,
galloping to meet the enemy's vanguard.
The soldiers fought desperately,
each worth a hundred,
and the Northern Hàn troops were routed.
Palace Guard Xiàjīn's Mǎ Rényǔ said to the troops:
"If the imperial carriage faces the enemy,
what use are we?"
He leaped on his horse, drew his bow, and shouted loudly,
killing several dozen men in succession.
Morale was further boosted.
(The Palace Guard
was established by Zhōu,
a designation for the various squads of the Palace Front.
Xiàjīn
was the Hàn dynasty's Shū County,
renamed Xiàjīn in the first year of the Táng Tiānbǎo era,
belonging to Bèizhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It belongs to Dàmíng Prefecture,
250 lǐ northeast of the prefectural seat.
Yǔ
is pronounced like wáng jǔ.
Chéng
is pronounced like shéng zhèng.
Hū
is pronounced like huǒ gù.
Last year, Mǎ Quányì followed the Emperor into court from Chánzhōu
and was already appointed as a Palace Front Commander,
but had not yet reached the rank of Dispersed Officer Commander.
Right Rotation Leader
held the leading position among the Palace Front right rotation squads,
his rank still below that of Dispersed Officer Commander.
Xíng
is pronounced like hù gāng.)
"The enemy's momentum is at its peak;
they will be captured by us.
I beg Your Majesty to hold the reins and not move,
and calmly watch the generals defeat them."
He then led several hundred cavalry forward and broke into the enemy formation.
The Northern Hàn ruler learned that the Emperor had personally arrived at the front lines.
He praised and rewarded Zhāng Yuánhuī,
urging him to press forward with the momentum of victory.
Yuánhuī advanced to reconnoiter the enemy formation,
but his horse stumbled,
and he was killed by the Zhōu troops.
Yuánhuī
was a valiant general of Northern Hàn,
and the Northern army's morale collapsed from this point.
At that time, the south wind grew even stronger,
and the Zhōu soldiers fought with redoubled vigor.
The Northern Hàn troops suffered a major defeat.
The Northern Hàn ruler personally raised a red banner to rally his troops,
but could not stop the rout.
Although Northern Hàn originated from the Shatuo,
they claimed the surname Liú,
inheriting the legacy of (Emperor) Gāo and (Emperor) Guāng of Hàn,
hence their banners and flags were still red.
Zhì (banner/flag)
is pronounced chāng zhì.
(The Khitan) did not dare to come to their aid,
and moreover resented the Northern Hàn ruler's words,
so they withdrew their entire army intact.
Examination of Discrepancies says: *Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties*:
"Liú Chóng sought aid from the Khitan,
obtaining several thousand swift cavalry.
Upon seeing Shìzōng's small force,
he regretted it,
and summoned his generals to discuss, saying:
'I observe the Zhōu army is easy to deal with.
The Khitan multitude should not be used.
If we decide the battle with our own army alone,
not only will we defeat the enemy,
it will also be enough to make the Khitan see it and be convinced in their hearts.'
All the generals agreed,
so he sent a man to tell the Khitan commander:
'The situation between the Chái family and us, host and guest, is already clear.
We certainly won't trouble your remaining blades.
We dare to request you lead your troops to a high place and observe, that will suffice.'
The Khitan did not know his scheme,
and complied.
When Shìzōng entered the battle formation,
his entire army, their courage roused, vied to advance,
each man worth a hundred.
The Khitan watched and feared them,
therefore they did not dare to aid, and Chóng was defeated."
Now we follow the *Veritable Records of Shìzōng* and the *Old History of the Five Dynasties*.
Fán Àinéng and Hé Huī led several thousand cavalry fleeing south,
bows drawn and blades bared,
plundering the supply train.
The laborers and porters fled in panic,
with many losses and desertions.
The Emperor sent close attendants and officers of the Imperial Guard to pursue them, convey his order, and stop them,
but none were willing to obey the decree.
Some of the messengers were killed by the soldiers,
who spread rumors, saying:
"The Khitan have arrived in great force,
the Imperial army is utterly defeated,
the remaining troops have already surrendered to the enemy."
Liú Cí encountered Àinéng and others on the road.
Àinéng and the others tried to stop him,
but Cí did not comply,
leading his troops northward.
At that time, the Northern Hàn ruler still had over ten thousand remaining troops,
who took up a defensive formation behind a stream.
As dusk approached,
Cí arrived,
and again joined the various armies in attacking them.
Bó (薄)
means to press/approach.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu.
The following zú fù (卒復) is the same.
They killed Wáng Yánsì,
pursued them to Gāopíng,
where corpses filled the valleys and mountains,
and abandoned imperial items, supplies, equipment, weapons, and miscellaneous livestock were too numerous to record.
That evening,
the Emperor spent the night in the open field.
He captured infantrymen who had surrendered to the enemy,
and had them all killed.
When Fán Àinéng and others heard of the Zhōu army's great victory,
they and their soldiers gradually began to return,
though some did not arrive until dawn.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
the army rested at Gāopíng.
Several thousand Northern Hàn soldiers who had surrendered were selected to form the "Xiàoshùn" Command,
and the former Wǔshèng Campaign Military Administrator Táng Jǐngsī was ordered to lead them,
sending them to garrison north of the Huái River.
The remaining two thousand or so men were given traveling funds and supplies and released.
"Zī" (貲)
should be
(They) hid and fled into the mountains and valleys,
and only emerged after several days.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the Emperor reached Lùzhōu.
The Northern Hàn ruler, wearing coarse clothes and a bamboo hat,
and riding the yellow steed gifted by the Khitan,
led over a hundred cavalry and fled back via Diāokē Ridge.
Diāokē Ridge
is northwest of Gāopíng,
entering by the Jiāngzhě Ridge road.
Shuài (帥)
is read as shuài (率).
Traveling at night, they lost their way.
They mistakenly went towards Jìnzhōu,
traveled over a hundred *lǐ*,
then realized it,
and killed the guide.
They fled north day and night.
Wherever they arrived,
before they could even lift their chopsticks to eat the food they obtained,
if word came that Zhōu troops were approaching,
they would hastily depart.
The Northern Hàn ruler, aged and exhausted,
slumped over his horse,
galloping day and night,
nearly unable to endure,
and barely managed to enter Jìnyáng.
The Emperor wanted to execute Fán Àinéng and others to enforce military discipline,
but hesitated, undecided.
On the jǐhài day,
while napping in his tent at the traveling palace during the day,
with Zhāng Yǒngdé attending at his side,
the Emperor consulted him on the matter.
Zhāng Yǒngdé
was Tàizǔ's son-in-law,
being both a relative
and exclusively in charge of the Diànqián troops,
guarding and attending the Emperor's side.
Therefore, the Emperor consulted him on the matter
to decide whether it was feasible or not.
"Àinéng and the others ordinarily had no great achievements,
yet unworthily held high command with symbols of authority.
Seeing the enemy, they fled first.
Death would not atone for their responsibility.
Moreover, Your Majesty is just planning to conquer the four seas.
If military law is not established,
even if you have warriors like bears and panthers,
a host of a million men,
how can you employ them effectively!"
The Emperor threw his pillow to the ground,
and shouted loudly in approval.
He immediately had Àinéng, Huī, and over seventy of their subordinate army commanders and above arrested.
He reprimanded them, saying:
"You all are veteran generals of successive reigns,
not incapable of fighting.
The reason you now flee at the mere sight of the enemy
is nothing else
but that you intended to treat Us as a rare commodity,
to be sold to Liú Chóng!"
He had them all beheaded.
The Emperor, because Hé Huī had previously defended Jìnzhōu with merit
(the event is seen in scroll 290, Tàizǔ's Guǎngshùn 1st year),
initially considered it, but then, because the law could not be set aside,
subsequently executed him as well,
but provided a coffin cart for his burial.
Huì chē (槥車)
means a small coffin.
Huì (槥)
is pronounced wèi.
(Thus) he did not implement a policy of undue leniency.
On the gēngzǐ day,
rewards were given for the merits at Gāopíng.
Lǐ Chòngjìn was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ.
Xiàng Xùn was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner of Yìchéng.
Zhāng Yǒngdé was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn.
"Concurrently" means
holding a concurrent provincial military command in addition to one's substantive post.
The salary and stipends were more generous than for nominal (yáolǐng) appointments.
This was a substantive appointment to a military commission.
The Emperor promoted Tàizǔ Huángdì to Diànqián Dū Yúhòu.
At the end of the Later Wèi,
Yǔwén established the post of Yúhòu Dūdū to command the scout cavalry.
The office of Yúhòu likely began at this time.
During the Five Dynasties, the Diànqián Dū Yúhòu ranked below the Deputy Commander-in-Chief,
and together with the Commander and Deputy Commander-in-Chief, managed the Diànqián Imperial Guard units.
Yánzhōu was subordinate to Lǐngnán,
at that time held by Southern Hàn,
(his title) was merely a nominal (yáolǐng) governorship.
Nowadays, the nominal (yáojùn) governorships held by military officers are precisely of this category.
But those who shed their graded official rank and receive a substantive appointment as governor
are called "substantive appointment" (zhèngrèn) governors.
However, they also never actually administered the commandery and governed the people.
Liú Xù says: Yánzhōu
was in the territory of the Qín-era Guìlín Commandery.
During the Táng Qiánfēng period,
they recruited and settled raw Lǎo tribesmen,
and established Yánzhōu.
In Sòng Kāibǎo 7th year,
Yánzhōu was abolished,
and Láibīn County was attached to Xiàngzhōu.
Mǎ Quányì was appointed as Sànyuán Commanding Officer.
From the remaining officers and commanders, several dozen were promoted and appointed.
There were even soldiers promoted from the ranks to command army units.
Zhào Cháo was released from imprisonment.
Imprisoning Zhào Cháo was to intimidate the masses;
after victory in battle, he was released.
The ruler of Northern Hàn gathered his scattered troops,
repaired armor and weapons,
and fortified city walls and moats to prepare against Zhōu.
Yáng Gǔn led his forces north to station at Dàizhōu,
and the ruler of Northern Hàn sent Wáng Dézhōng to escort Gǔn,
taking the opportunity to seek aid from the Khitan.
The Khitan ruler sent Dézhōng back with a reply,
promising to dispatch troops to rescue Jìnyáng.
On the Rényín day,
Fú Yànqīng was appointed as the overall commander of the Hé dōng campaign headquarters and concurrently in charge of the Tàiyuán administrative office,
with Guō Chóng as his deputy,
Xiàng Xùn as the overall supervisor,
Lǐ Chóngjìn as the commander of cavalry and infantry,
and Shǐ Yànchāo as the vanguard commander,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to set out from Lùzhōu;
it was also ordered that Wáng Yànchāo and Hán Tōng enter from Yīndì Pass,
and after Northern Hàn was defeated and fled,
the troops stationed east of Jìnzhōu were shifted north to attack Fénzhōu and Bìngzhōu.
Liú Cí was also appointed as the accompanying imperial commander,
with Bái Chóngzàn, the military governor of Bǎodà, as his deputy.
They advanced to attack Jìnyáng, taking advantage of their victory.
"Accompanying imperial"
below,
should have
"overall"
character.
19. The Han Empress Dowager Lǐ, Zhāoshèng, passed away in the Western Palace.
After Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
the Han Empress Dowager Lǐ moved to reside in the Western Palace,
as recorded in the first year of Guǎngshùn in the previous volume.
20. In summer,
the fourth month,
Yùxiàn of Northern Hàn surrendered.
Yù,
an ancient county,
belonged to Tàiyuán Prefecture in the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is two hundred lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
However, after Sòng captured Tàiyuán,
the administrative seat was moved to Yángqū.
Sòng Bái said: Yùxiàn,
originally the fief of the Jìn minister Yù Bǐng,
became Yù County in the Hàn dynasty.
According to this, Yùxiàn before this was located west of the current county,
which is the old Yù County city eighty lǐ northeast of Yángqū County.
In the Later Wèi, it was abolished and incorporated into Shí'ài County.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
Yuánqiú County was established from part of Shí'ài County,
belonging to Liáozhōu,
named after the old Yuánqiú city,
which is the current county.

He rose,

Yàntōng was greatly pleased,

The various barbarians of the streams and caves
cast bronze into large drums.
When first completed,
they are hung in the courtyard,
and wine is set out to summon their kindred.
The children of wealthy and powerful families use gold and silver to make large hairpins,
which they hold to strike the drum until the end,
then leave them as gifts for the host,
named
"bronze drum hairpins."
Their custom favors mutual killing,
often creating feuds and grudges.
When they wish to attack each other,
they sound these drums,
and those who come are as numerous as clouds.
"Qiánlǎng's single speech was worth more than tens of thousands of troops,

Qián,

Jìn lost Yōu;
Zhōu lost Bìng.)
Only then can we understand the methods to reclaim them.
When they were first lost,
it was always because the ruler was benighted and the ministers corrupt,
the military arrogant and the people distressed,
treacherous cliques blazed within,
and military men ran amok abroad.
Small causes led to great effects,
and minor accumulations became significant.
Now, to reclaim them,
nothing is better than doing the opposite of what was done before.
Promoting the worthy and dismissing the unworthy
is how to gather talent;
bestowing kindness, showing compassion, and being sincere and trustworthy
is how to win their hearts;
(隱 means to show compassion.)
rewarding achievements and punishing faults
is how to exhaust their efforts;
eliminating extravagance and practicing frugality
is how to enrich resources;
employing labor at appropriate times and imposing light taxes
is how to make the people prosperous.
('Employing labor at appropriate times' means using them according to the seasons.
斂 is read as liǎn.)
When governance is orderly,
resources are ample,
and the scholars and people are attached,
then raising an army and employing it
will ensure no undertaking fails to succeed!
When the people of those lands see that we possess the inevitable momentum to conquer,
then those who know their internal situation will be willing to act as spies,
and those familiar with their mountains and rivers will be willing to serve as guides.
Once the people's hearts are won over,
Heaven's will is sure to follow.
Generally, in the way of attack and conquest,
one must start with what is easy.
Táng shares a border with us for nearly two thousand lǐ,
making it easy to harass.
(Táng and the Central Plains use the Huái River as the border,
from the source of the Huái east to the sea is nearly two thousand lǐ.
易 is read as yì.)
If they defend the east, harass the west;
if they defend the west, harass the east.
They will certainly rush about to rescue.
In their rushing about,
we can discern their actual conditions of weakness and strength.
Then, avoid the strong and attack the weak,
avoid the solid and strike the void.
There is no need for a large-scale campaign initially;
just use light troops to harass them.
Southerners are timid and cowardly;
upon hearing of even a minor alarm,
they will certainly mobilize their entire army to rescue.
If the army is mobilized frequently, the people will be exhausted and resources depleted.
If they do not send their entire army, we can take advantage of their weakness to capture territory.
In this way,
all the prefectures north of the river will gradually become ours.
(The emperor's capture of the area north of the river followed Wáng Pǔ's plan.)

The Guǎng version:
"Kuí appointed the deputy campaign commander Máo Lì as the commander of the Yuánzhōu camp army,

The Hú Xiāng Story:
"Kuí fled back to Lǎngzhōu overnight.

Now, according to the Shízōng Shílù:
"On the bǐngyín day of the second month of Xiǎndé 3,

leading a large army into Huáinán territory;

It seems these were matters reported by Jìnkuí before his defeat,
which only reached the imperial presence in the third month,

Only the Hú Xiāng Story and Dīng Shú's Records of the Mǎ Clan's Conduct record Kuí attacking Yuánzhōu and Shūsì's rebellion.

Shūsì rebelled."

These are all erroneous.

Tàizōng, pitying his poverty and age,

Yǎn was originally a petty man,
his words vulgar and crude.
He did not intend to write a proper book,

turning nothing into something,
too numerous to count.
He harbored a grudge against Zhōu Xíngféng,

Not wanting Xíngféng to be uninvolved in Shūsì's plot,

Generally, the most severe accounts of Xíngféng's wickedness
all come from Yǎn.
Shú was also a person from the early dynasty.
It is suspected his account was derived from Yǎn's book.
None can be taken as reliable.
Now we follow the Shí Guó Jìnián.
Someone advised Shūsì to then seize Lǎngzhōu.
Shūsì said:
"I am merely escaping death.
How dare I presume to elevate myself?

refers to Zhōu Xíngféng.
He said Xíngféng would surely give him Tánzhōu.
Chǔ,
read as chǔ.
He sent the regiment training judge Lǐ Jiǎn
(Pān Shūsì was the Yuèzhōu regiment training commissioner,

Wèi,
means to inform,
to tell.
"Shūsì treacherously killed his commanding officer.

If I immediately appoint him as military commissioner,

How can I clear myself!
It is proper to temporarily make him campaign marshal.

Observing this,

(Zhōu Xíngféng was Wǔ'ān campaign marshal,

"Shūsì is still dissatisfied?

Someone advised Xíngféng:

ordering him to come to the capital city to receive the appointment.
Then he will be like meat on the chopping block!"
Xíngféng followed this advice.
As Shūsì was about to depart,
those close to him stopped him.
Shūsì relied on the fact that he had always served Xíngféng as an elder brother,

(The matter of Xíngféng and Shūsì being close and friendly
first appears in the second year of Tàizǔ's Guǎngshùn, ninth month, scroll 291.)
Xíngféng sent envoys to welcome and await him,
lining the roads.
Upon arrival,
Xíngféng personally went out to the suburbs to greet him,

Because of our past friendship,

Shūsì knew he could not escape,
