[the Emperor] appointed the Commanding Officer of the Imperial Guard and Military Commissioner of Guīdé, Lǐ Chóngjìn, as the Pacification Commissioner of Lúzhōu, Shòuzhōu, and other prefectures.
He appointed the Military Commissioner of Wǔníng, Wǔ Xíngdé, as the Field Commander at the foot of Háozhōu's walls.
The Táng Right Guard General Lù Mèngjùn led over ten thousand troops from Chángzhōu toward Tàizhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Chángzhōu north to Tàizhōu is 197 lǐ.
Mèngjùn recaptured it,
meaning he recaptured Tàizhōu.
Mèngjùn advanced to attack Yángzhōu,
encamping at Shǔgāng.
Hán Lìngkūn abandoned Yángzhōu and fled.
Shǔgāng is west of Yángzhōu city.
Yángzhōu city is southeast of Shǔgāng.
East, south, and north of the city are all flat land,
with ditches and canals crisscrossing.
Only Shǔgāng and the various mountains connect west to Lúzhōu and Chúzhōu.
Whenever northern troops invaded Yángzhōu from the south,
they generally came along the mountains,
occupying high ground to build fortifications overlooking it.
Now Lù Mèngjùn occupied Shǔgāng to cut off the Zhōu troops' route of reinforcement,
hence Hán Lìngkūn feared and fled.
Lìngkūn re-entered Yángzhōu.
Reinforcements arrived,
so he re-entered Yángzhōu.
Liùhé County,
belonging to Yángzhōu,
is 130 lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Liú Xù said: Liùhé
was the Tángyì County of the Hàn Línhuái Commandery.
In Jìn, the Qín Commandery was established.
In Northern Qí, Qín Prefecture was established.
In Suí, Fāng Prefecture was established.
Later it was abolished.
In Táng, Wǔdé first year, Liùhé County was established.
"Any Yángzhōu soldier who passes Liùhé
will have his feet broken!"
To return northwest from Yángzhōu,
one must pass Liùhé,
hence the statement.
Zhé,
pronounced ér shè fān.
Since the Emperor arrived at Shòuchūn,
he ordered the various armies to attack the city day and night,
but it long remained uncaptured.
There was heavy rain,
and the camps were several feet deep in water.
Siege equipment and soldiers were lost in considerable numbers.
At the time, the Zhōu troops used square boats to carry catapults,
and from the middle of the Féi River attacked Shòuchūn city.
They also bound several hundred thousand large bamboo poles,
placing plank huts on top,
calling them
"bamboo dragons,"
and loaded armored soldiers to attack with them.
It happened that the Féi River suddenly flooded,
and the catapult boats and bamboo dragons all drifted to the southern bank,
where they were burned by the Táng troops.
Lǐ Démíng did not arrive by the appointed time.
Lǐ Démíng returned to Jīnlíng and was executed.
Someone advised the Emperor to proceed east to Háozhōu,
claiming that Shòuzhōu had already been captured.
He followed this advice.
On the jǐsì day,
the Emperor proceeded east from Shòuchūn along the Huái River.
On the yǐhài day,
he reached Háozhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Shòuzhōu
east to Háozhōu is 380 lǐ.
Hán Lìngkūn defeated the Táng army east of the city,
this refers to east of Yángzhōu city.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Earlier,
when Mèng Jùn deposed Mǎ Xī'è and established Xīchóng,
the event is recorded in volume 290, the first year of Tàizǔ's Guǎngshùn era.
There was a beautiful daughter of the Yáng family,
who was presented to Xīchóng.
When Lìngkūn entered Yángzhōu,
Xīchóng gave the Yáng woman to Lìngkūn,
and Lìngkūn became infatuated with her.
After capturing Mèng Jùn,
he was about to send him in shackles to the Emperor;
the Yáng woman was behind a curtain,
suddenly clutched her chest and wailed bitterly,
Lìngkūn, startled, asked her the reason,
she replied:
"Mèng Jùn, when he was in Tánzhōu in the past,
killed two hundred members of my family.
Seeing him today,
I beg to avenge this injustice."
Lìngkūn then killed him.
History says one should not kill recklessly,
even a woman can seek revenge.
17 The Táng Prince of Qí, Jǐngdá, led twenty thousand troops from Guābù across the river,
halted over twenty lǐ from Liùhé,
set up stockades and did not advance.
The generals wanted to attack him,
but Emperor Tàizǔ said:
"They set up stockades to fortify themselves,
because they fear us.
Now our troops number less than two thousand.
If we go to attack them,
then they will see our numbers are few;
it is better to wait for them to come and then attack,
we will certainly defeat them!"
After several days,
the Táng troops advanced towards Liùhé,
Emperor Tàizǔ fiercely attacked,
and routed them,
killing and capturing nearly five thousand men.
The remaining troops, still over ten thousand,
fled across the river,
many drowned fighting for boats,
and thus the Táng's elite troops were exhausted.
In this battle,
there were soldiers who did not exert their full effort.
Emperor Tàizǔ pretended to supervise the battle,
and cut their leather hats with his sword.
The next day,
he inspected all their leather hats,
and found several dozen with sword marks.
He beheaded them all,
and from then on, none of his troops dared not to fight to the death.
Previously,
the Táng sovereign heard that Yángzhōu was lost,
and ordered troops from all sides to retake it.
On Jǐmǎo,
Hán Lìngkūn reported defeating over ten thousand Yáng
zhōu troops at Wāntóu Weir.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Yángzhōu Jiāngdū County has Wāntóu Town,
located fifteen lǐ north of present-day Yángzhōu city.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Táng probably established Liánzhōu at Liánshuǐ County.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Liánshuǐ,
is sixty lǐ southwest of Chǔzhōu.
Over ten thousand men at Qūxī Weir.
Qūxī,
is ten lǐ southwest of Xūyí County.
According to Zhāoxìn Tújīng: Qūxī Weir,
is also called Xīnhé Weir.
18 On Bǐngxū,
Xuànguī, Commissioner of the Southern Court of the Palace Administration, was appointed Military Commissioner of Huáinán and concurrently Riverine Recruitment Commissioner.
A report from Wōkǒu stated that the newly built pontoon bridge was completed.
On Dīnghài,
the Emperor went from Háozhōu to Wōkǒu.
Wōkǒu,
is the mouth where the Wō River enters the Huái.
Jùnxiàn Zhì: Wōkǒu City,
is ninety lǐ southeast of Háozhōu.
Wō,
yīn gē.
The Emperor was eager to advance,
wanting to go personally to Yángzhōu,
but Fàn Zhì and others, citing exhausted troops and scarce provisions,
tearfully remonstrated and stopped him.
The Emperor once became angry with Hanlin Academician Dòu Yí,
and wanted to kill him;
Fàn Zhì entered to save him.
The Emperor saw him coming,
knew his intention,
and immediately rose to avoid him.
Zhì hurried forward and prostrated on the ground,
kowtowing and remonstrating:
"Yí's crime does not deserve death.
I, as Chief Minister,
have caused Your Majesty to wrongly kill a close minister.
The fault lies entirely with me."
He followed this with tears.
The Emperor's anger subsided,
and he released Yí.
19 The Northern Hàn buried Emperor Shénwǔ at the northern mountains of Jiāochéng.
Suí divided Jìnyáng County to establish Jiāochéng County,
taking the ancient Jiāochéng northwest of the county as its name.
It was initially administered at Jiāoshān.
In the first year of Táng Tiānshòu (690 AD),
the administration was moved to Quèbō Village.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is one hundred lǐ southwest of Yángqǔ County.
Sòng Bái said: Dàtōng Supervisorate,
originally the area of ancient Jiāochéng,
managed the east and west iron-smelting offices.
The East Office was in Miánshàng County,
the West Office was in the northern mountains of Jiāochéng County.
20 In the fifth month,
on Bǐng
chén, the first day,
Wōkǒu was made the Zhènhuái Army garrison.
21 On Bǐngshēn,
the Táng Military Commissioner of Yǒng'ān, Chén Huì, defeated Fúzhōu troops at Nántáijiāng.
Present-day Fúzhōu has Diàolóngtái Mountain nine lǐ to the south,
overlooking the river.
Nántáijiāng is probably this location.
Xuēshǐ Dìlǐ Zhì: Fúzhōu Fútáng County,
in the early Jìn Tiānfù era, was renamed Nántái County,
likely named after the river,
and later reverted to its old name.
The Táng sovereign renamed Yǒng'ān as the Zhōngyì Army.
In the second year of Jìn Kāiyùn (945 AD),
Táng captured Jiànzhōu,
and established the Yǒng'ān Army.
Renamed,
gōng héng fān.
He was Déchéng's father.
22 On Wùxū,
the Emperor left Imperial Guard Commander Lǐ Chóngjìn and others to besiege Shòuzhōu,
and returned north from Wōkǒu;
on Yǐmǎo,
he reached Dàliáng.
From Wōkǒu to Dàliáng is seven hundred and forty lǐ.
23 In the sixth month,
on Rénshēn,
prisoners in the various prefectures of Huáinán were pardoned,
unjust taxes and corvée imposed by the Lǐ clan were abolished,
and matters inconvenient for the people
were to be reported by local officials.
24 Imperial Guard Infantry Commander and Military Commissioner of Zhāngxìn, Lǐ Jìxūn, encamped south of Shòuzhōu city.
The Táng general Liú Rénshàn, seeing Jìxūn unprepared,
led troops out and attacked him,
killing several hundred soldiers,
and burning his siege equipment.
25 The Táng Vice-Director of the Bureau of Equipment, Yuán Zhū, while reporting on affairs, discussed military strategy.
The Táng sovereign, considering him capable,
ordered him to lead troops and recover the various prefectures north of the river.
26 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Xīnmǎo, the first day,
Zhōu Xíngféng was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng,
with authority over military affairs of Wǔ'ān, Jìngjiāng, and others.
Xíngféng, having unified Hú and Xiāng,
corrected the abuses of his predecessors,
paid attention to the people's welfare,
abolished all oppressive taxes of the Mǎ clan,
removed greedy officials and crafty people who harmed the populace,
and selected honest and fair officials as prefects and magistrates.
Lǎngzhōu had mixed Han and non-Han inhabitants,
and the old generals of Liú Yán and Wáng Kuí were mostly arrogant and overbearing.
Xíngféng uniformly governed them by law,
showing no leniency,
causing widespread resentment and fear.
A senior general and more than ten of his followers plotted a rebellion.
Xíngféng, knowing of it,
convened a grand meeting of all generals,
and seized him during the assembly.
He enumerated his faults, saying:
"I wear coarse clothes and eat simple food,
filling the government storehouses,
precisely for you all.
How have I wronged you that you rebel?
Today's meeting
is to bid you farewell!"
He immediately had him beaten to death.
Those present trembled with fear.
Xíngféng said:
"The rest of you are not guilty,
you should all be at ease."
They drank merrily and the meeting ended.
Xíng Féng was full of schemes and
adept at uncovering hidden plots.
Whenever any of his generals or soldiers plotted rebellion or intended to desert,
Xíng Féng would always detect it beforehand,
capture and execute them,
causing his entire command to tremble with fear.
However, he was suspicious and cruel by nature.
He often dispatched agents in secret to spy on affairs in the various prefectures.
The one sent to Shào Prefecture,
having nothing to report,
merely said that the prefect, Liú Guāngwěi, frequently held banquets and drank.
Xíng Féng said:
"Guāngwěi gathers for drinking so often,
does he intend to plot against me?"
He immediately summoned him back
and had him killed.
The Personal Guard Commander and Héng Prefecture Prefect, Zhāng Wénbiǎo, fearing he might incur guilt,
requested to return to his administrative seat;
he sought to relinquish his military authority and return to Héng Prefecture.
Wénbiǎo presented lavish gifts during festivals and annual occasions,
and was extremely deferential in serving those around Xíng Féng,
thereby managing to avoid punishment.
Later, as Xíng Féng approached death,
he said to his son, Bǎo Quán:
"I rose from the fields,
joining the local militia.
Of the ten men who served alongside me, all were executed,
only Zhāng Wénbiǎo remains alive."
At that time, Wáng Kuí, Zhāng Fǎng, Hé Jìngzhēn, Zhū Quánxiù, and Pān Shūsì had all already died.
Only Pú Gōngyì, Yǔwén Qióng, Péng Wànhé, and Wénbiǎo remained.
The histories do not mention anything else about them,
so these three men must have subsequently been killed by Xíng Féng one after another,
and only Wénbiǎo alone was spared.
When Xíng Féng died,
then Wénbiǎo rebelled.
Xíng Féng's wife, the Lady of Yún State, Dèng shì,
was plain in appearance but resolute and decisive,
skilled at managing a livelihood.
She once admonished Xíng Féng for being too severe in his application of laws,
saying that no one felt close to or would rally to him.
Xíng Féng angrily said:
"What does a woman like you know!"
Dèng shì was displeased.
She then requested to go to the village estate to oversee the fields and gardens,
and subsequently did not return to the official residence.
"Zhī" means
to go.
"Shù"
is pronounced as "chéng yǔ fān."
"Fù"
is pronounced as "fú yòu fān."
"Fǔ shè"
refers to the official residence in Lǎng Prefecture.
She did not come;
one day,
she personally led her servants to come and deliver taxes.
Xíng Féng went to see her,
and said:
"I am the military governor,
why must you, my lady, toil like this!"
Dèng shì said:
"Taxes
are government property.
You, sir, are the military governor.
If you do not pay taxes first,
how can you lead your subordinates!
Moreover, have you forgotten the time when you were the village head and paid taxes on behalf of others to avoid being flogged?"
Xíng Féng wished to return with her,
but she refused,
unwilling to return to the official residence.
"You, sir, have executed and killed far too many.
I often fear that one day there will be a sudden change,
and the village estate will be easier to flee to and hide in."
Xíng Féng felt ashamed and angry.
His subordinates said:
"The lady's words are forthright,
you, sir, should accept them."
Xíng Féng's son-in-law, Táng Dé, requested an appointment as an official.
Xíng Féng said:
"Your talent is insufficient to serve as an official.
If I favor you privately now, that is possible;
but if you perform poorly in office,
I dare not exempt you from the law,
and then the bond of kinship between us would be severed."
He gave him plow oxen and farming tools and sent him away.
Xíng Féng, in his youth, had once been tattooed as punishment for an offense,
and was consigned to the copper mines of Chén Prefecture.
Someone advised Xíng Féng:
"You, sir, have markings on your face,
I fear they may be mocked by imperial envoys.
I request you use medicine to remove them."
Xíng Féng said:
"I have heard that in Hàn times there was Qíng Bù,
and it did not prevent him from being a hero.
Why should I be ashamed!"
The matter of Qíng Bù is seen in the eighth scroll, the second year of Qín Èr Shì.
From the time of Liú Yán and Wáng Kuí onward,
they repeatedly raised armies.
The accumulated merits of generals and officials, as well as the subjugated barbarians they controlled,
resulted in those holding the title of Inspectorate Official reaching the rank of the Three Dukes numbering in the thousands.
"Jī mí mán yí"
refers to the various barbarian tribes of the streams and gorges.
Since Mǎ Xīguǎng was deposed,
he shut his door and did not go out.
The matter of Mǎ Xīguǎng's deposition is seen in the two hundred eighty-ninth scroll, the second year of Hàn Qiányòu.
He was appointed as the Military Governor's Administrative Assistant.
Zhòng Yǎ said:
"Xíng Féng once served me,
how can I become his staff official!"
He pleaded illness and did not come.
Xíng Féng pressured and coerced him, firmly summoning him.
He personally handed him the official document,
but Zhòng Yǎ ultimately declined and would not accept it.
Xíng Féng was angry,
and exiled him to Shào Prefecture.
Later, he summoned him back.
It happened to be Xíng Féng's birthday.
The various circuits each sent envoys to offer congratulations.
Xíng Féng had a proud expression,
and said to Zhòng Yǎ:
"Since I concurrently govern three prefectures,"
the three prefectures
are the military prefectures of Wǔpíng, Wǔ'ān, and Jìngjiāng.
Zhòng Yǎ said:
"Within the borders of the Palace Attendant,"
Zhōu Xíng Féng was given the additional title of Palace Attendant,
hence Xú Zhòng Yǎ addressed him as such.
"Sīkōngs are found everywhere,
how can the neighbors not be afraid!"
Xíng Féng again exiled him to Shào Prefecture,
but in the end could not bend him to his will.
There was a monk named Rén Jí,
who was trusted by Xíng Féng.
He participated in all matters of the military government.
He was also given the additional title of Inspectorate Sīkōng.
He took several wives,
and when he went out, his entourage and retinue were like those of a prince or duke.
On the 27th, Xīnhài day,
the Xuānyì Empress, Fú shì, passed away.
The Táng general Zhū Yuán captured Shū Prefecture.
The prefect, Guō Lìngtú, abandoned the city and fled.
Lǐ Píng captured Qí Prefecture.
The Táng sovereign appointed Yuán as the Shū Prefecture Regimental Training Commissioner,
and Píng as the Qí Prefecture Prefect.
Yuán also captured Hé Prefecture.
Zhū Yuán and Lǐ Píng
were both men sent by Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to seek aid from Táng.
The matter is seen in the two hundred eighty-eighth scroll, the first year of Hàn Qiányòu.
Initially,
the men of Táng forced the people to exchange tea and salt for grain and cloth, which they levied,
calling it "extensive levy."
They also established military agricultural colonies in Huáinán.
The people suffered greatly from this.
When the Zhōu army arrived,
they vied to present oxen and wine to welcome and provision them.
However, the generals and commanders did not show them compassion,
but rather devoted themselves to plundering and taking captives,
treating the people like dirt and weeds.
The people all became disappointed,
gathered in the mountains and marshes,
erected fortresses and walls to defend themselves,
took up farming tools as weapons,
and piled up paper to make armor.
People of the time called them
the "White Armor Army."
The Zhōu troops attacked them,
but were repeatedly defeated by them.
Many of the Táng prefectures previously captured by Zhōu
were regained by Táng.
The Táng relief forces were encamped at Zǐjīn Mountain.
Zǐjīn Mountain is south of Shòuchūn;
some say it is Bāgōng Mountain.
The Huáinán Military Governor, Xiàng Xùn, submitted a memorial requesting to combine the forces from Guǎnglíng to attack Shòuchūn with full strength,
and after capturing the city,
to then plan further advances.
An edict granted permission.
Xùn sealed the government storehouses and handed them over to the officials in charge of Yáng Prefecture.
He ordered Yáng Prefecture's subordinate generals to divide and patrol the city in sections.
Not the slightest violation occurred.
The people of Yáng Prefecture were moved and pleased.
When the army returned,
some carried dried provisions to see them off.
The defending general of Chú Prefecture also abandoned the city and left.
They all led their troops towards Shòuchūn.
The Tang generals requested to occupy strategic positions to intercept the Later Zhou army.
Sòng Qíqiū said:
"If we do this,
the resentment will only deepen."
He then ordered the generals to each defend their positions,
and not to rashly attack the Zhou troops.
As a result, the siege of Shòuchūn became increasingly urgent.
Prince Qí Jǐngdá stationed his army at Háozhōu,
providing distant support for Shòuzhōu,
but military and administrative affairs were all handled by Chén Jué,
with Jǐngdá merely signing off on documents.
Though he commanded fifty thousand troops,
he had no intention of engaging in decisive battle.
Alas!
The fall of Xiāngyáng in recent years,
was it not due to the crime of relief troops not advancing!
No one dared to speak of it.
29 In the eighth month,
on the Wùchén day,
the Duanming Palace Academician Wáng Pǔ and the Deputy Director of the Directorate of Astronomy Wáng Chùnà
compiled the Xiǎndé Qīntiān Calendar,
and presented it to the emperor.
Earlier,
Wáng Chùnà had privately created the Míngxuán Calendar at home,
which was based on the Chóngxuán Calendar used during the Tang dynasty and clarified it.
The emperor, considering Wáng Pǔ knowledgeable in calendrical calculations,
ordered him to compile and finalize it.
It was divided into four sections: calculating the sun, calculating the moon, calculating the stars, and calculating the cycles,
combined into a calendrical classic.
They also wrote a one-volume detailed calendar of the seven luminaries for the third year of the Xiǎndé era,
which became the Qīntiān Calendar.
30 The Palace Front Commanding General and Yìchéng Military Commissioner Zhāng Yǒngdé was stationed at Xiàcài.
The Tang general Lín Rénzhào led naval and land forces to relieve Shòuchūn;
Yǒngdé engaged him in battle.
Rénzhào loaded boats with firewood and fodder,
and taking advantage of the wind, set them ablaze,
intending to burn the pontoon bridge at Xiàcài.
Suddenly, the wind shifted direction,
and the Tang troops were defeated and retreated.
Yǒngdé had over a thousand feet of iron cables
placed about ten paces from the pontoon bridge,
stretched across the Huái River,
anchored with large logs,
thus preventing the Tang troops from approaching.
31 In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Duanming Palace Academician, Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Provisional Administrator of Kāifēng Prefecture Wáng Pǔ was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue,
and concurrently Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
32 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Chóngjìn reported that the Tang troops had invaded Shèngtáng.
The Iron Cavalry Commanding Officer Wáng Yànshēng and others repelled them,
beheading over three thousand.
Yànshēng
was from Shǔ.
33 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the emperor said to his attending officials:
"In recent dynasties, the collection of grain and cloth
often did not wait until the harvest or spinning was completed."
"Attending officials"
is followed by
the word "said,"
which completes the meaning of the text.
"Recent dynasties"
means modern times.
"Dynasty"
is pronounced zhāo;
the same below.
From now on, the summer tax will be levied in the sixth month,
and the autumn tax in the tenth month.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The levying of the two taxes
both begins on the first day of the month.
34 The Shānnán East Circuit Military Commissioner, Grand Commandant, and concurrently Secretariat Director Ān Shěnqí had guarded Xiāngzhōu for over ten years.
In the twelfth year of the Hàn Tiānfù era,
Ān Shěnqí was stationed at Xiāngyáng,
and by now it had been ten years.
He was appointed Grand Preceptor
and sent back to his garrison.
After his departure,
the emperor asked the chancellor:
"Did you all see him off?"
They replied:
"We escorted him to the south of the city,
and Shěnqí deeply felt the imperial grace."
Since the Five Dynasties,
when regional commanders came to court,
some were detained and not sent back,
or were reassigned;
now he was promoted and sent back to his garrison,
hence his gratitude.
"In recent dynasties, many have not treated the feudal lords with sincerity and trust.
Even if some feudal lords wished to demonstrate loyalty and integrity,
they had no means to do so.
If the ruler can but avoid breaking his trust,
why worry that the feudal lords will not give their allegiance!"
35 On the Rénwǔ day,
Zhāng Yǒngdé reported defeating Tang troops at Xiàcài.
At that time, the Tang forces again attacked Yǒngdé with their navy.
Yǒngdé ordered skilled swimmers at night to dive beneath their ships,
and tether them with iron chains,
then launched an assault.
The ships could neither advance nor retreat,
and many drowned.
Yǒngdé took off his golden belt to reward the skilled swimmers.
36 On the Jiǎshēn day,
Tàizǔ Huángdì was appointed as the Dìngguó Military Commissioner and concurrently Palace Front Commanding General.
The Dìngguó Army
was the same as the Kuāngguó Army of Tóngzhōu.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
to avoid the imperial name,
it was changed to Dìngguó Army.
The history also records it using the later changed military designation.
37 Zhāng Yǒngdé and Lǐ Chóngjìn were not on good terms.
Yǒngdé secretly submitted a memorial accusing Chóngjìn of having disloyal intentions,
but the emperor did not believe it.
At the time, both generals commanded heavy troops,
causing widespread anxiety and fear.
One day, Chóngjìn rode alone to Yǒngdé's camp.
Lǐ Chóngjìn was then at the foot of Shòuzhōu city,
and Zhāng Yǒngdé was camped at Xiàcài.
He said to Yǒngdé:
"You and I are fortunate to be relatives and both serve as generals.
Why is the suspicion between us so deep?"
Yǒngdé's suspicions were then dispelled,
and the minds of the troops were also put at ease.
When the Tang ruler heard of this,
he sent a wax-sealed letter to Chóngjìn,
tempting him with great benefits.
The letter contained slanderous and divisive language;
Chóngjìn presented it to the emperor.
Earlier,
the Tang envoys Sūn Shèng and Zhōng Mó had followed the emperor to Dàliáng.
The emperor treated them very generously.
At each court assembly,
they were placed behind the officials of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
They were often summoned for audiences,
served fine wine,
and questioned about Tang affairs.
Shèng only said,
"Our ruler fears Your Majesty's divine prowess,
and serves Your Majesty with undivided loyalty."
After obtaining the Tang wax-sealed letter,
the emperor was greatly angered.
He summoned Shèng
and reproached him for not speaking truthfully.
Shèng maintained a stern expression and defended himself,
asking only for death.
When questioned about Tang's actual situation,
he remained silent and did not answer.
In the eleventh month,

the emperor ordered the Chief Recipient of Edicts Cáo Hàn to escort Shèng to the Right Army Patrol Office.
The Imperial Guard Army was divided into Left and Right Armies,
each with its own patrol office

Hàn drank several rounds of wine with him,
and calmly questioned him,
but Shèng ultimately said nothing.
Hàn then said to him:
"There is an imperial decree
granting you, sir, death."
He addressed him by the official title conferred by Tang.
Shèng asked for his robe and tablet,
straightened his clothes and cap,
faced south, bowed, and said:
"Your subject respectfully repays the state with his death."
He then submitted to execution.
Over a hundred of his followers were also killed,
and Zhōng Mó was demoted to Military Advisor of Yàozhōu.
Later, the emperor, admiring Shèng's loyalty and integrity,
regretted having him killed.
He summoned Mó
and appointed him as Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud.

The Prince of Qí, Lǐ Jǐngdá, from Háozhōu sent the Relief Commissioner and Yǒng'ān Military Commissioner Xǔ Wénzhěn, the Army Commander Biān Hào, and the Northern Front Recruitment Commissioner Zhū Yuán leading tens of thousands of troops,
to sail up the Huái River to rescue it.
They encamped at Zǐjīn Mountain,
setting up over ten stockades like a string of pearls,
exchanging beacon and fire signals morning and evening with the city,
and also built a covered roadway reaching to Shòuchūn,
intending to transport grain to supply it,
stretching for several tens of lǐ.
Just as it was about to reach Shòuchūn,
Lǐ Chóngjìn intercepted and attacked,
routing them heavily,
with five thousand dead,

On the Dīngwèi day,
Chóngjìn reported this.
On the Wùshēn day,
an edict was issued that the Emperor would proceed to the Huái region the following month.
Liú Rénshàn requested that Biān Hào defend the city,

the Prince of Qí, Lǐ Jǐngdá, did not permit it,
and Rénshàn, frustrated and aggrieved, fell ill.
His youngest son, Chóngjiàn, at night took a boat to cross to the north of the Huái,
but was captured by a junior officer.
Rénshàn ordered him to be cut in two at the waist.
None among his attendants dared to intervene.
The Army Supervisor Zhōu Tínggòu wept at the central gate to plead for him;
Rénshàn refused.
Tínggòu again sent someone to plead with Rénshàn's wife for help.
The lady said:
"It is not that I do not love Chóngjiàn,
but military law cannot be bent for private favor,
and reputation and integrity cannot be compromised.
If we pardon him,
then the Liú family will be a gate of disloyalty,
and what face would I and my lord have to show the officers and soldiers!"
She urged that the execution be carried out,
and only then performed the mourning rites.
The officers and soldiers were all moved to tears.
Commentators, considering the Táng relief forces still strong,
mostly requested to withdraw the troops.
The Emperor was doubtful.
Lǐ Gǔ was ill and resting at his residence.
In the second month,
on the Bǐngyín day,

Gǔ submitted a memorial,

"Shòuchūn is in dire straits and exhausted,

The Emperor was pleased.

(Sacrificial vessels:
items such as zūn, yí, fǔ, guǐ, biān, dòu.
Sacrificial jades:

the blue bì to ritually honor Heaven, the yellow cóng to ritually honor Earth, the green guī to ritually honor the East, the red zhāng to ritually honor the South, the white hǔ to ritually honor the West, the black huáng to ritually honor the North.)
At that time, the ritual officials and erudites, in accordance with the edict, deliberated on the regulations for sacrificial vessels and jades.
The Chancellor of the National University, Yǐn Zhuō, cited Cuī Líng'ēn's Sānlǐ Yìzōng, which says: The blue bì
is used to ritually honor Heaven,
its length is twelve inches,
modeling the twelve hours of Heaven.
He also cited explanations from the Jiāngdū Collection and the Báihǔ Tōng,
saying that bì are all round on the outside and square on the inside.
It also says,
the yellow cóng is used to ritually honor Earth,
its length is ten inches,
modeling the number of Earth.
The cóng is square on the outside and round on the inside,
octagonal and with a hole.
The Erudite of the National University, Niè Chóngyì, believed that the bì is round both inside and out,
with a diameter of nine inches.
According to the diagrams of Ruǎn and Zhèng Xuán, both say nine inches.
The Zhōulǐ Yùrén zhí,
also mentions a nine-inch bì.
And he cited the Ěryǎ, which says: When the rim is twice the hole, it is called a bì;
when the hole is twice the rim, it is called a yuàn;
when the rim and hole are equal, it is called a huán.
Guō Pú's commentary says: The hole,
is the aperture.
The rim,
is the edge.
But it does not record measurements.
Chóngyì also cited the Dōngguān Yùrén, which says: The hole of a bì is three inches.
The Ěryǎ says: When the rim is twice the hole, it is called a bì.
That means each side of the rim is three inches,
together with the hole making nine inches total,
thus it is clear that the bì is nine inches.
Chóngyì also said: The yellow cóng is octagonal to symbolize Earth,
each corner is cut out by one inch and six fen,
making a total length of eight inches,
and a thickness of one inch.
According to the Zhōulǐ diagram and Ruǎn's diagram, neither has a hole.
He also cited the Dōngguān Yùrén, which says: The cóng
is octagonal and without a hole.
Chóngyì also said: Cóng, huáng, guī, bì
are all vessels for ritually honoring Heaven and Earth,
yet the Ěryǎ only mentions that bì, huán, yuàn these three have holes,
and does not mention the others, cóng, huáng and various vessels,
thus it is clear that the yellow cóng is octagonal and without a hole.
At that time, Tián Mǐn, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and those below him considered Chóngyì's citations from the main text of the Zhōulǐ to be correct,
and so followed him.
