but ultimately, it was Hào and Zhāoyuǎn who caused Shǔ's destruction.
8. Zhōu troops attacked Chǔzhōu.
After over forty days,
the Táng Chǔzhōu Fángyùshǐ Zhāng Yànqīng firmly held out and would not surrender.
Yǐsì day:
The Emperor personally supervised the generals in attacking it,
encamping beneath the city walls.
Dīngwèi day:
it was captured.
Yànqīng and the Dūjiān Zhèng Zhāoyè still led their troops in resisting and fighting.
When their arrows and blades were all exhausted,
Yànqīng raised a rope-bed to fight and died.
Of the over one thousand troops under his command,
to the death, not a single one surrendered.
When Táng lost Huáinán,
there were still those who died defending its cities and borders.
9. Gāo Bǎoróng sent Zhǐhuīshǐ Wèi Lín
to lead a hundred warships east down the river to join in attacking Táng,
reaching Èzhōu.
10. Gēngxū day:
Shǔ established the Yǒngníng Army in Guǒzhōu,
placing Tōngzhōu under its jurisdiction.
11. Táng made Tiāncháng into Xióngzhōu,
appointing Jiànwǔjūnshǐ Yì Wényūn as its Cìshǐ.
Second month,
Jiǎyín day:
Wényūn surrendered the city.
12. Wùwǔ day:
The Emperor departed from Chǔzhōu;
Dīngmǎo day:
he reached Yángzhōu.
He ordered Hán Lìngkūn to mobilize over ten thousand laborers
to build a small city in the southeastern corner of the old city to administer it.
This is the present-day large city of Yángzhōu.
The old city of Yángzhōu occupied Shǔgāng to the west,
and encompassed Léibēi to the north.
"Zhì"
is pronounced "zhí."
13. Yǐhài day:
Huángzhōu Cìshǐ Sī Chāo reported that together with Kònghè Yòuxiāng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Wáng Shěnqí, they had attacked Táng's Shūzhōu,
capturing its Cìshǐ Shī Rénwàng.
14. Bǐngzǐ day:
Jiànxióng Jiédùshǐ Zhēndìng Yáng Tíngzhāng reported defeating Northern Hán troops beneath the walls of Xízhōu.
At that time, Xízhōu Cìshǐ Sūn Yì died suddenly.
Tíngzhāng said to the Dūjiān, Xiánjùshǐ Lǐ Qiānpǔ:
"Now the imperial carriage is on a southern campaign,
Zézhōu has no defending general."
("Zézhōu"
should be
"Xízhōu.")
"If we memorialize and wait for a reply,
then this isolated city will be in danger."
He immediately sent a dispatch for Qiānpǔ to temporarily administer Xízhōu affairs.
When Qiānpǔ arrived, he repaired the defenses.
Not long after,
Northern Hán troops indeed arrived.
The various generals requested to quickly rescue them,
but Tíngzhāng said:
"Xízhōu's walls are strong and its generals excellent,
it will not be easily taken."
The Northern Hán attacked the city for a long time without success.
Tíngzhāng, estimating they were weary and unprepared,
secretly made an agreement with Qiānpǔ.
Each recruited over a hundred daring men to raid their camp at night.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Jìnzhōu northwest to Xízhōu is 250 lǐ.
Yáng Tíngzhāng must have secretly moved his army there,
agreeing with Xízhōu,
to act in coordination from inside and out.
They beheaded over a thousand;
the Northern Hán troops then withdrew and left.
15. Third month,
Rénwú day, the first day of the month:
The Emperor went to Tàizhōu.
16. Dīnghài day:
Táng issued a general pardon,
and changed the reign title to Jiāotài.
17. The Tang Crown Prince Jǐngsuì submitted ten memorials in succession resigning his position,
stating:
"Now that the state is in peril and I cannot support it,
I request to leave and take up a regional governorship.
Prince Yān Hóngjì, as the legitimate eldest son, has military achievements;
Hóngjì
was the legitimate eldest son of the Tang ruler.
His military achievements
refer to using Chái Kèhóng to defeat the Wúyuè army and lift the siege of Chángzhōu,
as recorded in the third year of the previous volume.
'Eldest'
is pronounced zhǎng.
I respectfully present the crown prince's seal and documents."
Prince Qí Jǐngdá also resigned from his position as marshal due to military defeat.
The Tang ruler then established Jǐngsuì as Prince of Jìn,

conferring upon him the titles of General of Heavenly Strategy, Marshal of the Jiangnán West Circuit Military Forces, Grand Governor of Hóngzhōu, Grand Commandant, and President of the Department of State Affairs.
He appointed Jǐngdá as Marshal of the Zhèxī Circuit and Grand Governor of Rùnzhōu.
Jǐngdá, because military operations were ongoing in Zhèxī,
firmly declined.
Although the Wúyuè army had retreated after defeat at Chángzhōu,
they were still remotely coordinating with the Central Kingdom.
Hóngjì was established as crown prince,
participating in decision-making on various governmental matters.
Hóngjì was a suspicious, harsh, and severe person.
Among Jǐngsuì's attendants, those who had not yet left the Eastern Palace
were immediately expelled.
This sets the stage for Hóngjì's poisoning of Jǐngsuì.
He did not dare to involve himself in affairs,
devoting himself solely to the enjoyment of classical texts.
Cóngjiā was the later ruler Yù.
18. On Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor went to Yíngluán Garrison.
Yíngluán Garrison
was originally Táng's Báishā.
When the Wú ruler Yáng Pǔ arrived at Báishā,
to review the naval forces,
Xú Wēn came from Jīnlíng to see him,
and thus Báishā was made Yíngluán Garrison.
The location of Báishā
originally belonged to Jiāngdū.
Táng divided Jiāngdū to establish Yǒngzhēn County.
Under Wú it was Yíngluán Garrison,
under Sòng it was Zhēnzhōu.
He dispatched the navy to attack the Táng army,
defeating them.
The Emperor heard that several hundred Táng warships were anchored at Dōngbù Island,
intending to head for the estuary to block the routes to Sūzhōu and Hángzhōu.
Dōngbù Island
is in the great river southeast of Tàizhōu,
originally a maritime island of sand.
Sòng Bái said: Dōngbù Island is southeast of Tōngzhōu,
within the boundaries of Hǎimén County, Tōngzhōu.
Bù
is pronounced bù.
"Zhōu"
should be
"island".
The Right Divine Martial Commander-in-Chief Sòng Yánwò led the naval forces,
proceeding down the river.
On Jiǎwǔ,
Yánzhāo reported a great defeat of the Táng army at Dōngbù Island;
the Emperor sent Lǐ Chóngjìn to lead troops towards Lúzhōu.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
Yáng Xíngmì rose from Lúzhōu.
After establishing his state,
it became an important garrison.
When the Zhōu army crossed the Huái,
Shū, Qí, and Huáng first submitted and attached themselves,
only Lú had not fallen,
likely because it had many stationed troops,
and the Zhōu army did not dare to lightly attack it.
Qù
is pronounced qū.
The Táng ruler, hearing the Emperor was on the river,
feared he would cross south,
and was ashamed to lower his title and declare himself a vassal.
So he sent the Vice-Minister of War Chén Jué to present a memorial,
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Ten Kingdoms Chronicle:
"Sent the Commissioner of Military Affairs Chén Jué to present a memorial."
The Veritable Records records his memorial stating:
"Now I send Left Admonisher, Vice-Minister of War, your subject Chén Jué to personally hear your imperial command."
This was probably the official title he held at the time.
Now we follow this.
To receive orders from the Central Kingdom.
At that time in Huáinán, only Lú, Shū, Qí, and Huáng had not been taken.
On Bǐngshēn,
Jué arrived at Yíngluán,
saw the strength of the Zhōu troops,
and reported to the Emperor,
requesting to send someone across the river to obtain the memorial,
offering the four prefectures' territory,
drawing the river as the boundary,
to seek a cessation of hostilities,
his words were very sorrowful.
The Emperor said:
"I originally raised the army only to take north of the river.
If your ruler can submit the entire country,
what more could I ask for!"
Jué bowed in thanks and withdrew.
On Dīngyǒu,
Jué requested to send his subordinate, Gate Reception Commissioner Liú Chéngyù, to Jīnlíng.
The Emperor bestowed a letter to the Táng ruler,
addressing him as
"The Emperor respectfully inquires of the State Master of Jiāngnán",
comforting and accepting him.
On Wùxū,
Wúyuè reported dispatching the

Commanding Officer of the Upper Guard, Prefect of Chùzhōu Shào Kěqiān, and Prefect of Xiùzhōu Lù Yànzhū, with four hundred warships and seventeen thousand soldiers to station on the south bank of Tōngzhōu.
After Zhōu conquered the Jìnghǎi Army,
it established Tōngzhōu.
The south bank of Tōngzhōu is the location of Fúshān Town in Chángshú County, Sūzhōu,
which was the Nánshā of the Eastern Jìn.
The Táng ruler again sent Liú Chéngyù to present a memorial calling himself State Master of Táng,
requesting to offer the four prefectures north of the river,
and to annually deliver tribute goods amounting to one hundred
thousand.
Thereupon, the area north of the river was completely pacified,
gaining fourteen prefectures,
and sixty counties.
Guāng, Shòu, Lú, Shū, Qí, Huáng, Chú, Hé, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Yáng, Tài, and Tōng, fourteen prefectures.
On Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor bestowed a letter to the Táng ruler,
instructing that:
"The armies along the river and those of Liǎngzhè, Húnán, and Jīngnán shall all be disbanded and return.
The three routes of Lú, Qí, and Huáng
are also ordered to gather their troops near the outskirts.
Referring to the armies Zhōu dispatched to attack Lú, Qí, and Huáng.
'Near the outskirts'
means outside the near suburbs.
You may send someone to summon the commanders and hand over the cities and towns to them.
River boats and ships that need to come and go
shall all be ordered to proceed to the north bank to be guided."
All Táng boats and ships on the north bank
were permitted to be guided to the south bank.
On Xīnchǒu,
Chén Jué took his leave to depart,
and another letter was bestowed upon the Táng ruler,
instructing that it was not necessary to pass the throne to his son.
On Rényín,
the Emperor went from Yíngluán back to Yángzhōu.
On Guǐmǎo,
an edict ordered the Wúyuè and Jīngnán armies to each return to their own circuits;
bestowed upon Qián Hóngchù thirty thousand bolts of silk to reward his army,
and upon Gāo Bǎoróng ten thousand bolts.
The Wúyuè army was at Nánshā,
the Jīngnán army reached Èzhōu,
each was rewarded to disband and return.
Reward,
pronounced kào.
On Jiǎchén,
the Bǎoxìn Army was established at Lúzhōu,
with the Right Dragon Martial Commander-in-Chief Zhào Kuāngzàn as military governor.
On Bǐngwǔ,
the Táng ruler sent Féng Yánsǐ to present silver, silk, cash, tea, and grain totaling one million to reward the army.
Silver in taels, silk in bolts, cash in strings, tea in catties,
grain in piculs,
each counted in ten thousands,
the total number being one million.
On Jǐyǒu,
he ordered Sòng Yánwò to lead three thousand naval troops to patrol up the river.
On Gēngxū,
an edict ordered that the tombs of the former Huáinán military governor Yáng Xíngmì, the former Shēngfǔ military governor Xú Wēn, and others be given an appropriate number of guarding households;
their usurped posthumous titles were abolished,
but their former garrison towns were preserved.
Shēngfǔ is Jīnlíng.
Jīnlíng
was Táng's Shēngzhōu,
hence called Shēngfǔ.
Also entrusted the senior officials to inspect them periodically.
On Xīnhài,
the Táng ruler sent his Lord Línrǔ Xú Liáo to come in his place to offer birthday congratulations.
Meaning he presented wine for the birthday toast,
not for the imperial birthday.
The Emperor was born on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month.
Shàng
is pronounced shàng.
19. In this month,
the Biàn estuary was dredged,
guiding the river's flow to reach the Huái,
whereupon boats from the Jiāng and Huái regions could begin to pass through.
This was the transport route of the Táng period.
Since the Jiāng and Huái regions were divided and held separately,
water transport was blocked,
the waterways silted up,
now they were dredged again.
20. In summer,
the fourth month,
on Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor returned north from Yángzhōu.
21. The new Ancestral Temple was completed.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the spirit tablets were moved into the temple.
In the third year of the Guǎngshùn era of Emperor Tàizǔ,
construction of the Ancestral Temple began in Dàliáng,
and it was only now completed.
*Wǔdài Huìyào*: In the seventh month of the first year of the Guǎngshùn era of Emperor Tàizǔ,
the posthumous title of Ruìhé Emperor was conferred upon his great-great-grandfather Jǐng,
with the temple name Xìnzǔ;
the posthumous title of Míngxiàn Emperor was conferred upon his great-grandfather Chén,
with the temple name Xīzǔ;
the posthumous title of Yìshùn Emperor was conferred upon his grandfather Yùn,
with the temple name Yìzǔ;
the posthumous title of Zhāngsù Emperor was conferred upon his father Jiǎn,
with the temple name Qìngzǔ.
22. On the Xīnyǒu night,
a fire broke out in the southern part of Qiántáng city,
spreading to the inner city,
nearly destroying all government offices and residences.
At dawn on the Rénxū day,
the fire was about to reach the Zhènguó Granary.
Wúyuè King Qián Hóngchù, who had been ill for a long time,
forced himself to get up and went out to direct the firefighting efforts.
The fire was extinguished,
and he said to his attendants:
"My illness has been cured because of this disaster."
The people's minds were somewhat calmed.
23. When the Emperor was on his southern campaign,
the Khitan took advantage of the emptiness to invade.
On the Rénshēn day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng,
and ordered
Zhāng Yǒngdé to lead troops to guard the northern border.
24. In the fifth month,
on the Xīnsì day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
25. An edict was issued to reward and comfort the soldiers of the southern campaign and the newly submitted people of Huáinán.
26. On the Xīnmǎo day,
Emperor Tàizǔ was appointed to concurrently hold the position of Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ,
and Ān Shěnqí was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Pínglú.
27. Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, Guō Chóng, attacked the Khitan at Shùchéng,
and captured it.
Shùchéng,
was the Shùzhōu county of the Bóhǎi commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
renamed Shùchéng during the Suí dynasty,
and belonged to Yíngzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
In the sixth year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng dynasty, Shùchéng was demoted to a town,
and placed under Héjiān.
28. The ruler of Táng, to avoid the taboo of the Zhōu emperor's ancestor's name,
changed his name to Jǐng.
This was to avoid the taboo of the Zhōu Xìnzǔ's name.
Gēng,
pronounced as gēng.
He styled himself "Lord of the State,"
and all imperial rituals and regulations were reduced and downgraded.
He abolished his reign title,
adopted the Zhōu calendar,
and still reported this to the Ancestral Temple.
Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Co-manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, Féng Yánsì, was dismissed and made Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent;
Vice Director of the Chancellery and Co-manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, Yán Xù, was dismissed and made Junior Tutor;
Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner and Vice Minister of War, Chén Jué, was dismissed and retained only his substantive office rank.
Initially,
Féng Yánsì had persuaded the ruler of Táng with a strategy to seize the Central Plains,
and thus gained favor.
Yánsì once mocked Lièzǔ's military restraint as petty,
saying:
"The loss at Ānlù was merely a few thousand soldiers,
yet he stopped eating and sighed for ten days over it.
This refers to Lǐ Chéngyù's defeat at Ānzhōu in the fifth year of the Tiānfú era of Jìn Gāozǔ,
recorded in scroll 282.
Sàng,
pronounced sàng.
Wéi,
pronounced wèi.
How could such a person accomplish great deeds!
Is he not like the present ruler who has tens of thousands of troops campaigning abroad,
yet plays polo and feasts as usual,
truly a heroic ruler!"
Yánsì and his associates, in their discussions,
often took the world as their own responsibility,
echoing and supporting each other.
Hànlín Academician Cháng Mèngxī repeatedly said that Yánsì and others were frivolous and boastful,
and not to be trusted;
the ruler of Táng did not listen.
Mèngxī said:
"Treacherous words appear loyal,
if Your Majesty does not realize this,
the state will surely perish!"
When they submitted to Zhōu,
Yánsì's associates were talking among themselves,
and some referred to Zhōu as the "Great Court."
Mèngxī laughed loudly and said:
"You gentlemen always wanted to make your ruler a Yáo or Shùn,
how is it that today you yourselves have become a 'Minor Court'!"
The crowd fell silent.
Since the ruler of Táng submitted,
the Emperor only sent letters through his envoys,
and had never sent an envoy to his state.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
he first ordered Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud Féng Yánlǔ and Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Regalia Zhōng Mó to serve as envoys to Táng.
These two men
were originally both officials of Táng.
They also brought the current year's Qīntiān calendar.
When Liú Chéngyù returned from Jīnlíng,
see the third month above.
Huán,
pronounced huán.
Or as the original character.
He reported that Jiāngnán had no salt fields,
but the seashore had saline land,
suitable for boiling salt.
Lǔtián,
now called jiǎndì.
Lǔ,
pronounced lǔ.
Jiǎn,
pronounced jiǎn.
He requested that Hǎilíng be assigned to them to support the army.
The Emperor said:
"Hǎilíng is north of the river,
making it difficult for officials to reside together."
This means it was difficult for Zhōu officials and Táng officials to live intermingled.
At this time,
an edict was issued to supply 300,000 hú of salt annually to Jiāngnán,
and the captured Jiāngnán soldiers
were gradually returned.
29. In the sixth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, Lǐ Yún, reported attacking the Shíhuì Pass of Northern Hàn,
capturing six of its stockades.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Jìnzhōu reported that Military Supervisor Lǐ Qiānpǔ attacked Northern Hàn,
and defeated them at Xiàoyì.
Xiàoyì,
was the territory of Zhōngyáng county during the Hàn dynasty,
called Yǒng'ān during the Later Wèi,
renamed Xiàoyì in the first year of the Zhēnguān era of the Táng dynasty,
belonging to Fénzhōu,
located southeast of the prefecture.
In the fifth year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Xiàoyì was demoted to a town,
and placed under Jièxiū county.
Sòng Bái said: Xiàoyì county,
originally the territory of Císhì county of the Hàn dynasty,
during the Cáo Wèi, Zhōngyáng county was moved to its present location.
After the Yǒngjiā era, it was merged into Xíchéng.
During the Later Wèi, Xíchéng was again divided, and Yǒng'ān county was established thirty lǐ east of the present Língshí county.
In the first year of the Zhēnguān era, because the county name was the same as a county in Fúzhōu,
it was changed to Xiàoyì,
named after the virtuous conduct of a county man named Zhèng Xīng.
30. Gāo Bǎoróng sent an envoy to advise the ruler of Shǔ to become a vassal to Zhōu.
The ruler of Shǔ replied that he had sent Hú Lì with a letter to Zhōu the year before last but received no answer.
See the previous year in the scroll above.
31. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
the *Great Zhōu Penal Code* was first implemented.
32. The Emperor wanted to equalize land taxes.
On the Dīnghài day,
he had Yuán Zhěn's *Diagram of Equalized Fields* widely distributed to the various circuits.
The edict at the time said:
"Recently, I perused Yuán Zhěn's *Chángqìng Collection*,
and saw the memorial on equalizing fields he submitted while in Tóngzhōu.
Comparing the benefits and harms of that time,
he exhaustively described the situation,
enabling all the people within that region
to receive its benefits.
Preserved in the records,
it can be consulted.
Therefore, I ordered it made into a plain diagram,
directly recording the facts."
Zhěn,
pronounced zhěn.
33. In the intercalary month,
the Táng Qingyuán Military Commissioner and concurrently Secretariat Director Liú Cóngxiào
(Táng established the Qingyuán Army in Quánzhōu.)
placed a silk memorial inside a leather belt,
and came via a byway to declare his submission.
34. When the Táng Jiāngxī Marshal, Prince Jìn Lǐ Jǐngsuì, went to Hóngzhōu,
see the third month above.
He requested a senior minister to assist him.
The ruler of Táng appointed Vice Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner and Vice Minister of Works Lǐ Zhēnggǔ as Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhènnán.
Zhēnggǔ was arrogant, ruthless, arbitrary, and willful.
Although Jǐngsuì was tolerant and generous,
after a long time he could not bear it,
and often wanted to behead Zhēnggǔ,
then surrender himself to the authorities.
His attendants admonished him and he stopped,
but Jǐngsuì became dispirited and unhappy.
Crown Prince Hóngjì, while residing in the Eastern Palace, committed many unlawful acts.
The ruler of Táng was angered
and once struck him with a polo mallet, saying:
"I shall summon Jǐngsuì back again."
Yuán Cóngfàn, the Commissioner of the Zhāoqìng Palace, had followed Jǐngsuì as the Deputy Commander of Hóngzhōu.
Someone slandered Cóngfàn's son to Jǐngsuì.
Jǐngsuì wanted to kill him,
and from this, Cóngfàn harbored resentment.
Hóngjì heard of this
and secretly sent Cóngfàn to poison him.
In the eighth month,
on the Gēngchén day,
Jǐngsuì, having played polo and being extremely thirsty,
was offered a drink by Cóngfàn.
Jǐngsuì drank it and died.
Before the burial,
his body had already decomposed.
The ruler of Táng did not know of this
and posthumously honored him as Imperial Younger Brother,
bestowing the posthumous title Wénchéng.
On the Xīnshì day,
the Middle Ancestor of Southern Hàn passed away,
at the age of thirty-nine.
Jìxīng ascended the imperial throne,
changed his name to Chǎng,
and changed the era name to Dàbǎo.
Chǎng was sixteen years old,
and state affairs were all decided by the eunuch Gōng Chéngshū, Commissioner of the Yùqīng Palace.
The History of Ōu states: The Liú clan built detached palaces for excursions and hunting,
including the Southern Palace, Dàmíng, Chānghuá, Gānquán, Wánhuá, Xiùhuá, Yùqīng, and Tàiwēi Palaces,
all of which had commissioners appointed to oversee them.
Officials of the central ministries and departments merely held nominal positions.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Táng first established a Memorial Presentation Office in Dàliáng.
This was because they were now subjects.
On the Rénchén day,
[the Emperor] ordered Cáo Bīn of Língshòu, Commissioner of the Western Upper Pavilion Gate, to be sent as an envoy to Wúyuè,
bestowing upon the King of Wúyuè, Qián Hóngchù, two hundred sets of cavalry armor and
five thousand sets of infantry armor, along with other weapons.
After completing his mission, Bīn hurried back,
refusing to accept any gifts.
The people of Wúyuè pursued him with light boats to give him gifts,
repeating this several times.
Bīn said:
"If I ultimately do not accept,
it would be to steal a reputation."
He then fully recorded the quantities
and, upon returning, presented them.
The Emperor said:
"Former envoys on missions
begged and were never satisfied,
causing all regions to look down upon the court's commands.
That you could act thus
is very good;
however, since they gave these to you,
you may keep them for yourself."
Only then did Bīn bow and accept them,
but he distributed them all among relatives and acquaintances,
keeping none at home.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Féng Yánlǔ and Zhōng Mó arrived from Táng.
The ruler of Táng submitted a handwritten memorial thanking him for his grace.
"Handwritten memorial" means
written by his own hand.
"The grace of Heaven and Earth is generous,
the grace of parents is profound.
A son does not thank his father,
how can a man repay Heaven?
Only with a loyal heart
can one requite the great creation."
He also requested to be treated as a regional governor,
and to be granted imperial edicts.
He further stated:
"There are matters of sentiment for which I have ordered Zhōng Mó to memorialize,
requesting that he be allowed to return early."
The ruler of Táng also ordered Mó to inform the Emperor
that he wished to abdicate in favor of the Crown Prince.
In the ninth month,
on the Dǐngsì day,
[the Emperor] appointed Yánlǔ as Vice Minister of Justice and Mó as Supervising Secretary.
The ruler of Táng
again sent Yīn Chóngyì, Minister of Personnel and Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to congratulate him on the Tiānqīng Festival.
The Emperor was born on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month,
which was established as the Tiānqīng Festival.
The Emperor planned to attack Shǔ.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
he appointed Gāo Fáng, Vice Minister of Revenue, as Commander of the Southwest Land and Water Forces,
with Lǐ Yù, Senior Advisor to the Heir Apparent, as his Deputy.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,

the Emperor returned Féng Yánlǔ, along with General of the Left Imperial Gate Guard Xǔ Wénzhěn, General of the Right Thousand Bull Guard Biān Hào, and Minister of the Imperial Armory Zhōu Tínggòu, to Táng.
Féng Yánlǔ's capture is recorded in the 292nd scroll, third year.
Xǔ Wénzhěn and Biān Hào's capture is recorded in the previous scroll, last year.
Zhōu Tínggòu's surrender is also recorded in that year.
They were discarded and not employed again.
Gāo Bǎoróng sent a second letter to the ruler of Shǔ.
The first letter
is mentioned above in the sixth month.
The ruler of Shǔ gathered his generals and ministers to discuss it.
Lǐ Hào said:
"To comply would bring humiliation upon our sovereign and father;
to defy would surely bring the Zhōu army upon us.
Can our generals resist Zhōu?"
The generals all said:
"With Your Majesty's sagely brilliance
and our impregnable rivers and mountains,
how can we submit at the mere sight of their banners!
We have fed our horses and sharpened our weapons
precisely for a day like this.
We, your subjects, request to defend the altars of state with our lives!"
On the Dīngyǒu day,
the ruler of Shǔ ordered Hào to draft a letter
firmly rejecting it.
An edict ordered Ài Yǐng of Xūchéng, Senior Adviser to the Left, and thirty-three others to travel to various prefectures
to equalize and fix the land taxes.
Xūchéng County was attached to Yùnzhōu.
It was the Xūchāng County of Táng.
Later, Táng avoided the taboo of the temple name of the Revered Ancestor
and changed it to Xūchéng.
Ài
is a surname.
The *Annals of Master Yàn*
mentions a senior official named Ài Kǒng in Qí.
The *Comprehensive Accounts of Customs*
mentions Páng Jiǎn's mother, née Ài.
"Travel"
is pronounced xiàng, fourth tone.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
an edict ordered all prefectures to combine villages,
generally forming groups of one hundred households,
with each group appointing three elders as heads.
"Elder"
means old.
Each group had three elders serve as its heads.
"Head"
is pronounced zhǎng, third tone.
Wooden carvings of a plowman and a silkworm woman were made
and placed in the palace courtyard.
He ordered Sòng Yánwò, Military Commissioner of Wǔshèng, to patrol the river with a naval force.
Gāo Bǎoróng memorialized,
having heard that the imperial army was about to attack Shǔ,
requesting to lead a naval force towards the Three Gorges.
An edict praised him.
In the eleventh month,
on the Gēngxū day,
an order was issued for Dòu Yǎn to compile the *Great Zhōu Comprehensive Rites* and the *Great Zhōu Standard Music*.
Dòu Yǎn's request last year to fix rites and music is recorded in the previous scroll.
On the Xīnhài day,
Southern Hàn buried Emperor Wénwǔ Guāngmíng Xiào in the Zhāo Mausoleum,
with the temple name Middle Ancestor.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
the ruler of Táng again sent Zhōng Mó, Vice Minister of Rites, for an audience.
Lǐ Yù reached Cháng'ān.
Someone said
"Shǔ's Guī'ān Garrison is over three hundred *lǐ* south of Cháng'ān,
and can be taken by surprise attack."
The Guī'ān Garrison
was likely within the boundaries of Shǔ's Jīnzhōu.
He sent a dispatch to Wáng Yànchāo, Military Commissioner of Yǒngxìng,
requesting two hundred soldiers.
Yànchāo considered the road to Guī'ān treacherous and difficult to capture,
but Yù said:
"I have received a secret decree."
Yànchāo had no choice but to give them to him.
Yù led them to go.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Chéngxūn, the Garrison Commander of Shǔ's Guī'ān, relying on the dangerous terrain, ambushed them,
killed Yù,
and his entire force was lost.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
the ruler of Shǔ appointed Zhào Chóngtāo, Commander of the Right Imperial Guard Infantry, as Northern Campaign Commander.
On the Bǐngxū day,
he appointed Mèng Yíyè, Commander of the Imperial Guard and Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn, concurrently Secretariat Director, as Campaign Commander of Zhāowǔ and Wénzhōu.
The Zhāowǔ Army
was in Lìzhōu.
From Lìzhōu to Wénzhōu,
he was entrusted with controlling the strategic passes of Jiāngyóu and Jiàngé.
Hán Bǎozhēn, Military Commissioner of Shānnán West Circuit, was appointed Northern Area Campaign Commander,
leading an army of sixty thousand,
and stationed them in separate key locations to prepare against Zhōu.
On the Bǐngxū day,
an edict ordered that all various tax households and salary households be strictly returned to the prefectures and counties.
In early Táng,
various offices established capital funds for government offices,
using trade to generate interest,
which was calculated based on the number of officials for monthly allowances.
Later, these office capital funds were abolished,
and seven thousand wealthy households from across the land were made government clerks,
collecting taxes from them,
and distributing them according to the number of officials.
These were the so-called tax households.
Táng also lightly levied a year's tax,
entrusting it to wealthy households,
and used the monthly interest to pay salaries.
These were the so-called salary households.
51. Initially,
the Grand Tutor of Táng and concurrently Grand Councilor of the Right, Duke of Chǔ, Sòng Qíqiū, had formed many factions and cliques,
wishing to monopolize and solidify his power at court.
Impetuous careerists vied to attach themselves to him,
praising and lauding him as the state's senior statesman.
The Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioners Chén Jué and Deputy Commissioner Lǐ Zhēnggǔ, relying on Sòng Qíqiū's influence,
were especially arrogant and insolent.
When Xǔ Wénzhěn and others were defeated at Zǐjīn Shān,
Jué fled back from Háozhōu along with Qíqiū and Jǐngdá.
(For events, see the previous year in the preceding scroll.)
The Lord of Táng once sighed, saying:
"How has my state come to this in a single day!"
With this, tears fell.
Zhēnggǔ said:
"Your Majesty should train troops to resist the enemy;
what use is weeping?
Have you perhaps drunk too much,
or is your wet nurse not present?"
The Lord of Táng's countenance changed,
yet Zhēnggǔ's manner remained completely self-possessed.
It happened that the Director of Astrology memorialized:
"The celestial phenomena show an anomaly;
the ruler should abdicate his position to avert disaster."
The Lord of Táng then said:
"With calamities and difficulties pressing heavily,
I wish to lay aside the myriad affairs of state,
and settle my mind in serene tranquility.
To whom can I entrust the state?"
Zhēnggǔ said:
"Lord Sòng
is the master architect of the state.
If Your Majesty is weary of the myriad affairs,
why not hand over the entire state to him!"
Jué said:
"Your Majesty should reside deep within the palace;
all state affairs should be delegated to Lord Sòng,
to act first and report afterwards.
We ministers will merely enter to attend upon you from time to time,
to discuss Buddhism and Daoism, nothing more."
The Lord of Táng was inwardly angered,
and immediately ordered the Secretariat Drafter of Yùzhāng, Chén Qiáo, to draft an edict to implement this.
(Hóngzhōu is Yùzhāng Commandery.)
Chén Qiáo said:
"Once Your Majesty signs this edict,
your servant will never see you again!"
He then exhaustively argued why it should not be done.
The Lord of Táng laughed and said:
"So you also know it is wrong?"
He then stopped the plan.
Consequently, when the Prince of Jìn was sent out to govern a commandery,
Zhēnggǔ was appointed as his deputy.
(For events, see above.)
He was also removed from his close court positions.
Zhōng Mó had always been on good terms with Lǐ Démíng,
and because of Démíng's death, he bore a grudge against Qíqiū.
(Lǐ Démíng's death is recorded in the third year of the preceding scroll.)
He said to the Lord of Táng:
"Qíqiū, taking advantage of the state's peril,
hastily plotted usurpation and theft of the throne.
Chén Jué and Lǐ Zhēnggǔ were his wings and claws.
In principle, this cannot be tolerated."
When Chén Jué returned from Zhōu,
(see the third month above)
he said, "I heard that Jiāngnán's successive years of defying orders
were all due to the plans of Chief Minister Yán Xù.
You should execute him for me."
The Lord of Táng knew that Jué had long been at odds with Xù,
and therefore did not believe him.
Zhōng Mó requested to verify this with Zhōu
(to investigate and verify the truth or falsehood of his words with Zhōu).
He submitted a memorial stating:
"The prolonged resistance to the Imperial Army
was entirely due to my own foolish delusion,
not Yán Xù's crime."
The Emperor (of Zhōu) heard this
and said in great surprise:
"If it is truly so,
then Xù is a loyal minister."
(Meaning, if Yán Xù indeed devised plans for his lord to resist Zhōu, he was a loyal minister.)
"How could I instruct someone to kill a loyal minister!"
Mó returned
and reported this to the Lord of Táng.
The Lord of Táng wished to execute Qíqiū and others,
and again sent Mó to report and seek instructions from the Emperor.
The Emperor, considering them ministers of another state,
expressed neither approval nor disapproval.
On the jǐhài day,
the Lord of Táng ordered the Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Yīn Chóngyì, to draft an edict exposing the crimes and wickedness of Qíqiū, Jué, and Zhēnggǔ.
He permitted Qíqiū to return to his former seclusion at Jiǔhuá Shān,
with his official titles and ranks all remaining as before.
(Sòng Qíqiū's seclusion at Jiǔhuá Shān is recorded in scroll 277, the second year of the Chángxīng era of Táng Míngzōng, which was the third year of the Tàihé era of Wú Ruìhuáng.)
He was to be settled in Xuānzhōu.
Zhēnggǔ was stripped of his offices and ranks
and ordered to commit suicide.
Their associates and partisans were not interrogated.
Envoys were sent to report this to Zhōu.
52. On the bǐngwǔ day,
Shǔ appointed the Patrol and Pacification Commissioner of the Xiá region, Gāo Yànchóu, as Campaign Commander.
53. Ān Yǒujìn, a servant of the Military Commissioner of Pínglú, Grand Preceptor, and Grand Councilor of the Right, Prince of Chén, Ān Shěnqí, had an affair with Shěnqí's favorite concubine.
The concubine, fearing the affair would be exposed,
plotted with Yǒujìn to kill Shěnqí.
Yǒujìn refused.
The concubine said:
"If not,
I will turn around and accuse you."
Yǒujìn, afraid, complied.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
Shěnqí was drunk and sleeping soundly.
The concubine took the sword Shěnqí used as a pillow
and gave it to Yǒujìn, who killed him with it.
They then killed all the serving maids in the tent to eliminate witnesses.
Several days later,
his son, Shǒuzhōng, finally learned of it
and arrested Yǒujìn and others,
executing them.
2. Initially, when the officials were about to set up the ceremonial guard,
they had the musical instruments set up in the palace courtyard the night before.
(Setting them up the previous night is called 'setting up overnight'.)
(The character 縣 is read as xuán;
the same applies below.)
Seeing that among the bells and chime stones there were some set up but not struck,
he asked the musicians,
but none could answer.
He then ordered Dòu Yǎn to investigate and discuss ancient and modern practices,
to examine and correct the ceremonial music.
Wáng Pǔ was broadly knowledgeable about musical temperament.
The Emperor consulted him on musical matters.
Pǔ submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Ritual is used to regulate form,
music to govern the heart.
When form is harmonious externally and the heart is harmonious internally,
there has never been a case where the world was not well-ordered.
Therefore, when ritual and music are cultivated above,
the myriad states are transformed below.
The teachings of the sage succeed without severity,
and his governance is orderly without strictness."
(These are words of Confucius recorded in the Classic of Filial Piety.)
(治 is read with the pronunciation zhì.)
Music is born from the human heart, and sound is formed by objects.
Once the sound of objects is formed,
it can again influence the human heart.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor blew a pipe nine inches long
and obtained the correct sound of the Yellow Bell.
Half of it produced the clear sound,
double of it produced the slow sound.
By the method of adding or subtracting one-third, the twelve pitches were generated.
(Taking one-third and adding or subtracting it, generating upwards and downwards, the twelve pitches were completed.)
This formed one key.
Altogether, with twelve keys and eighty-four modes, the system was fully prepared.
It suffered the destruction of learning under Qín,
and throughout successive dynasties, those who dealt with music rarely could use it.
In the era of Táng Tàizōng,
Zǔ Xiàosūn and Zhāng Wénshōu examined and corrected the grand music,
completing the eighty-four modes.
(See scroll 192, the first year of the Zhēnguàn era.)
(The character 調 is read as diào;
the same applies below.)
Instruments and craftsmen were lost by eighty or ninety percent.
By the time of Huáng Cháo,
they were utterly swept away without a trace.
At that time, there was the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Erudite, Yīn Yíngsūn,
who, according to the Artificers' Record,
cast twelve bó bells
and two hundred and forty biān bells.
(Large bells are called bó.
Sixteen small bells hung together on one rack are called biān bells.)
(Bó is pronounced bó.)
Those currently displayed are these.
Although they have the shape of bells and chime stones,
they utterly lack harmonious resonance.
The bó bells are struck without regard to musical pitch,
merely in a cyclical pattern.
The biān bells and biān chime stones are merely hung there.
The string, bamboo, gourd, and clay instruments only have seven notes,
named the palace note of the Yellow Bell.
Of these, nine melodies survive.
Upon examination, three melodies conform to the pitches,
while six melodies involve various modes.
Indeed, the decay and deficiency of music
has never been worse than today.
Your Majesty’s military achievements are already illustrious,
and you now turn your attention to rites and music.
Since I have studied musical temperament,
you have shown me the ancient and modern records of music
and commanded me to deliberate upon them.
I have carefully followed the ancient method,
using black millet to determine the standard foot,
and made a pipe for the huángzhōng pitch, nine inches long and three-tenths of an inch in diameter,
which corresponds to the present sound of huángzhōng.
Proceeding from this,
I derived the twelve pitches.
Considering that blowing the various pipes interchangeably
is inconvenient for producing sounds,
I then made a pitch-standard,
with thirteen strings,
each nine feet long.
This pitch-standard
is actually the legacy of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
who in turn based it on Jīng Fáng’s method.
By setting bridges in sequence,
I obtained the eleven pitches,
along with the clear sound of huángzhōng,
and cyclically used seven pitches to form a mode.
The master of the mode
is the gōng note;
then follow zhǐ, shāng, yǔ, jué, biàngōng, and biànzhǐ.
When the sound of the mode’s master is produced,
it returns to the pitch of its fundamental note,
and the seven sounds respond in succession without confusion,
thus forming a key.
In all, there are eighty-one keys.
Wáng Pǔ’s words say: “Having received the imperial command, I accordingly followed the Zhōu method,
using black millet to verify and fix the foot measure,
nine inches long,
with an inner diameter of three-tenths of an inch,
to make the huángzhōng pipe,
which corresponds to the currently existing sound of huángzhōng.
Using the method of mutual generation from above and below to deduce,
I obtained the twelve pitch pipes.
Considering that blowing the various pipes interchangeably
is inconvenient for producing sounds,
I then made a pitch-standard,
with thirteen strings to propagate the sounds,
each nine feet long when strung,
all like the sound of huángzhōng;
on the eighth string, setting a bridge at six feet,
gives línzhōng;
on the third string, setting a bridge at eight feet,
gives tàicù;
on the tenth string, setting a bridge at five feet, three inches, and four-tenths,
gives nányú;
on the fifth string, setting a bridge at seven feet, one inch, and three-tenths,
gives gūxiǎn;
on the twelfth string, setting a bridge at four feet, seven inches, and five-tenths,
gives yìngzhōng;
on the seventh string, setting a bridge at six feet, three inches, and three-tenths,
gives ruíbīn;
on the second string, setting a bridge at eight feet, four inches, and four-tenths,
gives dàlǚ;
on the ninth string, setting a bridge at five feet, six inches, and three-tenths,
gives yízé;
on the fourth string, setting a bridge at seven feet, five inches, and one-tenth,
gives jiǎzhōng;
on the eleventh string, setting a bridge at five feet and one-tenth of an inch,
gives wúyì;
on the sixth string, setting a bridge at six feet, six inches, and eight-tenths,
gives zhōnglǚ;
on the thirteenth string, setting a bridge at four feet and five inches,
gives the clear sound of huángzhōng.
Among the twelve sounds,
cyclically using seven sounds forms a mode;
the master of the mode is solely the gōng note,
then follow zhǐ, shāng, yǔ, jué, biàngōng, and biànzhǐ.
When the sound of the mode’s master is produced,
it returns to the pitch of its fundamental note,
and the seven sounds respond in succession without confusion,
thus forming a key.
Each mode has seven keys,
and there are twelve modes of sounds,
making eighty-four keys in total,
from which songs and melodies for singing and playing arise.
The sounds of cyclical modulation had long been lost,
but in one day, Wáng Pǔ restored them,
based solely on my own insight.
The Comprehensive Mirror extracted the essentials,
and now I record them in full.
Based solely on my own insight,
I beg to assemble all officials to examine its merits and faults.”
The edict approved this.
All officials considered it appropriate,
and thus it was implemented.
At that time, the Minister of War Zhāng Zhāo and others deliberated, saying:
"In ancient times, when Dìhóng created music,
he observed the sounds of the winds from the eight solar terms,
and measured the proper qi of the four seasons.
The purity and turbidity of qi cannot be conveyed by brush,
and the goodness or badness of sounds cannot be transmitted by mouth.
Therefore, the Fú clan cast bells,
and Líng Lún cut bamboo,
to calculate the mutual generation of the pitch pipes,
and the harmonious sounds of the gōng and shāng notes.
These were then disseminated through wind and string instruments,
and proclaimed through bells and stone chimes,
after which the sentiments of heaven and earth were harmoniously united,
and the qi of yīn and yáng became balanced and aligned.
The eight qi followed the pitch pipes without deviation,
and the five tones formed patterns without disorder.
The melodies of Kōngsāng and Gūzhú were sufficient to honor the spirits,
and the forms of Yúnmén and Dàxià did not detract from observing virtue.
However, the method of rotating the pitches according to the monthly pitch pipes
was fully encompassed within the duties of the Grand Master.
After the Qin dynasty extinguished learning,
the elegant Way declined.
What the Zhì clan adjusted in the early Han dynasty
only preserved drumming and dancing;
the method of rotating the twelve pitch standards
was lost to the world.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán of Han,
Jīng Fáng, skilled in the Yìjīng and distinguishing sounds,
explored ancient meanings,
and using the equalization method of the Zhōu officials,
employed the five tones each month,
even to the point of tuning with the pitch pipes,
rotating them to serve as the gōng note,
thus creating sixty modes.
He further divided the daily method into three hundred sixty parts,
transmitted it to the Music Bureau,
and restored the arrangement of suspended instruments to the old standard,
with no discrepancy in the pitch pipes.
Suffering the decline of the Han dynasty,
the elegant music was lost and deficient.
Regarding Jīng Fáng's pitch pipe standards,
there were frequent discussions,
but the matter ultimately did not succeed.
Qián Yuè merely recorded their names,
and Shěn Zhòng only outlined their theories.
The sixty-pitch method
fell silent and was not continued.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was always proficient in music theory,
and personally created four tōng and twelve flutes to arrange the eight sounds.
He also drew upon the ancient five proper and two altered notes,
rotating them to serve as the gōng note,
obtaining eighty-four modes,
which, compared to the tuning of the pitch pipe standards,
were identical in sound but different in number.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
this music was again cut off.
At the beginning of the Suí dynasty, when establishing elegant music,
factions obstructed discussions,
and for years it was not accomplished.
However, Duke Peì, Zhèng Yì, based on the seven tones of the Qiūcí pipa to correspond with the monthly pitch pipes,
with the five proper and two altered notes,
harmonized the seven modes,
rotating them to serve as the gōng note,
again creating eighty-four modes.
The artisan Wàn Bǎocháng further reduced the number of strings,
slightly making it more ancient and subdued.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Suí did not value elegant music,
ordering his ministers to gather for discussion.
The Erudite Hé Tuǒ refuted the memorial,
and the eighty-four modes presented by Zhèng and Wàn were all abolished.
What was performed at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples in the Suí dynasty
was only the Huángzhōng pitch standard,
and for welcoming the qi at the five suburban sacrifices,
Ruíbīn was mixed in,
but only seven modes were used.
The other five bells
were suspended but not played.
For banquet music at the three courts,
the màn music of nine sections was used.
Until the dynastic change,
it could not be altered.
Táng Tàizōng then ordered the former artisans Zǔ Xiàosūn and Zhāng Wénshōu to organize and compare the seven tones and eighty-four modes equalized by Zhèng Yì and Bǎocháng,
only then were string and wind instruments both employed,
and bells and stone chimes all played together.
The sounds of the seven beginnings were revived,
and the melodies of the four side halls were all tuned.
Since the turmoil of Ān and Shǐ,
and the devastation of Xiánqín,
the instruments with raised teeth and feathered decorations
were swept away without remainder.
The artisans who struck and patted
for years had no successors.
What was performed at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples
was no different from the Southern Winnowing Basket.
Wandering and drifting without return,
those who understood music were nearly extinct.
We humbly believe that the origin of sound
comes from the human heart.
Kuí and Kuàng could not live forever,
and human affairs cannot always be peaceful.
When people perish, sound ceases;
when the world is in chaos, music collapses.
If one does not understand the essence of ritual and music,
how can one comprehend the foundation of creation!
We, based on the detailed memorial of the Privy Councilor Wáng Pǔ,
adopted Jīng Fáng's method of pitch pipes,
refined Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's comprehensive music,
examined Zhèng Yì and Bǎocháng's seven equalizations,
compared Xiàosūn and Wénshōu's nine alterations,
accumulated millet grains to examine their measures,
listened to sound poems to gauge their sentiments,
followed the earlier texts on weights and measures,
obtained the main principles of complete numbers and harmonious sounds,
applied them to bell stands,
sufficient to harmonize with the Sháo music.

On the nineteenth day of this month, we gathered at the Tàicháng Temple and ordered the Director of Music Jiǎ Jùn to perform the seven equalizations of the Huángzhōng mode according to Wáng Pǔ's new method.
The pitch pipes were harmonious,
without encroaching upon one another.
As for the various modes of the other eleven pipes,
we hope to teach and practice them according to the new method,
to prepare for use in ritual temples.
For the grand ceremonies of the five suburban sacrifices to heaven and earth, ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and the three courts,
it is appropriate to use the various modes of the twelve pipes,
as recorded in the Táng History and the Kāiyuán Rituals,
commonly practiced in recent times.
During the Guǎngshùn period,

the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Biān Wèi received an edict to determine the dance names, musical pieces, and lyrics for the aforementioned sacrificial ceremonies and court assemblies.
The temple office should have records.
We fear that what was determined may not harmonize with the melodies and sounds of the new method.
We request to order the Tàicháng Temple to examine, review, and test them.
If there are discrepancies,
we request that the temple, according to the new method's tones,
separately compose musical pieces and dance tunes,
and have singers practice and recite them."
This was approved.
3 Sòng Qíqiū arrived at Jiǔhuá Mountain.
The Táng ruler ordered his residence locked,
with food and drink passed through a hole in the wall.
Qíqiū sighed and said:
"In the past, I offered a plan to confine the clan of the Abdicated Emperor Yōu in Tàizhōu.
The matter is recorded in volume 281, the second year of the Jìn Tiānfú era.
He then hanged himself and died.
Examination of discrepancies: The Jiāngbiǎo Zhì states:
"Qíqiū arrived at Qīngyáng,
abstained from food for several days,
and his family also looked pallid.
A palace envoy said: 'Only when the Lord passes away
will food be provided.'
His family members stuffed his mouth with cotton, and he died."
Now we follow the Jiāngnán Lù and the Jìnián.
Initially,
the Hanlin Academician Cháng Mèngxī was in charge of the Xuānzhèng Academy,
participating in confidential government affairs.
He deeply detested Qíqiū's faction,
and repeatedly said to the Táng ruler:
"If this group is not removed,
the state will surely face peril and ruin."
He had daily disputes with Féng Yánjǐ, Wèi Cén, and their followers.
After a long time,
the Xuānzhèng Academy was abolished.
Mèngxī, depressed and unable to fulfill his ambitions,
no longer participated in affairs,
indulged in alcohol, fell ill, and died.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, volume 285, the third year of the Jìn Qíwáng Kāiyùn era,
already recorded Cháng Mèngxī's indulgence in alcohol.
Last year, it also recorded Mèngxī laughing at the faction of Féng Yánjǐ.
It seems his indulgence in alcohol was not for just one day;
after a long time, he fell ill and died.
The Táng ruler said:
"Cháng Mèngxī throughout his life wanted to kill Qíqiū;
it is a pity he did not live to see it!"
He posthumously awarded Mèngxī the title of Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
4 In the second month,
on the first day, bǐngzǐ,
Wáng Pǔ was ordered to go to Héyīn to inspect the river embankments,
and a sluice gate was established at the Biàn River estuary.
On the rénwǔ day,
the Imperial Guard Commander-in-Chief Hán Tōng and the Southern Court Commissioner of the Palace Administration Wú Tíngzuò
("Tíngzuò"
should be
"Yánzuò".
[Chapter note: The Kong edition correctly has
"Yán";

Since Táng's military campaigns in Huáinán and the cession of territory north of the river—
in the winter, twelfth month of the second year of Xiǎndé,
Zhōu troops crossed the Huái.
In the spring, third month of the fifth year,
Táng ceded the territory north of the river—
annual tributes and offerings,
depleted the treasury,
money became scarcer,
and prices soared.
Zhōng Mó, Vice Minister of Rites, requested the minting of large coins,
one equivalent to fifty;
Hán Xīzǎi, Zhōngshū Shèrén, requested the minting of iron coins.
The ruler of Táng initially refused both,
but Zhōng Mó persistently pleaded,
and he eventually agreed.
That month,
they began minting coins worth ten,
inscribed
"Yǒng Tōng Quán Huò,"
and also minted coins worth two,
inscribed
"Táng Guó Tōng Bǎo,"
which circulated alongside the Kāiyuán coins.
The Kāiyuán coins
were minted in the early years of Táng's Wǔdé era.
19 In the eighth month,
on Wùzǐ,
the ruler of Shǔ appointed Lǐ Hào as Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn.
Right Supplements Officer Lǐ Qǐ submitted a memorial:
"According to precedent,
no prime minister has concurrently held a regional military commission."
The ruler of Shǔ said:
"Lǐ Hào's household has many expenses,
so I am providing him with a generous salary."
Qǐ,
a native of Qióngzhōu,
was by nature stubborn and straightforward.
Lǐ Hào once said to him:
"With your talent,
if you could be cautious and silent,
you would become a Hanlin Academician."
Qǐ replied:
"Only when I have no tongue
will I not speak!"
20 On Gēngyín,
the Emperor's younger brother Zōngràng was enfeoffed as Prince of Cáo,
and his name was changed to Xīràng;
Xījǐn was enfeoffed as Prince of Jì,
and Xīhuì as Prince of Qí.
The character
"Zōng"
was changed to
"Xī"
to avoid the Emperor's personal name.
Ōu Shǐ states: In the second year of Qiándé of our dynasty,
in the tenth month,
Xījǐn passed away.
The fates of Xīràng and Xīhuì are unknown,
likely concealed.
Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.
21 In the ninth month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
the Crown Prince of Táng, Hóngjì, passed away.
The relevant officials cited his achievements in Zhèxī—
referring to sending Chái Kèhóng to defeat Wúyuè troops at Chángzhōu—
but Jùróng County Assistant Quánjiāo Zhāng Jì submitted a memorial:
Jùróng County belonged to Shēngzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Located ninety lǐ east of the prefecture.
Quánjiāo,
a Hàn-dynasty county name,
was established as Běiqiáo Commandery in the Liáng,
soon renamed Línchú Commandery,
changed to Chúshuǐ County in the Suí,
and in the early years of Dàyè,
restored to Quánjiāo,
belonging to Chúzhōu in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Located fifty lǐ south of the prefecture.
Jù,
pronounced as the character.
Jì,
pronounced qí jì fān.
"The virtue of a crown prince
lies primarily in filial piety and respect.
Now to give him a posthumous title based on military achievements
is not the way to guard against subtle faults and uphold virtue."
So his posthumous title was changed to Wénxiàn;
and Zhāng Jì was promoted to Assistant of Shàngyuán.
Táng's capital was at Jīnlíng,
with Shàngyuán as the capital county,
and Jùróng as an adjacent county.
Promotion from an adjacent county assistant to a capital county assistant was considered a promotion.
22 Zhōng Mó, Vice Minister of Rites and Administrator of the Department of State Affairs of Táng, was sent multiple times as an envoy to Zhōu,
conveying Shìzōng's commands to the ruler of Táng.
Both Shìzōng and the ruler of Táng treated him generously,
and relying on this, he became arrogant and overbearing in his own state,
involving himself in the affairs of all three departments.
When the Crown Prince Wénxiàn was overseeing the court administration,
Zhōng Mó sought to concurrently hold an official post in the Eastern Palace but failed.
He then recommended his friend Yán Shì to serve as Sīyì Láng,
in charge of official communications from various departments.
Regarding the death of Lǐ Démíng,
see the third year of the previous scroll.
Zhōng Mó heard that Táng Hào had accepted bribes,
and once confronted him face-to-face about it.
Táng Hào was very frightened.
Zhōng Mó was on good terms with Zhāng Luán, the Dūyúhòu of the Tiānwēi Army.
They often spoke privately at his residence late into the night, dismissing others.
Táng Hào slandered them to the Southern Tang ruler, saying:
"Zhōng Mó and Zhāng Luán are of different temperaments,
yet they are excessively intimate.
Zhōng Mó has frequently been sent as an envoy to the superior state (Zhou),
and Zhāng Luán is a northerner.
I fear they may be plotting something treacherous."
He also said:
"Many people are illicitly minting the Yǒngtōng large coins,
resulting in numerous lawbreakers."
After the death of Crown Prince Wénxiàn,
the Southern Tang ruler intended to install his younger maternal brother, Prince Zhèng Lǐ Cóngjiā.
Zhōng Mó had once served as an envoy to Zhou together with Duke Jì Lǐ Cóngshàn,
and they were close friends.
He said to the Southern Tang ruler:
"Cóngjiā lacks virtue and is weak-willed,
and he is also fanatically devoted to Buddhism.
He is not fit to be a ruler.
Cóngshàn is resolute, decisive, and dignified.
He should be the heir."
The Southern Tang ruler became angry because of this.
To interfere in the relationship between father and son,
and to want to depose the elder and establish the younger,
it was fitting that Zhōng Mó met his death.
(The Crown Prince) resided in the Eastern Palace.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhōng Mó requested that Zhāng Luán patrol the capital with his troops.
This precisely matched the slander by Táng Hào,
and thus he quickly incurred punishment.
Jiào,
pronounced as jí diào fān.
(Zhōng Mó) was demoted to Guózǐ Sīyè,
and exiled to Ráozhōu.
Zhāng Luán was demoted to Deputy Commissioner of Xuānzhōu.
Not long after,
both were executed.
The Yǒngtōng coins were abolished.
23 In the eleventh month,
on the first day, Rényín,
Ruìwǔ Xiàowén Emperor was buried at Qìnglíng.
The mausoleum is located in Guǎnchéng County, Zhèngzhōu.
24 The Southern Han ruler, because Zhōng Yǔnzhāng, a Zhōngshū Shèrén,
was an old subordinate from his princely establishment,
promoted him to Shàngshū Yòuchéng and Cānzhèngshì,
and placed great trust in him.
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng requested the execution of several people who violated the law to rectify discipline,
but the Southern Han ruler could not comply.
The eunuchs heard of this and despised him.
The Southern Han ruler was about to perform sacrifices at the Yuánqiū altar.
Three days prior,
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng led the ritual officials onto the altar,
looking around and directing the placement of the spirit tablets.
The Nèishì Jiān Xǔ Yànzhēn saw this and said:
"This is rebellion!"
He immediately climbed onto the altar with his sword.
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng shouted at him.
Yànzhēn galloped into the palace,
and reported that Zhōng Yǔnzhāng intended to stage a rebellion on the day of the suburban sacrifice.
The Southern Han ruler said:
"I have treated Yǔnzhāng generously.
How could there be such a thing?"
Yùqīng Gōngshǐ Gōng Chéngshū, Nèishì Jiān Lǐ Tuō, and others jointly corroborated it,
believing Yànzhēn's words to be true.
They then arrested Zhōng Yǔnzhāng,
imprisoned him under the Hánzhāng Tower,
and ordered eunuchs and the Minister of Rites Xuē Yòngpī to jointly interrogate him.
Yòngpī had always been on good terms with Yǔnzhāng.
He told him that death was unavoidable.
Yǔnzhāng grasped Yòngpī's hand and wept, saying:
"This old man is now like meat on a chopping block,
destined to be cooked by his enemies.
I only regret that my sons Yōng and Chāng are young,
and do not know of my injustice.
When they grow up,
please tell them for me."
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng, being slandered,
faced an unpredictable crime.
He was precisely afraid of implicating his wife and children,
yet he spoke these words,
which brought disaster upon himself.
Zhǎng,
pronounced as zhī liǎng fān.
Wèi,
pronounced as yú wèi fān.
Yǔ,
pronounced as niú jù fān.
(Yòngpī) scolded him:
"Does the rebel want his sons to seek revenge?"
He then reported again to the Southern Han ruler:
"Yǔnzhāng ascended the altar together with his two sons,
secretly praying for something."
All were beheaded.
From then on, the eunuchs became even more domineering.
Lǐ Tuō
was from Fēngzhōu.
On Xīnhài,
the Southern Han ruler performed sacrifices at the Yuánqiū altar,
and issued a general pardon.
Not long after,
he appointed Gōng Chéngshū as Zuǒ Lónghǔ Guān Jūnróng Shǐ and Nèi Tàishī.
All military and state affairs were decided by him.
Generally, any courtier with talent and ability, or the top candidate in the imperial examinations
(the top candidate in the imperial examinations,
was called zhuàngtóu)
had to first undergo castration,
and only then could they advance.
There were also those who castrated themselves to seek advancement,
and those who were castrated to avoid death.
As a result, there were nearly twenty thousand eunuchs.
Those who were noble, prominent, and wielded power,
were mostly eunuchs.
They called scholars "outsiders,"
not allowing them to participate in affairs.
Ultimately, this led to the state's downfall.
The Southern Han perished in the fourth year of Kāibǎo of Song.
Zú,
pronounced as zǐ xù fān.
25 Southern Tang renamed Hóngzhōu as Nánchāng Fǔ,
establishing the Southern Capital.
They appointed Hé Jìngzhú, the military governor of Wǔqīng, as the Liúshǒu of the Southern Capital.
The Wǔqīng Army was in Héngzhōu,
belonging to Húnán.
Hé Jìngzhú held the title remotely.
(The ruler) intended to move the capital to Yùzhāng.
26 When the Zhou people attacked Qín and Fèng,
there was panic in Shǔ;
Xú Jífǔ, a Dūguān Lángzhōng, who prided himself on his talent and strategy,
was dissatisfied with his official career.
He secretly formed a faction,
plotting to install Wáng Lìngyí, the Shàofǔ Shǎojiàn and grandson of the Former Shu founder, as their leader to stage a rebellion.
(The Former Shu ruler Wáng Jiàn
had the temple name Gāozǔ.)
At this time,
someone from his faction informed on them.
They were arrested,
and Xú Jífǔ committed suicide.
In the twelfth month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
Wáng Lìngyí was ordered to commit suicide.
27 Dòu Yí, a Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì and Vice Minister of War, was sent as an envoy to Southern Tang.
It was snowing.
The Southern Tang ruler intended to receive the imperial edict under the eaves.
Dòu Yí said:
"The envoy has come bearing an imperial edict,
and dares not neglect the old rituals.
If the snow wets our robes,
please wait for another day."
The Southern Tang ruler then bowed to receive the edict in the courtyard.
28 The Khitan ruler sent his maternal uncle as an envoy to Southern Tang.
Jīng Hǎnrú, the Tuánliàn Shǐ of Tàizhōu, recruited an agent to kill him.
The Southern Tang people held a night banquet for the Khitan envoy at the Qīngfēng Post Station.
When they were drunk,
(the envoy) got up to relieve himself.
Jīng
is a surname;
there was the assassin Jīng Kē in Yān.
The state of Chǔ was originally called Jīng,
hence this surname from before Chǔ.
Gēng,
pronounced as gōng héng fān.
When they looked for him,
his head was missing.
From then on, Khitan severed relations with Southern Tang.
Hǎnrú
was from Jìzhōu.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Your subject Guāng states: Previously, I received an imperial order to compile the events of rulers and ministers throughout history.
I also received a sacred decree bestowing the name Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
It is now completed.
I humbly reflect that I am by nature ignorant and dull,
my learning is crude and superficial,
in all matters and affairs,
I fall below others,
yet only regarding the histories of the past,
I have roughly devoted my full attention,
from youth to old age,
I have been fond of them without tiring.
I have often lamented that since Simǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
the texts have become exceedingly numerous,
even scholars of common background
cannot read them all,
let alone the sovereign,
who has ten thousand affairs daily,
how could he find the leisure to peruse them all!
I have often, without measuring my own abilities,
wished to delete the lengthy parts,
gather the essential points,
focusing solely on what concerns the rise and fall of the state,
what is tied to the weal and woe of the people,
the good that can serve as a model,
the evil that can serve as a warning,
to compile a book in annalistic form,
so that the sequence is orderly,
the refined and the crude are not mixed,
but with the limited strength of a private individual,
there was no way to accomplish it.
I then had the fortune to encounter Emperor Yīngzōng,
who possessed a nature of profound wisdom,
and implemented a governance of culture and enlightenment,
who thought of surveying the affairs of antiquity,
to expand and magnify the grand plan,
and thus deigned to command me,
ordering me to compile and edit.
The wish I had long held,
was realized in a single morning,
I leapt with joy to receive the command,
fearing only that I would prove unworthy.
The late Emperor further commanded me to select and appoint officials myself,
to establish a bureau at the Chóngwén Institute,
permitting the borrowing of books from the Lóngtú Pavilion, Tiānzhāng Pavilion, the Three Institutes, and the Imperial Library,
bestowing upon me the imperial store's brushes, ink, silks, and satins, as well as funds from the imperial presence to supply fruits and pastries,
assigning eunuchs to handle matters,
the honor of such favor and treatment,
was unmatched even by close ministers.
Unfortunately, before the book could be presented to the Emperor,
the late Emperor departed and abandoned his ministers.
Your Majesty succeeded to the great lineage,
reverently inheriting the former will,
honoring it with a preface from the imperial crown,
bestowing upon it an excellent name,
whenever the Classics Colloquium was opened,
you often commanded me to present and read it.
Although I am stubborn and foolish,
to receive such profound recognition and treatment from two reigns,
even should I lose my body and head,
it would not suffice to repay,
if within the reach of my intellect and strength,
how would I dare to hold anything back!
I was then assigned to administer Yǒngxīng Army,
but due to declining health and inability to manage demanding duties,
I begged for a sinecure post.
Your Majesty graciously complied with my wish,
indulgently granting me rest and care,
assigning me to the Western Capital Remaining Bureau of the Censorate and to oversee the Chóngfú Palace at Sōngshān in the Western Capital,
for six successive appointments,
still allowing me to keep the editorial bureau with me,
providing me with salary and rank,
without pressing official duties.
Since I had no other affairs,
I was able to refine my thoughts to the utmost,
exhaust all I had,
when daylight was insufficient,
I continued through the night.
I perused all the old histories,
gathered material from miscellaneous records,
the bamboo slips and documents piled high,
vast as a sea of smoke,
I selected the obscure and hidden,
checked and calculated down to the slightest detail.
Starting from the Warring States period above,
ending with the Five Dynasties below,
covering one thousand three hundred and sixty-two years in all,
I compiled two hundred and ninety-four scrolls;
also briefly listed the event titles,
with years as the warp and states as the weft,
to facilitate searching,
making a table of contents of thirty scrolls;
also consulted various texts,
evaluated their similarities and differences,
to bring them to a single path,
making a textual criticism of thirty scrolls: totaling three hundred and fifty-four scrolls.
Since opening the bureau in the Zhìpíng era,
until now it is finally completed,
the years and months have been long,
within it there are contradictions,
I dare not vouch for myself,
the gravity of my offenses and faults,
surely cannot be escaped.
I, Guāng, am truly fearful and apprehensive,
kowtow and kowtow.
I further reflect that I have been separated from the imperial court,
for fifteen years,
although my body is outside,
my sincere heart,
morning and evening, waking and sleeping,
how could it not be by Your Majesty's side!
But considering my own ineptitude and lameness,
there is nothing I can apply myself to,
therefore I devoted myself solely to writing and editing,
to repay the great kindness,
hoping to exhaust my meager dust-like efforts,
to slightly benefit the sea and mountains.
I am now bones frail and weary,
my vision dim and nearsighted,
my teeth few,
my spirit and awareness declining and exhausted,
what I do before my eyes,
I forget as soon as I turn around,
my energy and strength,
are all spent on this book.
I humbly hope Your Majesty will be lenient regarding the crime of my reckless composition,
and consider my sincere intention of loyalty,
in moments of leisure and repose,
occasionally deign to peruse it,
observe the rise and fall of former ages,
examine the gains and losses of the present,
praise the good and pity the evil,
adopt the right and discard the wrong,
sufficient to encourage the splendid virtue of investigating antiquity,
and ascend to an unparalleled perfect governance,
so that all living beings within the Four Seas,
may all receive its blessings,
then even if my bones are laid in the Nine Springs,
my will and wish will be forever fulfilled.
Respectfully I present this memorial to report for your attention.
I, Guāng, am truly fearful and apprehensive,
kowtow and kowtow,
respectfully stated.

Sīmǎ Guāng
Imperial Edict of Commendation
Edict to Sīmǎ Guāng: On the completion of the compilation of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
The study of history has long been neglected,
the recording lacks method,
the discussions lack clarity,
how could it suffice to demonstrate warning and encouragement,
and illuminate the long term!
You, with broad learning and extensive knowledge,
penetrate through past and present,
from the late Zhōu above,
down to the Five Dynasties,
expounding and compiling,
have completed a book that stands as a school of its own,
in praise and blame, selection and rejection,
there is basis and reliance.
Having perused it,
I deeply admire and praise it!
Now I bestow upon you silver, silk, court robes, a belt, saddle, bridle, and horse,
as detailed in a separate record,
you may receive them.
Therefore, this commendation,
I trust you will duly understand.
In the winter cold,
I hope you are well and at peace.
Sending this letter,
I shall not elaborate further.
The fifteenth day.
